0.title: The Cross at the Centre: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
0.overview:
Of all the churches Paul founded, none gave him more grief — or more glory — than the church at Corinth. Corinth was one of the great cities of the ancient world: a rebuilt Roman colony on the narrow isthmus of Greece, sitting athwart the trade routes of the Mediterranean, a cosmopolitan, polyglot, ferociously commercial city where every culture, every religion, and every vice was for sale. The Greek verb korinthiazesthai — to live like a Corinthian — had become a byword for sexual immorality. Into this city Paul came on his second missionary journey around AD 50, stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:11), and planted a church that would make him simultaneously the most celebrated and most embattled apostle in his own lifetime.

He wrote this letter from Ephesus around AD 54–55, provoked by reports from Chloe’s household and a letter from the Corinthians themselves. What he had heard was alarming: the church had fractured into personality factions (“I follow Paul”; “I follow Apollos”; “I follow Cephas”; “I follow Christ”); a man was openly sleeping with his stepmother and the church was arrogant about it; members were suing each other in pagan courts; spiritual gifts had become instruments of status and one-upmanship; the Lord’s Supper had been turned into a class exercise in social humiliation; and some were denying the bodily resurrection entirely. This is a church in crisis — not the crisis of persecution from outside, but the far more dangerous crisis of pride, worldliness, and theological confusion from within.

Paul’s answer to every single one of these crises is the same: the cross. The word of the cross (1:18) is the only wisdom that addresses human arrogance. The crucified Christ (1:23) is the only foundation (3:11) on which a community can be built. The resurrection of Christ (15:20) is the only ground on which the resurrection of the dead makes sense. Every pastoral problem in the letter — from church discipline to spiritual gifts to the collection for the Jerusalem poor — is resolved by returning to the gospel of the crucified and risen Lord. This is why Martin Luther set the theology of the cross (theologia crucis) against the theology of glory (theologia gloriae), and why this letter is the most searching diagnostic of the church’s recurrent temptation to dress the gospel in the clothing of worldly wisdom and power.

The governing conviction is that this letter was written to the twenty-first century as much as the first — because the Corinthian church is every church, and the Corinthian heart is every heart, that has tried to hold the gospel and the values of the world simultaneously.

1.title: Divisions, the Cross, and the Wisdom of God
1.overview:
Corinth in the 50s AD was a boom town. Destroyed by Rome in 146 BC, it was refounded by Julius Caesar in 44 BC as a Roman colony, settled largely with freed slaves, and grew rich on trade between its two harbours on either side of the isthmus. It hosted the Isthmian Games and was full of people climbing the social ladder: one inscription found there records that a man called Erastus paved a street at his own expense in return for public office, perhaps the same Erastus, “the city treasurer”, who sent greetings in Romans 16:23. Status, eloquence, wisdom and success were prized. Paul spent eighteen months planting the church there (Acts 18), and a few years later, from Ephesus, he wrote this letter after hearing of serious problems.

The first problem is division. Church members were lining up behind favourite teachers (Paul, Apollos, Peter, even “Christ”) as though they were rival schools of philosophy. Paul’s answer goes to the root: the gospel itself overturns human ideas of wisdom and status. Its message is a crucified Messiah, which sounded like nonsense to Greeks and like an outrage to Jews, yet it is God’s power and wisdom. God deliberately chose ordinary, unimpressive people, so that no one could boast except in the Lord, who has given us Christ as our wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, writing with a colleague called Sosthenes, introduces himself as an apostle by God’s calling. He addresses the church in Corinth as God’s own people, made holy in Christ and called to be saints, together with believers everywhere who call on the name of Jesus, the Lord of all, and wishes them grace and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called by the Will of God

Paul’s self-designation as an apostle “by the will of God” is not modesty but theology. The divine will is the only ground of any apostolic or ministerial commission. This will become crucial in the letter: when the Corinthians reject Paul’s apostleship, they are not rejecting a self-appointed teacher but the will of the God who sent him. The same logic applies to their own calling: they are saints not because they volunteered but because they were called (v. 2). The sovereignty of grace is the foundation of every sentence.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s apostolic authority was contested at Corinth by those who preferred Apollos’s rhetorical polish or Cephas’s Petrine prestige. His opening — “called by the will of God” — quietly answers the challenge before it is raised. Now: In a church culture that prizes celebrity and charisma, the ground of ministry is still the same: divine calling, not human talent. The pastor who grounds his authority in his own gifts is standing on sand; the one who grounds it in the call of God can stand when the culture turns against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
From Paul, called by God’s will to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and from our brother Sosthenes.

Called. Paul did not choose the job. God called him (Galatians 1:15). In a church where people were choosing their favourite leaders, Paul begins by saying that leaders are chosen by God.

Sosthenes. Probably the ruler of the Corinthian synagogue who was beaten in front of the proconsul Gallio when the Jewish leaders’ case against Paul failed: “they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him” (Acts 18:17). If so, he later became a Christian and was now with Paul in Ephesus. The Corinthians would have known him well.

On a Tuesday. Every Christian has a calling from God, whether in church office or in an ordinary job. Start the week remembering who called you.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus, around AD 53–55, a few years after founding the church. Sosthenes may be the synagogue ruler beaten at Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To God’s church in Corinth: to those who have been made holy in Christ Jesus and called to be his holy people, together with all who everywhere call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours. Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

The church of God. Not Paul’s church, nor Apollos’s, nor Chloe’s. God’s. The first blow against factions.

Sanctified and called to be saints. Two sides of holiness. They have already been set apart as God’s in Christ (a settled fact, sometimes called definitive sanctification), and they are called to live as holy people (progressive sanctification). This to a church with incest, lawsuits, drunkenness at the Lord’s Supper and pride. They were saints by God’s act, not by their record.

With all who call on his name. Corinth was not the only church. Their factions forgot the wider church.

Call on the name. In the Old Testament, people “call upon the name of the LORD” (Genesis 4:26; compare Joel 2:32). Here they call on the name of Jesus. Paul assumes Jesus is to be worshipped as God.

On a Tuesday. If you feel too sinful to call yourself a saint, look at who Paul called saints. Holiness begins with what God has made you in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Corinth was a wealthy Roman colony and trading city on the narrow isthmus of Greece, with two ports and a mixed, mobile population. “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God constantly for the grace given to the Corinthians in Christ. They have been enriched in every way, especially in their speech and knowledge, because the message about Christ took firm root among them, and so they lack no spiritual gift as they wait for Christ to be revealed. Christ will keep them firm to the end, so that they will be blameless on his day. God is faithful, and it was he who called them into fellowship with his Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Faithfulness of God as the Ground of Perseverance

Verse 9 — “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son” — is one of the great perseverance texts in Paul. The guarantee of the Corinthians’ ultimate confirmation (v. 8) is not their grip on Christ but God’s grip on them. The calling is God’s act; the fellowship is God’s gift; the sustaining is God’s work. Reformed theology has always grounded the doctrine of perseverance here: the saints persevere not because they are strong but because the God who called them is faithful.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had turned their spiritual gifts into status symbols, measuring their standing before God and their superiority over others by the quality of their tongues and the depth of their knowledge. Paul’s thanksgiving subtly reorients them: the gifts are something you “were enriched in” — given, not earned. Now: The same pride attaches to spiritual accomplishment in every generation — the sense that one’s theological sophistication or spiritual experience gives one a higher standing. Paul’s corrective is the same: it is all grace. What do you have that you did not receive? (4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge—
verseByVerse.commentary:
I always thank my God for you because of the grace he has given you in Christ Jesus. In him you have been made rich in every way, in all your speaking and in all your knowledge.

Thanks first. Before tackling a long list of problems, Paul thanks God for them. Not flattery: he thanks God for what God has done, not for what they have done.

Speech and knowledge. The very gifts the Corinthians prized and misused. Corinthians loved eloquence and knowledge (chapters 1–4, 8, 12–14). Paul does not despise the gifts; he will correct their use.

A textual note. A few early manuscripts lack “my” in “my God”. The difference is slight; most manuscripts include it.

On a Tuesday. Before you criticise your church, thank God for something real in it. It will change the tone of your criticism.
verseByVerse.note: The Corinthians prized eloquent speech and knowledge — the very gifts later misused.

verseByVerse.quote: even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you— so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you, so that you do not lack any spiritual gift while you wait eagerly for our Lord Jesus Christ to be revealed.

Confirmed. Bebaioō: made firm, a legal word for a guaranteed contract. The gospel took hold in them, shown by changed lives and spiritual gifts.

Not lacking any gift. Charisma: a gift of grace. Chapters 12–14 will discuss the gifts.

As you wait. The gifts are for the time between Christ’s first and second comings.

Does this prove all gifts continue until Christ returns? Continuationists cite this verse: gifts are given “as you wait”, until the revelation of Christ. Cessationists reply that the verse says the Corinthians lacked no gift then, not that every gift continues unchanged until the end. Verdict: the verse does not settle the question. God gives gifts to his church throughout the age, but which gifts and in what form must be decided from other passages (see 13:8–12; Ephesians 2:20).

On a Tuesday. Waiting for Christ is not passive. Use whatever gift God has given you while you wait.

verseByVerse.quote: who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will keep you strong to the end, so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Sustain. The same verb as “confirmed” in verse 6. God, who made the gospel firm in them, will keep them firm.

Guiltless. Anenklētos: no charge can be brought. Not because they are sinless, but because Christ has dealt with their sin (Romans 8:33–34).

The day. The Old Testament “day of the LORD” is now “the day of our Lord Jesus Christ”: the day of his return and judgement.

Perseverance. This is said to a deeply flawed church. Their perseverance rests on God’s faithfulness (v. 9), not on their performance. This is the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints (Westminster Confession 17).

On a Tuesday. If you fear you will not make it to the end as a Christian, this verse is for you. He will sustain you.

verseByVerse.quote: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is faithful, and he is the one who called you into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

God is faithful. The ground of everything. Paul will say it again in 10:13.

Fellowship. Koinōnia: sharing, partnership, participation. Believers share in Christ himself, and so with one another. This fellowship is the answer to division: you cannot be in fellowship with Christ and at war with his people.

Ten times. Paul has named the Lord Jesus Christ nine times in nine verses. Before he deals with factions around human leaders, he fills the page with Christ.

For worship. Thank God that his faithfulness, not yours, holds you in fellowship with his Son.

parallels.desc: the faithful God

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul appeals to them, in Christ’s name, to agree with one another and end their divisions. Members of Chloe’s household have told him about quarrels: each person has a favourite, Paul, Apollos, Peter or Christ. Is Christ split into pieces? Was Paul crucified for them, or were they baptised into Paul’s name? He is glad he personally baptised only a handful of them, so no one can claim to be his disciple. Christ sent him not mainly to baptise but to preach the gospel, and not with clever rhetoric, which would empty the cross of its power.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross Against Personality Cults

The Corinthian factions are a cautionary tale about what happens when human personality becomes the centre of Christian community. This text is a permanent warning: the church that rallies around a preacher’s gifts, style, or personality rather than around the crucified Christ has already drifted from the gospel. The preacher is, at most, a herald — the one who announces a message that does not belong to him. Paul’s refusal to preach with “eloquent wisdom” is not anti-intellectualism; it is a deliberate choice to let the gospel speak in its own register, with its own power, rather than dressing it in borrowed clothes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ancient world ran on patronage and sophistry: you attached yourself to the most impressive teacher, displayed his influence on your life, and measured your social standing by his. The Corinthian factions are simply the church doing what Corinthian culture always did. Now: Celebrity pastor culture is the contemporary version. The church that streams a famous preacher rather than investing in local pastors, or that divides over which theological tradition’s champion to follow, is still choosing Apollos over Christ — a more impressive package over the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers and sisters, I appeal to you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: agree with one another, and let there be no divisions among you, but be united in the same mind and the same purpose. For some people from Chloe’s household have told me that there are quarrels among you, my friends.

By the name. The name they all call on (v. 2) is the ground of unity.

Divisions. Schismata, from which we get “schism”: tears in a garment. Not yet separate churches, but rival groups in one church.

Chloe’s people. Chloe was probably a businesswoman, perhaps from Ephesus or Corinth, whose slaves or employees travelled between the cities. Paul names his source: he does not act on anonymous gossip.

What unity is. “Perfectly joined together” (katartizō, the word for mending nets). Not uniformity of personality, but agreement in the gospel and in purpose.

On a Tuesday. If you hear of a problem in your church, go to the people involved and say where you heard it, as Paul does. Anonymous complaints breed suspicion.
verseByVerse.note: Chloe’s people were probably members of her household or business who had travelled to Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos,” or “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What I mean is this: each of you says, “I belong to Paul,” or “I belong to Apollos,” or “I belong to Cephas,” or “I belong to Christ.” Has Christ been divided up? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptised in Paul’s name?

The parties. In Greek cities, students attached themselves to a famous teacher and boasted of him. The Corinthians did the same with Christian leaders.

Paul: the founder. Perhaps the Gentile believers loyal to him.

Apollos: an eloquent Alexandrian Jew, “a native of Alexandria … an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures” (Acts 18:24). He taught in Corinth after Paul (Acts 18:27–19:1). Those who prized eloquence may have preferred him.

Cephas: Peter’s Aramaic name. Perhaps Jewish believers, or those impressed by his link to Jesus.

Christ: either the most pious-sounding faction (“we follow only Christ, not men”), or Paul’s own retort. Most think it was a real party, claiming Christ as their private possession.

Is Christ divided? The question exposes the absurdity. There is one Christ and one body.

A textual note. The Greek can be read as a question, “Is Christ divided?”, or as an exclamation, “Christ has been divided!” Most translations take it as a question, which fits the questions that follow.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may not have denominations or prefer a particular teacher. Paul himself had co-workers. The sin is the spirit of party, pride and rivalry.

On a Tuesday. Online, Christians can become fans of a celebrity preacher and despise those who follow another. Paul, Apollos and Peter would not have it.
verseByVerse.note: Apollos had taught at Corinth after Paul. Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank God that I did not baptise any of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one can say you were baptised in my name. (Yes, I also baptised the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not remember baptising anyone else.)

Crispus. The synagogue ruler who “believed in the Lord, together with his entire household” (Acts 18:8).

Gaius. Probably the wealthy believer who later hosted Paul and the whole church in Corinth (Romans 16:23).

Stephanas. The first converts in Achaia, devoted to serving the saints (16:15).

I do not remember. A sign that Paul is writing naturally. Inspiration does not make the apostle omniscient about his own past.

The household of Stephanas. Paedobaptists point to household baptisms (also Acts 16:15, 33) as likely including infants. Credobaptists reply that in 16:15 the household of Stephanas “devoted themselves to the service of the saints”, which implies they were believers, and that Acts consistently links baptism with hearing and believing. Verdict: the credobaptist reading fits better, but these texts do not settle the question alone, and Christians on both sides hold their view in good conscience.

On a Tuesday. Your baptism ties you to Christ, not to the minister who baptised you.

parallels.desc: Crispus
Gaius
Stephanas

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Christ did not send me to baptise but to preach the gospel, and not with clever eloquence, so that the cross of Christ would not be emptied of its power.

Not to baptise. Not that baptism does not matter (Matthew 28:19), but that it is not the heart of the apostle’s commission. If baptism were the means of saving grace, Paul could hardly thank God he had baptised so few.

Baptismal regeneration? Some traditions (Roman Catholic, Orthodox, some Lutheran and Anglican) teach that baptism itself regenerates. Others cite Acts 2:38. Verdict: this verse is strong evidence against baptismal regeneration. The gospel preached and believed saves; baptism is the sign and seal of that salvation, to be received by believers.

Not with eloquent wisdom. Greek rhetoric was a highly developed art. Professional orators were celebrities, admired for performance as much as content. Paul refused to rely on rhetorical technique (2:1–5), because people would be persuaded by the speaker rather than the cross.

Emptied of its power. A message about a crucified man, delivered with manipulative brilliance, would draw attention to the speaker and hide the scandal and power of the cross.

On a Tuesday. When you explain the gospel to a friend, do not dress it up to make it sound less offensive. The power is in the cross itself.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized polished rhetoric; travelling orators were admired like celebrities.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Christ the Wisdom and Power of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The message of the cross seems foolish to those who are perishing, but to those being saved it is the power of God. Scripture foretold that God would confound the wisdom of the wise. Where are the sages, the scholars and the debaters now? God has made the world’s wisdom look foolish. Since the world in its wisdom did not come to know God, God was pleased to save believers through the apparent foolishness of preaching. Jews want miraculous signs and Greeks want wisdom, but Paul preaches a crucified Messiah, an offence to Jews and nonsense to Gentiles, yet to those God calls, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom. God’s foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and his weakness stronger than human strength.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of the Cross (Theologia Crucis)

Luther’s distinction between the theology of the cross and the theology of glory is nowhere more clearly grounded than in 1:18–25. The theologian of glory sees God in power, success, and wisdom that makes sense on human terms. The theologian of the cross sees God revealed precisely in weakness, foolishness, and the apparent defeat of Good Friday. The cross is not the means to something better; it is the place where God is most fully known. The cross was never Plan B after the fall. It was the plan from eternity — the place where the justice and the love of God were both satisfied at the same moment, in the same event, in the same Person.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul wrote into a culture where crucifixion was the ultimate symbol of shame, defeat, and criminal status. To preach a crucified Messiah was not merely theologically offensive but socially disqualifying. The early Christians were not brave about something trivial; they were staking their social standing and their lives on an executed criminal. Now: The pressure to make the gospel more palatable — to lead with Jesus-as-life-coach rather than Jesus-as-sin-bearer, to emphasise personal fulfilment rather than atonement — is the contemporary version of Paul’s Corinthian problem. The cross still offends the wisdom of the age. The answer is still to preach it anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is God’s power. For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the clever I will frustrate.”

The word of the cross. Not just a doctrine but the whole message centred on the crucified Christ.

Two groups. Perishing, being saved: present tenses, two roads. The same message produces opposite reactions (2 Corinthians 2:15–16).

The power of God. “For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (Romans 1:16). Not advice about God’s power, but the power itself at work.

Isaiah 29:14. In Isaiah, Judah’s politicians thought they were clever, seeking an alliance with Egypt against Assyria instead of trusting God. God said: “the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden.” Paul quotes the Greek version. God’s way of saving overturns human cleverness.

On a Tuesday. If a clever colleague ridicules the cross, do not be shaken. The ridicule was predicted. And the message still has power.

parallels.desc: the wisdom of their wise men shall perish

verseByVerse.quote: Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where is the wise person? Where is the scholar? Where is the debater of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of the world look foolish? For since, in God’s wisdom, the world did not come to know God through its own wisdom, God was pleased to save those who believe through the foolishness of what we preach.

Three types. The wise (Greek philosophers), the scribe (Jewish experts in the law), the debater (the clever arguer of either culture). Echoing Isaiah 19:12 and 33:18, where God mocks the wise men of Egypt and the officials of Assyria.

The world did not know God. Human wisdom, however brilliant, cannot reach God by itself. Romans 1:19–21 says that creation reveals God’s power, but people suppressed the truth. General revelation leaves us without excuse; it does not save.

The folly of what we preach. Not foolish preaching, but the foolish-seeming content: a crucified Messiah.

Natural theology? Some Christian thinkers (Thomas Aquinas) built a natural theology, arguing that reason can prove God’s existence. Others (Karl Barth) rejected natural theology entirely. Verdict: the Reformed view (Calvin, Westminster Confession 1.1) holds that creation reveals God clearly enough to leave everyone accountable, but that saving knowledge of God comes only through his word and Spirit. Reason is a gift, but it cannot find God without revelation.

On a Tuesday. You do not need to win every intellectual debate to share the gospel. God saves through the message preached, not through our cleverness.

verseByVerse.quote: For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jews ask for signs and Greeks look for wisdom, but we proclaim Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles. But to those whom God has called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

Signs. Jewish hearers wanted proof by mighty acts (Matthew 12:38; John 6:30). A Messiah would defeat Rome with power.

Wisdom. Greek hearers wanted a philosophy: rational, elegant, impressive.

Christ crucified. To a Jew, a crucified Messiah was a contradiction in terms: “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23). To a Roman, crucifixion was the shameful death of slaves and rebels, not mentioned in polite company. An early graffito from Rome shows a man worshipping a crucified figure with a donkey’s head, captioned “Alexamenos worships his god”. That was how the cross looked.

The called. Effectual calling. The same message is folly to some and power to others. The difference is God’s call (vv. 24, 26).

On a Tuesday. People today still want either proof (signs) or a sophisticated worldview (wisdom). Offer them Christ crucified. It is what they need, even if it is not what they want.
verseByVerse.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, reserved for slaves and rebels; for Jews, a crucified man was under God’s curse.

verseByVerse.quote: For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God’s foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and God’s weakness is stronger than human strength.

A deliberate paradox. God is not foolish or weak. But what looks foolish and weak in God’s actions, a crucified Saviour, outdoes all human wisdom and power.

For worship. The cross that looked like God’s weakest moment defeated sin, death and Satan. Worship the God who wins through what looks like defeat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to look at their own church. Not many of them were clever, powerful or well-born by worldly standards. God deliberately chose what the world thinks foolish, weak, low and contemptible, even what counts for nothing, to put the proud and the important to shame, so that no human being can boast before him. It is God who has placed them in Christ Jesus, and Christ has become for them wisdom from God: their righteousness, their holiness and their redemption. So, as Scripture says, anyone who boasts should boast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Doctrine of Boasting: Sola Gratia Applied

The logic of vv. 28–29 is the logic of grace pushed to its social conclusion: God chooses the things that are “not” to bring to nothing the things that “are” — “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.” This is the pastoral and sociological outworking of sola gratia. If salvation were partly dependent on human wisdom, power, or birth, then at least some people could boast. But when God saves fishermen, tax collectors, former persecutors, and the socially marginal, the only conceivable boast is in the grace that did what human merit could never have achieved. God’s choosing of the lowly things is not an arbitrary preference for lowliness but a deliberate demolition of every ground of human pride before him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth’s social hierarchy was steep and rigid: Roman citizens over freedpersons over slaves; the educated over the illiterate; patrons over clients. The church at Corinth crossed every one of these lines — and the crossing was theological, not merely sociological. It was evidence of the same gospel that the cross proclaimed. Now: The church that unconsciously mirrors the class and status structures of its surrounding culture is denying with its sociology what it affirms with its theology. The cross creates a community where the only legitimate boast is in the Lord — which means no other boast is legitimate at all.

verseByVerse.quote: For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Think about what you were when you were called, brothers and sisters. Not many of you were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what the world thinks foolish to shame the wise; God chose what the world thinks weak to shame the strong.

Look at yourselves. The church at Corinth was mostly ordinary people: slaves, freedmen, artisans, with a few wealthier members like Crispus, Gaius and Erastus. “Not many”, not “not any”.

Chosen. Three times in two verses: God chose. Election is not based on merit, intelligence or status. “It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you” (Deuteronomy 7:7). “Has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith” (James 2:5)?

To shame. God’s choice overturns the world’s ranking.

On a Tuesday. If you feel ordinary or unimportant, you are exactly the kind of person God loves to choose. And if your church is full of unimpressive people, it is in good company.

verseByVerse.quote: God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that count for nothing, to bring to nothing the things that count, so that no human being might boast in God’s presence.

Low and despised. Literally “ignoble” (the opposite of “noble” in v. 26) and “treated with contempt”.

Things that are not. People who were nobodies in Corinthian society. God creates out of nothing (Romans 4:17) in salvation as in creation.

No boasting. The purpose of God’s choice: no one can say “I deserved it.”

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “yea, and things which are not”) add “and”. The earliest read “even things that are not”. The meaning is the same.

On a Tuesday. There is no room for snobbery in the church: intellectual, social or spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is because of God that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness and redemption.

Because of him. Your union with Christ is God’s doing, not yours.

Wisdom from God. The Corinthians sought wisdom. True wisdom is a person, Christ, and it has three parts:

Righteousness: our right standing with God, Christ’s righteousness credited to us (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). Not a righteousness infused into us and then improved, but Christ himself as our righteousness. “The LORD is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6).

Sanctification: our holiness, also found in Christ, worked out by the Spirit.

Redemption: freedom bought at a price, beginning now and completed at the resurrection of the body (Romans 8:23).

Imputed or infused? Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent) holds that justification includes the infusion of righteousness into the believer. The Reformers taught that justification is God’s legal declaration based on Christ’s righteousness imputed, while sanctification is the inner renewal that always accompanies it. Verdict: Paul lists righteousness and sanctification separately, both in Christ. They are inseparable but distinct.

On a Tuesday. Everything you need before God is in Christ: wisdom, standing, holiness, freedom. You are not missing anything.

parallels.desc: the LORD is our righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
So that, as Scripture says, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

Jeremiah 9:23–24. Do not boast in wisdom, might or riches, but in knowing the Lord. Exactly the three things Corinth prized (v. 26: wise, powerful, noble). Paul will quote it again in 2 Corinthians 10:17.

The Lord. In Jeremiah, the LORD (Yahweh). For Paul, the Lord Jesus Christ. He applies the divine name to Jesus without hesitation.

For worship. Finish the day by boasting in the Lord: tell him what you admire in him. Then tell someone else.

parallels.desc: let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me

Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?<sup>14</sup>I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,<sup>15</sup>so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name.<sup>16</sup>(I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)<sup>17</sup>For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.<sup>18</sup>For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.<sup>19</sup>For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”<sup>20</sup>Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?<sup>21</sup>For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.<sup>22</sup>For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom,<sup>23</sup>but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles,<sup>24</sup>but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.<sup>25</sup>For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.<sup>26</sup>For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.<sup>27</sup>But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;<sup>28</sup>God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are,<sup>29</sup>so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.<sup>30</sup>And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,<sup>31</sup>so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

2.title: The Spirit, the Cross, and True Wisdom
2.overview:
Paul continues his answer to a church that prized clever speech and secret wisdom. He reminds them how he first came to Corinth: not as a dazzling orator, but weak, nervous and resolved to speak of nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified, so that their faith would rest on God’s power rather than on human brilliance. Yet the gospel is not anti-intellectual. There is a wisdom Paul speaks among the mature, but it is God’s wisdom, hidden in the past and now revealed, which the rulers of this age did not grasp, or they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

This wisdom cannot be discovered; it must be revealed, and God has revealed it by his Spirit, who knows God’s depths as a person’s own spirit knows his thoughts. The apostles have received that Spirit, and they speak in words he teaches. A person without the Spirit cannot accept these things; they seem foolish to him, because they can be understood only by the Spirit. But the person with the Spirit can discern them, and believers have the mind of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul recalls his arrival in Corinth. He did not come with impressive rhetoric or a display of cleverness to announce God’s message. He had made up his mind to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ, crucified. He came in weakness, fear and great trembling, and his preaching did not rely on persuasive technique but on a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, so that their faith would rest not on human wisdom but on God’s power.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of Proclamation

Paul’s deliberate simplicity in proclamation is not a pastoral strategy; it is a doctrinal commitment. The power of the gospel is the power of the Spirit working through the word of the cross — not the power of the preacher, the brilliance of the argument, or the emotional manipulation of the audience. Reformed theology has always insisted on this: it is the Spirit who regenerates, convicts, and converts; the preacher is the instrument, not the cause. If people are not converted by the preaching of Christ crucified, they will not be converted by anything the preacher can add.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In first-century Corinth, the travelling sophist was a celebrity figure — a rhetorical virtuoso who could hold an audience spellbound, charge a fee, and move on. The Corinthians expected their teacher to perform at that level. Paul’s refusal to do so was not incompetence but protest: he would not compete on the sophists’ terms. Now: The contemporary equivalent is the pressure to make church services “compelling” through production values, platform charisma, and emotional manipulation. Paul’s counter-word is not to be deliberately boring, but to trust the cross to do what polished performance cannot: actually save people.

verseByVerse.quote: And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I came to you, brothers and sisters, I did not come to announce God’s testimony with impressive speech or cleverness. For I decided to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.

Lofty speech. Travelling orators made a dramatic entrance into a city, displaying their skill to attract students and fees. Paul refused to play that game.

I decided. A deliberate choice. Paul was highly educated and could have argued like a philosopher. He chose not to.

After Athens? Paul came to Corinth from Athens, where he had debated philosophers on the Areopagus and “some mocked” (Acts 17:32). Some think he concluded his Athens approach had failed and changed method. Verdict: unlikely to be a repudiation. In Athens he also preached the resurrection and judgement (Acts 17:31), and some believed. But Corinth’s love of rhetoric made him especially careful not to compete on those terms.

Christ crucified. Not that Paul never taught anything else, but that everything was centred on and measured by the cross.

A textual note. Early manuscripts are divided between “the testimony of God” (ESV) and “the mystery of God” (in the earliest papyrus and several others). The two Greek words look similar. “Mystery” would anticipate verse 7; “testimony” recalls 1:6. The meaning is close either way: the message God has revealed.

On a Tuesday. When you talk about your faith, you do not have to be clever. Keep coming back to Jesus and what he did on the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I came to you in weakness, with fear and a great deal of trembling. My speech and my preaching did not rely on clever, persuasive words, but on a demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith would not rest on human wisdom but on God’s power.

Weakness and fear. Paul had been beaten at Philippi, chased from Thessalonica and Berea, mocked at Athens. He arrived in Corinth alone and anxious. The Lord encouraged him in a vision: “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you” (Acts 18:9–10).

Demonstration of the Spirit and power. Apodeixis: a technical term in rhetoric for a compelling proof. Paul’s proof was not a clever argument but the Spirit’s work. Does this mean miracles (2 Corinthians 12:12; Romans 15:19) or the Spirit’s power to convict and convert (1 Thessalonians 1:5)? Verdict: probably both, but especially the changed lives of the Corinthians themselves.

Faith resting on God. If people are argued into faith by brilliance, a more brilliant arguer can argue them out. Faith resting on God’s power stands.

A textual note. The phrase “plausible words of wisdom” has many variant forms in the manuscripts. The KJV’s “enticing words of man’s wisdom” adds “man’s”, which is not in the earliest. The sense is unaffected.

On a Tuesday. Nervous about speaking to a friend about Christ? So was Paul. Pray, speak simply, and trust the Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: Paul came to Corinth after the cool reception at Athens.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Yet Paul does teach wisdom among those who are mature, though not the wisdom of this age or of its rulers, who are passing away. It is God’s secret wisdom, hidden until now, which God planned before time for our glory. None of the rulers of this age understood it; if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. As Scripture says, no one has seen, heard or imagined what God has prepared for those who love him, but God has revealed it to us by his Spirit, who searches even the depths of God. Just as only a person’s own spirit knows his inner thoughts, only God’s Spirit knows God’s thoughts. Believers have received not the world’s spirit but God’s Spirit, so that they may understand what God has freely given. The apostles speak of these things in words taught not by human wisdom but by the Spirit. The unspiritual person rejects them as foolishness and cannot understand them, because they are discerned only through the Spirit. The spiritual person can evaluate everything but is not subject to merely human judgement. Who has known the Lord’s mind to instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Knowledge of God

Verses 10–16 are the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit (testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum). Calvin’s Institutes ground the believer’s certainty about Scripture not in external proofs but in the Spirit’s own witness to the heart. Paul’s argument here is the foundation: the things of God are spiritually discerned; the Spirit of God alone can reveal them; the Spirit has been given to those who are in Christ. The natural person (psychikos anthrōpos) is not merely unwilling but unable to receive spiritual things — a direct support for the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its noetic dimension.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians’ preference for Apollos’s sophisticated rhetoric over Paul’s plain proclamation was, at root, a preference for a wisdom they could evaluate by their own natural capacities. Paul’s response: the real wisdom — the wisdom that saves — cannot be evaluated that way. It requires the Spirit to receive it. Now: The recurring temptation to evaluate the gospel by academic or cultural criteria — to ask whether Christianity can hold its own in the university seminar — misses Paul’s point. The knowledge of God is not the endpoint of human inquiry; it is the gift of the Spirit to the humble heart. This is why apologetics serves evangelism but cannot replace it: ultimately, only the Spirit can open eyes to see the Lord of glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet we do speak wisdom among the mature, but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing. No, we speak God’s wisdom, a mystery that was hidden, which God destined before the ages for our glory.

The mature. Teleioi. Not an elite inner circle with secret knowledge, as later Gnostic groups claimed, but believers who have received the Spirit and accept the cross (vv. 12–15). In 3:1 Paul will say the Corinthians are not yet acting maturely.

Mystery. In Paul, not a puzzle, but God’s plan hidden in the past and now openly revealed in Christ (Romans 16:25–26; Ephesians 3:3–6).

Before the ages. The cross was not plan B. God decreed it before creation (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:20).

For our glory. God planned our salvation and our share in his glory before time began.

On a Tuesday. Christianity is not anti-thinking. There is depth to explore for a lifetime. But it is always the depth of the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of the rulers of this age understood this wisdom. If they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

Who are the rulers?

Human rulers: Caiaphas, Herod, Pilate, those who crucified Jesus. “Both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel” (Acts 4:27).

Spiritual powers: the demonic forces behind them (Ephesians 6:12; Colossians 2:15).

Verdict: primarily the human rulers, who acted in ignorance (Luke 23:34; Acts 3:17). Spiritual powers may stand behind them, but Paul’s main point is that the world’s powerful people did not see who Jesus was.

The Lord of glory. A title of God in Jewish writings (compare Psalm 24:7–10, “the King of glory”). The one crucified was God the Son. A man was nailed to a cross, and he was the Lord of glory.

For worship. Meditate on the phrase: the Lord of glory, crucified. Then sing it.

verseByVerse.quote: But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”— these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But, as Scripture says: “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the human heart imagined, God has prepared for those who love him.” These things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.

The quotation. A free combination of Isaiah 64:4 (“no eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for those who wait for him”) and perhaps Isaiah 65:17 (things that will not come to mind).

Not mainly about heaven. This verse is often read at funerals as if it described heaven, which we cannot imagine. But Paul’s point is the next verse: God has now revealed it by the Spirit. What was unimaginable is the gospel itself, God’s plan of salvation in Christ, now made known.

The Spirit searches. Not that the Spirit is ignorant and has to find out, but that he knows God completely from within. Only one who is himself God could do so. This verse is part of the Bible’s witness to the Spirit’s deity.

On a Tuesday. When you read the Bible, ask the Spirit who knows God’s depths to show you what you cannot see by yourself.

parallels.desc: from of old no one has heard or perceived

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For who knows a person’s thoughts except that person’s own spirit within them? In the same way, no one knows God’s thoughts except the Spirit of God. And we have received not the spirit of the world but the Spirit who comes from God, so that we may understand the things God has freely given us.

An analogy. No one knows what you are really thinking unless you tell them. Likewise, no one knows God’s mind except the Spirit, unless he reveals it.

The spirit of the world. The outlook of human wisdom apart from God.

The things freely given. Salvation, adoption, grace: gifts, which we understand only by the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. If you understand the gospel at all, thank the Spirit. You did not work it out yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we speak about these things not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit, explaining spiritual realities with spiritual words.

Words taught by the Spirit. Paul claims that not only the ideas but the words of the apostles’ teaching were given by the Spirit. This is the basis of the doctrine of verbal inspiration: “men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).

Interpreting spiritual truths. The last phrase is ambiguous. It could mean “explaining spiritual truths to spiritual people”, “combining spiritual truths with spiritual words”, or “comparing spiritual things with spiritual things”. Verdict: “explaining spiritual things with spiritual words” fits the verse best, but the general sense is clear: the Spirit gives both the content and the language.

On a Tuesday. When you study the Bible, pay attention to the words, not just the general ideas. The Spirit chose them.

verseByVerse.quote: The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The person without the Spirit does not accept the things that come from God’s Spirit. They seem foolish to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are discerned only through the Spirit.

The natural person. Psychikos: a person who has only natural human life, without the Holy Spirit. Not necessarily a stupid person: some of the most brilliant people reject the gospel.

Cannot. Not just “does not”, but “is not able”. This is the Bible’s teaching on spiritual inability, or total depravity: sin affects the whole person, including the mind, so that we cannot come to God by our own power. “The mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot” (Romans 8:7). Jesus: “unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3).

Do people have free will to accept the gospel? Arminian Christians teach that God gives all people enough grace (prevenient grace) to be able to accept or reject the gospel. Reformed Christians teach that the natural person cannot accept it until God regenerates him by the Spirit. Verdict: this verse supports the Reformed view: the Spirit must open the heart (Acts 16:14). Yet the gospel must still be preached to all, for it is through the message that the Spirit works.

On a Tuesday. Do not despair if a clever friend finds the gospel foolish. That is what Paul said would happen. Pray for the Spirit to open their eyes, as he opened yours.
verseByVerse.note: The “natural person” is someone without the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spiritual person can evaluate everything, but is not subject to being evaluated by anyone without the Spirit.

Judges all things. The believer with the Spirit can discern truth and error, and see things as they really are.

Judged by no one. Not that Christians are beyond correction (5:12; 14:29; Galatians 6:1), but that the unspiritual person is not qualified to assess spiritual matters. The world’s verdict on the cross is not the final word.

What it does not mean. The Corinthians may have used “spiritual” as a badge of superiority, claiming no one could correct them. Paul will deflate that in 3:1–4. Being spiritual does not mean being infallible.

On a Tuesday. Do not let the opinions of unbelieving commentators shake your confidence in the gospel. But do accept correction from mature Christians.

verseByVerse.quote: “For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

Isaiah 40:13. “Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel?” No human can advise God or know his mind by their own effort.

But we have the mind of Christ. Astonishing: through the Spirit, believers have access to the very way Christ thinks. Not omniscience, but his outlook, values and understanding, revealed in the gospel and formed in us by the Spirit (Philippians 2:5; Romans 12:2, “be transformed by the renewal of your mind”).

The Lord and Christ. In Isaiah, “the LORD”. Paul answers with “Christ”. Again he identifies Jesus with the LORD of the Old Testament.

On a Tuesday. Before a hard decision at work or in your family, ask: how would Christ think about this? You have his mind through his word and Spirit.

For worship. Thank God that the Spirit who knows God’s depths has opened them to you.

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel?
