3.title: God’s Field, God’s Building, God’s Temple
3.overview:
The Corinthians thought of themselves as spiritual and wise. Paul tells them bluntly that their quarrelling over leaders shows they are still spiritual infants, behaving like ordinary unconverted people. Their leaders are only servants. Using a farming picture, Paul says he planted and Apollos watered, but God made things grow, so the workers are nothing and God is everything. Then a building picture: Paul laid the only possible foundation, Jesus Christ, and others build on it. On the day of judgement, fire will test the quality of each builder’s work; good work will be rewarded, and poor work will burn up, though the builder himself will be saved, as if escaping through flames.

Then a warning: the church is God’s temple, where his Spirit lives, and anyone who destroys it will be destroyed by God. Paul ends where chapter 1 began, with the folly of the world’s wisdom. No one should boast about human leaders, because everything already belongs to believers, Paul, Apollos, Peter, the world, life, death, the present and the future, and they belong to Christ, and Christ to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul could not speak to them as spiritually mature people, but only as people still ruled by the flesh, infants in Christ. He gave them milk rather than solid food, because they were not ready, and they still are not. Their jealousy and quarrels prove it: they are behaving like ordinary people, saying “I follow Paul” or “I follow Apollos”. But Paul and Apollos are only servants through whom they believed, each doing the job the Lord assigned. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth, so the planter and the waterer are nothing; only God, who makes things grow, matters. The workers have one purpose, and each will be rewarded for his own work. They are God’s fellow workers; the church is God’s field and God’s building.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God in Ministry

The repeated insistence that God gives the growth is not a platitude; it is the Reformed doctrine of sovereign grace applied to the fruit of ministry. Paul preached; Apollos taught; but neither of them converted a single soul. Conversion is the work of God, not the achievement of the preacher. This means that the minister cannot take credit for results, cannot despair over apparent fruitlessness as if it were his own failure, and cannot be compared with another minister as if their different “results” reflected their different competencies. God gives where and when he wills.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian factions were measuring Paul and Apollos by their outputs — converts, rhetorical impact, visible results. Paul refuses this measuring rod: the results belong to God, not to the apostle. Now: The contemporary church is still tempted to evaluate ministry by attendance, conversion numbers, and cultural impact — and to attribute these to the skill and gifting of the human leader. Paul’s corrective: plant faithfully, water patiently, and trust the God of growth.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I, brothers and sisters, could not talk to you as spiritual people. I had to talk to you as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, because you were not ready for it. And even now you are still not ready.

Not spiritual. The Corinthians thought they were the spiritual ones (2:15). Paul punctures it.

People of the flesh. Sarkinos: made of flesh, still governed by natural human attitudes. They are true believers (“in Christ”) but immature.

Milk. The basic gospel. Not that milk is bad: “Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk” (1 Peter 2:2). But adults need solid food too (Hebrews 5:12–14).

The “carnal Christian”? Some twentieth-century teachers (notably Lewis Sperry Chafer and the Campus Crusade booklet on the Spirit-filled life) built on this verse a third category of person, between the unbeliever and the spiritual Christian: the “carnal Christian”, saved but living with no real change. Verdict: Paul is not describing a stable category to settle in, but rebuking a temporary immaturity he expects them to outgrow. A person who claims Christ but shows no change at all over years should ask whether they have truly been born again (2 Corinthians 13:5; 1 John 3:9).

On a Tuesday. How long have you been a Christian? Are you still on milk? Take a step: read through a whole book of the Bible, or join a serious study group.

verseByVerse.quote: for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you are still worldly. Since there is jealousy and quarrelling among you, are you not worldly and behaving like ordinary people?

The evidence. Not lack of knowledge or gifts (they had plenty, 1:5–7), but jealousy and strife. Spiritual maturity is measured by love, not by knowledge.

Like mere men. Like people without the Spirit, who rank leaders and compete for status.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “envying, and strife, and divisions”) add “and divisions”. The earliest lack it; it was probably added from Galatians 5:20.

On a Tuesday. If you are jealous of another Christian’s ministry, gifts or popularity, Paul has a word for it: immature. Confess it, and pray for their success.

verseByVerse.quote: For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when one of you says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not acting like ordinary human beings? What, after all, is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, each doing what the Lord gave him to do.

What, not who. Paul asks “what is Apollos?”, not “who”. Leaders are functions, not personalities to follow.

Servants. Diakonoi: table-servants, attendants. Not heroes or founders of schools.

As the Lord assigned. Each leader has a different task, given by Christ.

A textual note. Some later manuscripts (KJV “are ye not carnal?”) read “fleshly” instead of “human” in verse 4. The earliest read “human”.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the leaders who helped you to faith. But do not put them on a pedestal. They are servants, like you.

verseByVerse.quote: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I planted the seed, Apollos watered it, but God made it grow. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything; only God, who makes things grow.

A farming picture. Paul founded the church (Acts 18:1–11); Apollos taught it afterwards (Acts 18:27–28). Both did real work, but neither made anything grow.

God gave the growth. The tense is continuous: God was giving the growth all along. Only he can create life.

What it does not mean. Not that human work is pointless. Planting and watering are necessary. But growth is God’s gift.

On a Tuesday. A Sunday school teacher, a youth leader or a parent may see little fruit for years. Keep planting and watering. Growth is God’s business, and he is at work.

verseByVerse.quote: He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who plants and the one who waters work together with one purpose, and each will be rewarded for his own work.

One. Not rivals but one team, with one aim.

Wages. Each worker will receive a reward from God, according to his labour, not his success. Faithfulness is rewarded.

On a Tuesday. If you serve in a hidden role, God sees your labour and will reward it.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are fellow workers in God’s service. You are God’s field, God’s building.

God’s fellow workers. Either “fellow workers with God” or “fellow workers belonging to God”. The Greek stresses “God’s” three times: God’s workers, God’s field, God’s building. The emphasis is that everything belongs to God.

Field and building. Two pictures: agriculture (vv. 6–8) and construction (vv. 10–17). Jeremiah 1:10 combined them: “to build and to plant”.

For worship. Thank God that your church, with all its faults, is his field and his building.

parallels.desc: the planting of the LORD

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By God’s grace, Paul laid the foundation like a skilled master builder, and others are building on it. Everyone must be careful how they build, because no other foundation can be laid than the one already there, Jesus Christ. On that foundation people build with gold, silver and precious stones, or with wood, hay and straw. The day of judgement will expose each person’s work, because it will be revealed with fire, which will test its quality. If the work survives, the builder will be rewarded; if it burns up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as one escaping through fire. Paul then warns that the church is God’s temple, in which God’s Spirit lives. If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person, because God’s temple is holy, and they are that temple.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Temple

Paul’s identification of the church as God’s temple carries enormous theological weight in a letter written to a city famous for its pagan temples. The Corinthians lived in the shadow of the temple of Aphrodite; the city was saturated with temple culture, sexual licence, and temple feasts. Paul’s claim is that the living God has abandoned temples made of stone and taken up residence in a community of people — flawed, fractious, sin-prone people — through his Spirit. The church is not a building where God may be found; the church is the people in whom God actually dwells. This is the new covenant fulfilment of every OT temple theology: God with his people, no longer mediated through architecture and ritual, but through the Spirit given to all who belong to Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The divisions at Corinth were not merely social dysfunction; they were a theological emergency. A fragmented community cannot be a temple — the architectural metaphor itself requires unity, all the stones fitting together. The faction wars were, quite literally, demolition work on the place where God had chosen to live. Now: Every church split, every faction, every deliberate destruction of community is an assault on the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. This gives a theological gravity to church unity that mere social concern cannot supply: we are not trying to be nice; we are protecting the home of God.

verseByVerse.quote: According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the grace God gave me, I laid a foundation like a skilled master builder, and someone else is building on it. Each person must be careful how they build on it. For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.

Master builder. Architektōn: the chief builder or contractor who planned the project and laid the foundation. Corinth was full of new public buildings after its refounding; everyone knew the role.

By grace. Even Paul’s skill as a church planter was God’s gift.

The only foundation. Jesus Christ: his person, death and resurrection, as preached in the gospel. Isaiah prophesied “a tested stone, a precious cornerstone” laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16). The church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20).

Let each take care. A warning to all teachers and leaders, Apollos included. It is possible to build badly on the right foundation.

On a Tuesday. Is Christ actually the foundation of your life, or one part of the structure? Check what you would fall back on if everything else collapsed.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw— each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone builds on this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay or straw, the quality of each person’s work will become clear. The Day will make it known, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.

Two kinds of material. Gold, silver and precious stones are costly and survive fire; perhaps Paul thinks of the temple (1 Chronicles 29:2). Wood, hay and straw are cheap and burn. Corinth itself had been burned by the Romans in 146 BC: its marble and bronze survived, its timber did not.

What is the building? In context, the church, and the materials are the teaching and ministry of its leaders. Sound teaching that builds lasting faith is gold; teaching driven by human wisdom, popularity or personality is straw. The principle applies to all Christian service.

The Day. The day of the Lord, Christ’s return and judgement (1:8; 4:5).

Fire. A common biblical image for God’s testing judgement: “For he is like a refiner’s fire” (Malachi 3:2).

On a Tuesday. Ask what you are building with: a youth group built on entertainment, or on the word of God and prayer? Work done in your own strength for applause, or quietly for Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Fire tests metals; wood and straw burn up.

parallels.desc: like a refiner’s fire

verseByVerse.quote: If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If what someone has built on the foundation survives, that person will receive a reward. If it is burned up, that person will suffer loss, though they themselves will be saved, but only like someone escaping through the flames.

Reward. God graciously rewards faithful service. The New Testament speaks freely of rewards (Matthew 6:4; 25:21; 2 John 8), though all are gifts of grace.

Suffer loss. Loss of reward, not of salvation. The builder escapes like a man running from a burning house with nothing but his life.

Purgatory? Roman Catholic theology has used this passage to support purgatory: a cleansing fire after death for believers who die with unpurged sin. Verdict: the passage does not teach purgatory. The fire tests works, not people; it happens on “the Day” of judgement, not in a period after death; and its result is reward or loss, not purification from sin. Christ’s blood purifies from all sin (1 John 1:7; Hebrews 10:14). After death comes judgement (Hebrews 9:27), not a further process of cleansing.

Saved through fire. A sobering picture: a Christian can be truly saved and still have wasted much of his life’s work.

On a Tuesday. You are saved by grace, but not everything you do will last. Invest in what will survive the fire: people, prayer, the word, love.

parallels.desc: a brand plucked out of the burning

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit lives in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.

You are God’s temple. “You” is plural: the church together. Corinth had many temples: to Apollo, Aphrodite, Asclepius, the emperor. The Jews had one in Jerusalem. Now the living temple of the true God is a congregation of believers in Corinth.

The Spirit dwells. As God’s glory filled the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10–11), so the Spirit lives among his people.

Destroying the temple. Not just building badly (v. 15), but tearing down the church through division, false teaching or immorality. The penalty is severe: God will destroy him. This is not about true believers who build poorly, but about those whose work destroys the church.

Holy. Set apart for God. The church is sacred to him.

On a Tuesday. Gossip, factions and spreading false ideas are not small things. They damage God’s temple. Guard your church as holy ground.
verseByVerse.note: “You” is plural: the church together is God’s temple.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Folly of Boasting in Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to fool themselves. Anyone who thinks he is wise by this world’s standards should become a fool, in the world’s eyes, so as to become truly wise. The world’s wisdom is foolishness to God, as Scripture says: God traps the wise in their cunning, and knows how empty their reasoning is. So no one should boast about human leaders. Everything already belongs to them: Paul, Apollos and Peter, the world, life and death, the present and the future. All of it is theirs, and they belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything in Christ, Nothing Apart from him

Verses 21–23 are one of the great catalogue texts of what it means to be in Christ. Paul’s list — Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, present, future — is comprehensive: every apostle, every circumstance, every temporal horizon, even death itself, belongs to the believer in Christ. The Corinthians have been acting poor — squabbling over which apostle to claim — while they are infinitely rich. This is union with Christ expanded to cosmic scope: the one who is in Christ owns, in principle, everything that Christ owns. They need not cling to Paul or Apollos; they have all of them, and infinitely more besides.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were each claiming one-third of the apostolic inheritance — “I follow Paul,” etc. — when they could have had the whole. Their factionalism was a self-imposed poverty in the middle of infinite wealth. Now: The Christian who defines himself by his tradition (Calvinist, Arminian, Baptist, Anglican) rather than by Christ is doing the same thing — claiming a slice when the whole belongs to him. The traditions are real and valuable; they are yours in Christ. But Christ is not yours in the tradition.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness,” and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not deceive yourselves. If any of you think you are wise by the standards of this age, you should become “fools” so that you may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight. As Scripture says, “He catches the wise in their own craftiness,” and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”

Become a fool. Accept the gospel that the world calls foolish (1:18). True wisdom starts with admitting your own wisdom is not enough.

Two quotations. Job 5:13 (Eliphaz’s words, true in themselves though misapplied to Job) and Psalm 94:11, where the LORD knows that human thoughts are a mere breath. Paul adds “of the wise” to apply it.

What it does not mean. Not anti-intellectualism. Christians have founded universities and pioneered science. The point is to bring all learning under God and his revelation.

On a Tuesday. If you are a professional with expertise, use it gratefully. But be willing to look foolish to your colleagues for Christ.

parallels.desc: he catches the wise in their own craftiness
the LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath

verseByVerse.quote: So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So no more boasting about human leaders! For everything belongs to you: Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, the present and the future. All of it is yours.

Reversal. The Corinthians said “I belong to Paul”. Paul says “Paul belongs to you.” Leaders are gifts to the church, not owners of it.

All things. A breathtaking list. The world: God’s creation is the believer’s inheritance (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5). Life and death: even death serves the believer (Philippians 1:21). The present and the future: nothing can separate them from God’s love (Romans 8:38–39). “For those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28).

On a Tuesday. Why compete for status in the church when everything is already yours in Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

The chain. All things are yours; you are Christ’s; Christ is God’s. Everything ends in God.

Christ is God’s. Not that Christ is less than God, but that in his role as Mediator the Son serves the Father’s purpose (15:28). The Son is equal to the Father in nature (John 1:1; Philippians 2:6) and gladly does his will.

For worship. Say it aloud: all things are mine; I am Christ’s; Christ is God’s. Then praise God for such an inheritance.

4.title: Servants of Christ, Spectacles to the World
4.overview:
Paul finishes his answer to the factions by telling the Corinthians how to think about their leaders. Apostles are Christ’s servants and the managers of God’s revealed truth, and what counts for a manager is faithfulness. Paul is not troubled by the Corinthians’ assessment of him, or even by his own clear conscience, because the Lord is his judge, and on the last day he will expose hidden motives and give each person whatever praise is due. So the Corinthians must stop judging prematurely and stop puffing themselves up over one teacher against another, for everything they have is a gift.

Then Paul turns to biting irony. The Corinthians act as if they have already arrived, rich and reigning like kings, while the apostles look like condemned prisoners paraded at the end of a procession: hungry, ill-clothed, beaten, homeless, labouring with their hands, treated as the scum of the earth, yet blessing those who curse them. He writes not to shame them but to warn them as a father. They may have countless tutors, but only one father in the gospel, so they should imitate him. He is sending Timothy to remind them of his ways, and will come himself soon to see whether the arrogant have any real power, since God’s kingdom is a matter of power, not talk. Should he come with a rod, or with love and gentleness?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Servants and Stewards: The Judgment That Matters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: People should regard Paul and his fellow workers as Christ’s servants, entrusted with managing God’s revealed secrets, and the one thing required of such managers is that they prove faithful. Paul cares very little whether the Corinthians or any human court evaluates him; he does not even judge himself. His conscience is clear, but that does not prove him innocent; the Lord is the one who judges him. So they should not pass verdicts before the time. When the Lord comes he will bring hidden things to light and reveal the purposes of every heart, and then each person will receive whatever commendation comes from God. Paul has used himself and Apollos as an example so that they learn not to go beyond what Scripture says and not to be proud of one leader against another. What makes anyone superior? What do they have that they did not receive? And if it was a gift, why boast as if it were not?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Eschatological Judgment and Its Present Implications

Paul’s refusal to pre-judge himself or others (vv. 3–5) is not relativism but eschatological realism. The final judgment has not yet been rendered; therefore all present judgments — including self-assessment — are provisional. Reformed theology has always warned against both false confidence (I know I am right) and false despair (I know I am condemned): both pre-empt the judgment that belongs to God alone. The practical implication is freedom: neither to be destroyed by human criticism nor to be puffed up by human praise, because neither the critic nor the flatterer is the judge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were evaluating Paul and finding him wanting, not by the standard of faithfulness but by the standards of rhetorical eloquence and visible success. Paul refuses the evaluation: you are not my judge; the Lord is. Now: Ministry evaluation by attendance, public approval, or conference invitations is the contemporary equivalent. The minister who structures his ministry around what will get him praised by his peers has already chosen the wrong judge. The only evaluation that matters is the Lord’s — and it will assess what the heart actually was.

verseByVerse.quote: This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is how people should think of us: as servants of Christ and as stewards entrusted with God’s mysteries. And what is required of stewards is that they be found faithful.

Servants. Hypēretai: assistants, under-officers, originally the rowers on the lower deck of a warship. Subordinates who take orders.

Stewards. Oikonomoi: household managers, often trusted slaves, in charge of the master’s property and staff. The same title was held by Erastus, Corinth’s “city treasurer” (Romans 16:23 uses this word). A steward owns nothing; he manages what belongs to another.

The mysteries of God. The gospel truths once hidden and now revealed (2:7). The later Latin church sometimes read this of the sacraments (“mysteries” was translated sacramenta), and Eastern churches still call the sacraments mysteries. Verdict: Paul means the revealed gospel, which the apostles preach and guard. The sacraments are signs of that gospel, not the content of the stewardship.

Faithful. Not brilliant, popular or successful, but faithful. “Who then is the faithful and wise manager” (Luke 12:42)?

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “you seek” (zēteite) instead of “it is required” (zēteitai); the words sounded alike when read aloud. The ESV’s reading is better supported.

On a Tuesday. Every Christian is a steward of something: money, time, children, a job, the gospel. Ask at the end of the week not “Was I impressive?” but “Was I faithful?”
verseByVerse.note: A steward was a trusted household manager, often a slave, put in charge of his master’s goods.

verseByVerse.quote: But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for me, it matters very little to me if I am judged by you or by any human court. I do not even judge myself. I am not aware of anything against me, but that does not make me innocent. It is the Lord who judges me.

Human court. Literally “human day”, as opposed to the Lord’s day of judgement (3:13). The Corinthians were sitting in judgement on their teachers, comparing them like critics.

I do not judge myself. Not that self-examination is wrong (11:28; 2 Corinthians 13:5), but that Paul’s own verdict is not final either.

A clear conscience is not enough. Conscience is valuable but fallible. We can be unaware of sin. “Search me, O God, and know my heart!” (Psalm 139:23). Only God’s verdict counts.

On a Tuesday. If people are criticising you unfairly, you do not need to win their approval. And if your conscience accuses you, remember “God is greater than our heart” (1 John 3:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So do not judge anything before the right time, before the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and expose the motives of people’s hearts. Then each person will receive their praise from God.

Before the time. The Corinthians were passing final verdicts on leaders now. Only Christ can judge motives, and he will, at his return.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may never make judgements. Paul tells them to judge in the very next chapter (5:12). The point is not to judge motives and pass final verdicts. “Judge not, that you be not judged” (Matthew 7:1) is about condemning others, not about discernment.

Hidden things revealed. “On that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus” (Romans 2:16).

Commendation from God. Not condemnation but praise: the faithful will receive God’s “well done” (Matthew 25:21).

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to assume the worst about someone’s motives, stop. You cannot see their heart. Christ can, and will.

verseByVerse.quote: I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers, that you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written, that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Friends, I have applied all this to myself and Apollos for your benefit, so that you may learn from us the meaning of the saying, “Nothing beyond what is written,” and so that none of you will be puffed up in favour of one person against another. For who makes you superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not?

Not beyond what is written. A puzzling phrase, perhaps a slogan. Possible meanings:

Do not go beyond Scripture (the Old Testament texts Paul has quoted about wisdom and boasting).

Keep to the rules, as children learning to write traced the letters exactly.

Some think it is a scribal note that crept into the text.

Verdict: most likely “do not go beyond Scripture”: in Paul “it is written” always refers to Scripture. The Corinthians should measure leaders by God’s word, not by human standards of wisdom. This is an early form of the principle that Scripture is the supreme rule.

What do you have that you did not receive? One of the most humbling questions in the Bible. Talents, upbringing, intelligence, health, faith: all gifts. “A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven” (John 3:27). Augustine said this verse finally convinced him that even faith is God’s gift.

On a Tuesday. When you feel proud of your achievements, your children or your theology, ask Paul’s question. Then turn the pride into thanks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Apostles as Spectacle: The Cruciform Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to irony. The Corinthians act as if they already have everything, already rich and reigning as kings without the apostles. He wishes they really did reign, so that the apostles could share it. Instead God seems to have put the apostles at the end of the procession, like men condemned to die in the arena, a spectacle to the world, to angels and to people. The apostles are fools for Christ, weak and dishonoured, while the Corinthians think themselves wise, strong and honoured. To this very hour the apostles are hungry, thirsty, poorly clothed, beaten and homeless; they work hard with their own hands; when cursed they bless, when persecuted they endure, when slandered they answer kindly. They have become like the world’s rubbish and the dirt everyone wipes off.
verseByVerse.theology:
Realized Eschatology and the Cross-Shaped Life

The Corinthians’ problem was not merely social pride but theological confusion about which age they were in. They were living as if the resurrection age had fully arrived — treating this present life as the time of reigning and riches. Paul’s corrective is eschatological: we are still in the “between the times,” the age between the first and second coming, in which the pattern of the Christian life is cruciform, not triumphant. The “not yet” of eschatology shapes the “how” of Christian living. Suffering, weakness, and apparent defeat are not failures of faith but participation in Christ’s own pattern — the pattern of resurrection that comes through, not around, the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman spectacle of condemned criminals paraded before the crowd before their execution is the image behind v. 9 (“a spectacle to the world”). Paul uses the imagery of the arena: God has made the apostles last, like the condemned criminals brought on at the end of the show. This was not hyperbole; Paul had been beaten, imprisoned, and would eventually be executed. Now: The prosperity gospel is the contemporary version of Corinthian triumphalism: the claim that health, wealth, and success are the normal marks of Spirit-filled Christianity. Paul’s fools for Christ’s sake, hungry and homeless, are a permanent rebuke to any theology that makes suffering an anomaly rather than a participation in the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!
verseByVerse.commentary:
You already have everything you want! You have already become rich! You have begun to reign as kings, and without us! How I wish you really were reigning, so that we could reign with you!

Irony. Paul is mocking their self-satisfaction.

Already. The Corinthians lived as though the kingdom had fully arrived: they were spiritually full, rich and reigning now. Scholars call this “over-realised eschatology”: claiming now what belongs to the future. It may explain their contempt for the body, their tongues as the language of angels (13:1), and their doubts about a future resurrection (15:12).

What it does not mean. Believers do already reign with Christ in a sense (Ephesians 2:6), but the full kingdom is still to come, and its path runs through suffering (2 Timothy 2:12).

A modern parallel. Teachings that promise believers health, wealth and victory now as their right make the same mistake.

On a Tuesday. If your Christianity promises you comfort now and never mentions the cross, it is the Corinthian error.
verseByVerse.note: Paul speaks with irony: they acted as if the kingdom had already fully come.

verseByVerse.quote: For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it seems to me that God has put us apostles on display at the very end of the line, like men condemned to die, because we have become a spectacle to the whole world, to angels and to people.

Last of all. In a Roman triumph, captives destined for execution were paraded at the end. In the amphitheatre, the condemned were sent in last, to die fighting beasts or gladiators as the climax of the show.

Spectacle. Theatron: a theatre-show. The whole universe, human and angelic, watches.

On a Tuesday. Christians in many countries today are literally on display: jailed, beaten, executed. Pray for them. And remember that angels watch how ordinary Christians endure.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned prisoners were paraded last in a Roman triumph, or sent into the arena at the end of the games.

verseByVerse.quote: We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are fools because of Christ, but you are so wise in Christ! We are weak, but you are strong! You are honoured, but we are despised!

Three contrasts. Each repeats the language of chapter 1: foolish, weak, low (1:25–28). The apostles live out the message of the cross; the Corinthians think they have left it behind.

On a Tuesday. Which do you prefer, to be thought wise and strong, or to be faithful to Christ even if that looks foolish?

verseByVerse.quote: To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, poorly dressed, beaten and homeless. We work hard with our own hands. When we are cursed, we bless; when we are persecuted, we put up with it; when we are slandered, we answer gently. We have become like the rubbish of the world, the scum everyone scrapes off, even now.

Hunger and homelessness. Not occasional hardship, but the normal apostolic life.

Work with our hands. Manual labour was despised by the Greek and Roman elite as fit for slaves. Paul made tents and was proud of it: “these hands ministered to my necessities” (Acts 20:34).

Bless when cursed. Following Jesus: “pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

Scum and refuse. Perikatharmata and peripsēma: the dirt scoured from a pot, the filth wiped off. In some Greek cities these words were also used of the human scapegoats, outcasts chosen in times of plague or disaster to be driven out or killed to “cleanse” the city. Compare “You have made us scum and garbage among the peoples” (Lamentations 3:45).

On a Tuesday. When someone insults you at work or online for your faith, try Paul’s way: bless, endure, answer kindly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — A Father’s Warning and Appeal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says he is not writing to shame them but to warn them as his dear children. They may have countless guardians in Christ, but they do not have many fathers; through the gospel Paul became their father in Christ Jesus. So he urges them to imitate him. That is why he is sending Timothy, his loved and faithful son in the Lord, to remind them of his way of life in Christ, which he teaches in every church. Some have become arrogant, as though Paul were not coming. But he will come soon, if the Lord wills, and find out not what these proud people say but what power they have, because God’s kingdom is not a matter of talk but of power. Which do they want: that he come with a rod, or with love and a gentle spirit?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fatherhood of the Apostle and Spiritual Formation by Imitation

Paul’s claim to spiritual fatherhood over the Corinthian church is grounded in the gospel: “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (v. 15). The new birth produces a spiritual parentage — and the one through whose proclamation the Spirit brought new birth to a community is, in a real sense, their spiritual father. This is not about control but about formation. Paul asks to be imitated not as an authority but as a living embodiment of the gospel he preached — not his person but his pattern, the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had, in Paul’s absence, developed arrogant teachers who had dismissed the apostle. Timothy is sent to embody what Paul had taught by his life — because argument alone, without the living example, is insufficient. Now: The pastoral call to “be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (11:1) is the most demanding thing a minister can say — and the most necessary. Disciples need models, not merely doctrines. The church that produces only correct theology without cruciform character has missed the point of the apostolic office.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my dear children. You may have ten thousand guardians in Christ, but you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.

Guardians. Paidagōgoi: household slaves who took children to school, supervised their behaviour and disciplined them. They were not teachers or parents. Many people might supervise the Corinthians; only Paul gave them spiritual birth.

Father. Paul planted the church through the gospel. A spiritual father’s love is different from a tutor’s.

“Call no man father”? Jesus said, “call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew 23:9). Protestants have often used this against the title “Father” for priests. Yet Paul calls himself a father. Verdict: Jesus forbids giving any human the ultimate authority that belongs to God, not every use of family language for spiritual relationships. Paul’s fatherhood points them to Christ, not to himself.

On a Tuesday. If you led someone to Christ, you have a special responsibility to care for them as a parent, not just to supervise them.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “guides” was used of the household slave who took charge of children on their way to school.

verseByVerse.quote: I urge you, then, be imitators of me. That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I urge you: imitate me. That is why I sent Timothy to you, my dear and faithful son in the Lord. He will remind you of my way of life in Christ Jesus, which matches what I teach everywhere in every church.

Imitate me. Children copy their father. Paul will add “as I am of Christ” (11:1).

Timothy. Paul’s “true child in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2), sent from Ephesus via Macedonia (Acts 19:22; 1 Corinthians 16:10).

My ways in Christ. Teaching and life together. Paul taught the same thing in every church; the Corinthians had no special version.

On a Tuesday. Could you say to a younger Christian, “Watch how I live and copy it”? If not, what needs to change?

verseByVerse.quote: Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of you have become arrogant, as if I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord is willing, and then I will find out not what these arrogant people are saying but what power they have.

Arrogant. Physioō: to be puffed up, inflated. A favourite word in this letter (4:6, 18, 19; 5:2; 8:1; 13:4). Pride was Corinth’s besetting sin.

If the Lord wills. Paul’s plans are always subject to God (James 4:15).

On a Tuesday. Talking big about faith is easy. Ask whether there is any real spiritual power in your life: changed habits, answered prayer, love.

verseByVerse.quote: For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power. Which do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a gentle spirit?

Not talk but power. The Corinthians loved eloquent speech. God’s kingdom is shown by the Spirit’s power to change lives (2:4).

A rod. A father’s or a tutor’s rod of discipline. “Whoever spares the rod hates his son” (Proverbs 13:24). Paul means church discipline, as chapter 5 will show.

The choice is theirs. Paul would rather come in gentleness. Their repentance will decide.

On a Tuesday. Parents and leaders: give clear warning, prefer gentleness, but be willing to discipline in love.

For worship. Thank God for fathers and mothers in the faith who loved you enough to warn you.

In fact, I do not even judge myself.<sup>4</sup>For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. 5.title: The Leaven of Immorality: Church Discipline and the Holiness of God
5.overview:
Paul now deals with a scandal. A man in the church is living with his father’s wife, probably his stepmother, a relationship forbidden by the law of Moses and condemned even by Roman society. Worse, the church is proud of itself instead of grieving. Perhaps they thought their freedom in Christ meant the body did not matter. Paul, though absent, has already made his judgement: when they assemble with the Lord’s power, they must hand this man over to Satan, putting him outside the church, so that his sinful nature may be destroyed and he may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Paul uses a Passover picture. Just as Jewish households swept every scrap of yeast out of the house before the feast, the church must get rid of the old yeast of sin, because Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. Then he corrects a misunderstanding of an earlier letter. He never meant them to avoid all contact with immoral people in the world, which would mean leaving the world altogether. He meant that they must not share fellowship with someone who claims to be a believer but persists in serious sin. God judges outsiders; the church must judge those inside.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul has heard that there is sexual immorality in the church of a kind not even found among pagans: a man is living with his father’s wife. And instead of mourning and removing him, they are proud. Though absent in body, Paul is present in spirit and has already judged the man. When they gather in the name of the Lord Jesus, with Paul’s spirit and the Lord’s power present, they are to hand him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. Their boasting is wrong. Do they not know that a little yeast works through the whole batch of dough? They must clear out the old yeast so that they may be a new, unleavened batch, as in fact they are, for Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. So they should keep the festival, not with the old yeast of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.theology:
Church Discipline as a Gospel Act

The Reformed tradition has always identified church discipline as one of the marks of the true church (alongside Word and sacraments). Calvin’s Institutes IV.12 grounds discipline in the same logic Paul uses here: the holiness of the community is not a human achievement but a participation in the holiness of Christ who dwells in it. Excommunication is not the final word against the sinner but the penultimate word, designed to produce repentance. The church that refuses to discipline its members — in the name of grace, tolerance, or avoiding conflict — is, paradoxically, acting without grace: it is allowing the leavening of unrepentant sin to compromise the whole community and denying the sinner the painful mercy of confrontation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinthian pride in tolerating this relationship may reflect the influence of the “strong” in the community — those with social status and rhetorical sophistication who had reinterpreted gospel freedom as moral permissiveness. The man involved may have been a patron of the church, someone whose loss the community feared. Paul overrides all such calculations: the gospel has higher priorities than keeping wealthy members comfortable. Now: The contemporary church’s allergy to any form of discipline is well-documented and widely lamented. Churches afraid to confront unrepentant sin in their members have, ironically, become communities shaped more by the fear of conflict than by love for the sinner.

verseByVerse.quote: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife. And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is actually being reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind not even tolerated among pagans: a man is living with his father’s wife. And you are proud! Should you not rather have mourned, and removed the man who did this from among you?

His father’s wife. Probably his stepmother, not his own mother (Paul would have said so). The relationship was ongoing (“has”), perhaps marriage or cohabitation, possibly after the father’s death or divorce. The law forbade it: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife” (Leviticus 18:8; Deuteronomy 22:30). Roman law also prohibited marriage with a stepmother, and Roman writers such as Cicero spoke of such unions with horror.

Not even among pagans. A church in pagan Corinth had sunk below pagan standards.

Arrogant. Perhaps they took pride in their tolerance, or in a freedom that said what the body does does not matter (6:12–13). Perhaps the man was wealthy and influential, a patron the church did not want to offend.

Mourn. The right response to sin in the church is grief, as at a funeral.

On a Tuesday. When serious sin comes to light in your church, the first response should be tears, not gossip, and not pride in how accepting you are.
verseByVerse.note: “His father’s wife” probably means his stepmother. The law of Moses forbade it, and Roman law condemned it too.

verseByVerse.quote: For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For my part, though I am absent in body, I am present in spirit, and I have already passed judgement on the man who did this, as if I were present.

Present in spirit. Paul is with them in his concern and authority, as their apostle. Some think he means the Holy Spirit unites them across the distance.

Already judged. The facts were not in doubt (“it is actually reported”, v. 1). Paul does not need a long inquiry.

On a Tuesday. Discipline should never be hasty, but neither should obvious, public sin be left for years while the church debates.

verseByVerse.quote: you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you are gathered together in the name of the Lord Jesus, and my spirit is with you along with the power of our Lord Jesus, you are to hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

In assembly. Discipline is an act of the whole church gathered, not of one leader in private (Matthew 18:17).

Deliver to Satan. Put him out of the church, the realm where Christ rules, into the world, where Satan holds sway (2 Corinthians 4:4). Compare Hymenaeus and Alexander, “whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1:20).

The destruction of the flesh. Two main readings:

Physical suffering or even death, as with Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5) or the sick at the Lord’s Table (11:30).

The destruction of his sinful nature, the “flesh” in Paul’s moral sense: the shock of exclusion leading him to repentance.

Verdict: the second fits better with the goal, “that his spirit may be saved”. The purpose of excommunication is restoration, not revenge. Some believe this man is the one forgiven in 2 Corinthians 2:5–11, though that is uncertain.

A textual note. Manuscripts vary between “the day of the Lord”, “the day of the Lord Jesus” and “the day of our Lord Jesus Christ”. The shortest is probably original; the meaning is the same.

On a Tuesday. If your church has to exclude someone, keep praying for them, and keep the door open for their return.
verseByVerse.note: To “deliver to Satan” means to put the man out of the church into the world, where Satan rules, in the hope that he will repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little yeast works its way through the whole batch of dough? Clean out the old yeast so that you may be a new batch, without yeast, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.

Leaven. Ancient bread was raised with a piece of fermented dough from the previous batch. A small lump spread through the whole. Sin tolerated in one person affects the whole church (Galatians 5:9).

Passover. Before the feast of Passover and Unleavened Bread, Jewish households searched every corner by lamplight to remove every crumb of leaven (Exodus 12:15). Then the lamb was killed.

As you really are. In Christ they are already a new, unleavened batch. They must become what they are.

Christ our Passover. Jesus died at Passover time, as the true Passover lamb, whose blood shields God’s people from judgement (Exodus 12:13; John 1:29, “Behold, the Lamb of God”). The order matters: the lamb has already been sacrificed, so the leaven must go.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “Christ our passover is sacrificed for us”) add “for us”. The earliest lack it; it is a natural expansion.

On a Tuesday. Is there “old leaven” in your own life, a habit or sin you have tolerated? Remove it, because Christ died for you.
verseByVerse.note: Before Passover every Jewish household removed all leaven (yeast) from the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So let us keep the festival, not with the old yeast of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

The festival. The Christian life is a continual Passover celebration, rejoicing in redemption.

Malice and evil, sincerity and truth. The old life and the new. Sincerity (eilikrineia) is purity of motive, held up to the light (2 Corinthians 1:12).

For worship. At the Lord’s Supper, remember that you are celebrating the new Passover. Come with sincerity and truth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul clarifies what he wrote in an earlier letter about not associating with sexually immoral people. He did not mean people of this world who are immoral, greedy, swindlers or idolaters; to avoid them entirely they would have to leave the world. He meant that they must not associate with anyone who calls himself a brother or sister but lives in sexual sin or greed, worships idols, slanders, gets drunk or swindles, and they should not even eat with such a person. It is not Paul’s business to judge outsiders; God will judge them. But the church must judge those inside it, and, as the law says, expel the wicked person from among them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church’s Jurisdiction and God’s Jurisdiction

Paul’s distinction between inside and outside the community (v. 12–13) defines the scope of church discipline with precision. The church is not called to police the world; it is called to maintain the integrity of its own fellowship. “God judges those outside” — this is not indifference to the world’s sin but a recognition that the church is not the world’s court of law. The church’s mission to the world is evangelism, not judgment; its internal discipline is precisely what enables it to be a credible witness in the world it is trying to reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul had already written a previous letter (now lost) on this subject, and the Corinthians had misapplied it. Misapplied teaching on holiness tends in two directions: either becoming a withdrawal sect (refusing all contact with sinful unbelievers) or collapsing into permissiveness (refusing all internal accountability). The Corinthians had managed both: they read the earlier letter as a call to leave the world, and they were lax about discipline inside the church. Now: The same confusion persists: churches that are either socially withdrawn from the world (failing at evangelism) or internally undisciplined (failing at community). Paul’s answer is a third way: engaged with the world in love, honest with the community in accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people— not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In my letter I wrote to you not to associate with sexually immoral people. I did not at all mean the immoral people of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters. In that case you would have to leave the world altogether.

An earlier letter. Paul wrote to Corinth before 1 Corinthians, and that letter has not survived. The Corinthians misunderstood it, or chose to.

Not withdrawal from the world. Christians must live among unbelievers, work with them, be their neighbours and friends. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (Mark 2:15–17).

What it does not mean. Not a call to Christian separatism, isolating believers from society. Monastic withdrawal and closed sects have sometimes misread separation that way.

On a Tuesday. If all your friends are Christians, you may have misunderstood this verse in the opposite direction. Who are your non-Christian friends?
verseByVerse.note: The earlier letter Paul mentions has not survived.

verseByVerse.quote: But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now I am writing to tell you not to associate with anyone who calls himself a brother or sister but is sexually immoral, or greedy, or an idolater, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a swindler. Do not even eat with such a person.

Bears the name. Someone who claims to be a Christian. The church’s concern is the conduct of its own members.

Six sins. Sexual immorality, greed, idolatry, abusive speech, drunkenness, swindling. Greed and slander sit alongside sexual sin; churches often treat them more lightly.

Not even eat. In the ancient world, sharing a meal meant fellowship and acceptance. This probably includes, but is not limited to, the Lord’s Supper.

How far should this go? Some groups (for example strict Amish communities, or Jehovah’s Witnesses) practise shunning so severe that family members cut off all contact. Others ignore church discipline entirely. Verdict: Paul means persistent, unrepentant sin by a professing believer, dealt with by the church after warning (Matthew 18:15–17). Exclusion from church fellowship does not cancel family duties: a believing wife still lives with her husband, a son still honours his father. And the aim is always restoration: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother” (2 Thessalonians 3:15).

On a Tuesday. If a Christian friend is persistently living in serious sin, love them enough to speak to them privately first.

verseByVerse.quote: For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
What business of mine is it to judge outsiders? Are you not to judge those inside the church? God will judge those outside. “Expel the wicked person from among you.”

Inside and outside. The church does not police the morals of society. Its discipline applies to its members. God will judge the world.

Purge the evil. A formula repeated in Deuteronomy, where Israel was told to deal with serious offenders: “So you shall purge the evil from your midst” (Deuteronomy 17:7; 22:21–24). Israel did it by execution; the church does it by excommunication. The holiness of God’s people is at stake.

On a Tuesday. Christians often reverse Paul’s order: condemning the world’s sins loudly and ignoring their own. Start with the church, and with yourself.

For worship. Thank God that Christ our Passover was sacrificed so that his church can be holy. Pray for your church’s purity.

parallels.desc: so you shall purge the evil from your midst
