6.title: Lawsuits, Liberty, and the Temple of the Spirit
6.overview:
Two more problems show the Corinthians living by the standards of their city rather than of Christ. First, church members were suing each other in the public courts. In Roman Corinth, civil litigation was a contest of status: the wealthy and well connected usually won, and lawsuits were a way to humiliate rivals. Paul is appalled that believers, who will one day judge the world and even angels, cannot settle disputes among themselves, and that they would rather drag one another before unbelieving judges than suffer wrong. He reminds them that the unrighteous, including thieves and swindlers, will not inherit God’s kingdom, and that some of them used to be exactly that, before they were washed, made holy and justified in Christ by the Spirit.

Second, some were using slogans like “all things are lawful for me” and “food for the stomach and the stomach for food” to justify sleeping with prostitutes, as if what the body does did not matter to the soul. Paul answers that the body belongs to the Lord and will be raised. A believer’s body is a member of Christ, and union with a prostitute makes the two one flesh. So they must run from sexual immorality. Their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit; they are not their own; they were bought at a price, and must honour God with their bodies.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul is shocked that when a believer has a dispute with another, he dares to take it before unbelieving judges instead of before God’s people. Do they not know that the saints will judge the world, and even angels? Then surely they are competent to settle everyday matters. Why appoint as judges those whom the church has no reason to respect? Is there really no one wise enough among them to decide between brothers, so that brother sues brother in front of unbelievers? The very fact that they have lawsuits against each other is already a defeat. Why not rather be wronged or cheated? Instead they themselves wrong and cheat, and they do it to their own brothers and sisters.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Saints Will Judge the World: Present Implications

Paul’s argument from eschatology — “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (v. 2) — is a characteristic move: the future reality of the believer’s status shapes present behaviour. The saints who will participate in Christ’s eschatological judgment (Dan 7:22; Rev 20:4) have already, in their union with Christ, been granted a dignity that makes recourse to pagan courts for petty disputes absurd. The inconsistency Paul exposes is not merely practical but theological: why would those destined for cosmic judicial authority submit their neighbourhood disputes to judges who do not acknowledge Christ?
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman legal culture in Corinth was a social arena where disputes were used to assert status and damage opponents. Going to court was not merely a legal act but a social strategy. Paul refuses the framework: the cross creates a community in which the willingness to absorb loss is a greater display of power than the ability to win in court. Now: The Christian instinct to reach for legal remedies when wronged by a fellow believer is understandable but reveals how deeply the world’s categories of justice and self-protection have shaped us. Paul’s question — “Why not rather suffer wrong?” — is among the most countercultural sentences in the NT.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If any of you has a dispute with another believer, how dare you take it to be judged by unbelievers instead of by God’s people? Do you not know that God’s people will judge the world? And if you are going to judge the world, are you not capable of judging trivial cases?

The courts. In Roman Corinth civil cases were heard in public by magistrates or juries drawn from the elite. Justice favoured the rich and powerful; bribery and influence were common. Lawsuits were a way to climb the social ladder or humiliate a rival. Probably wealthy church members were suing poorer ones.

The unrighteous. Not that pagan judges were necessarily corrupt, but that they did not belong to God’s righteous people.

The saints will judge the world. Believers will share in Christ’s judgement at the end. Daniel saw that “judgment was given for the saints of the Most High” (Daniel 7:22). Jesus told the twelve they would sit “on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

On a Tuesday. When you have a grievance against a fellow Christian, your first step should be to go to them privately (Matthew 18:15), then involve wise people in the church, not lawyers.
verseByVerse.note: Roman civil courts were public, costly and often corrupt; lawsuits were a way for the powerful to win status.

parallels.desc: judgment was given for the saints of the Most High

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that we will judge angels? How much more, then, the matters of this life!

Judge angels. Probably the fallen angels, condemned at the last judgement (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). Believers will share in Christ’s verdict on them.

Everyday matters. Property, money, contracts, the stuff of lawsuits. If we will judge angels, we can handle a business dispute.

On a Tuesday. Keep your disputes in perspective. A quarrel over a fence or an invoice is small beside your eternal calling.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers, but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?
verseByVerse.commentary:
So if you have disputes about everyday matters, why do you appoint as judges people who have no standing in the church? I say this to shame you. Is there really no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between believers? Instead, one brother takes another to court, and in front of unbelievers!

No standing. Pagan judges, whose values the church does not share.

To your shame. The church that boasted of its wisdom (1:5; 3:18) could not find one wise person to arbitrate.

Before unbelievers. Public lawsuits between Christians shame the gospel. The watching world sees believers fighting over money.

Can Christians ever go to court? Paul is addressing civil disputes between believers. He is not forbidding all use of the courts. Paul himself appealed to Roman justice: “I appeal to Caesar” (Acts 25:11). And crimes, such as abuse, assault or fraud, must be reported to the civil authorities, whom God has appointed to punish wrongdoers (Romans 13:1–4). Verdict: for disputes between believers, Christians should seek reconciliation and, if needed, Christian arbitration or mediation. For crimes, especially against the vulnerable, the church must never use this verse to keep matters from the police. (See the study on Christians in business, chapter 7.)

On a Tuesday. If you are in a dispute with a Christian business partner or relative, look for a Christian mediator before you go to court.

parallels.desc: able men to judge the people

verseByVerse.quote: To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The very fact that you have lawsuits against each other means you have already been defeated. Why not rather accept being wronged? Why not rather be cheated? Instead, you yourselves do wrong and cheat, and you do it to your own brothers and sisters.

Already a defeat. Whoever wins the case, the church has lost.

Suffer wrong. Jesus: “Do not resist the one who is evil” (Matthew 5:39). Better to lose money than to lose a brother and dishonour Christ.

You do wrong. The plaintiffs were not innocent victims. Some were exploiting others.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must never stand up for justice for others, or let abusers continue. Accepting wrong done to oneself is different from tolerating wrong done to the vulnerable.

On a Tuesday. Is there a debt or wrong done to you by a fellow believer that you could simply write off for Christ’s sake? Consider it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–11 — The Unrighteous Will Not Inherit the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to be deceived: the unrighteous will not inherit God’s kingdom. Those who live in sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery or homosexual practice, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, slanderers and swindlers will not inherit it. Some of the Corinthians had lived exactly like that. But they were washed, set apart as holy and declared righteous in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification, Sanctification, and the New Identity

The triad of v. 11 — washed, sanctified, justified — covers the full scope of soteric transformation. Reformed theology typically orders justification before sanctification logically; Paul here places sanctification before justification in the list, which suggests he is not giving a logical order but a rhetorical one: moving from the most experientially tangible (washing, cleansing from the pollution of past sin) to the most legally decisive (justification, right standing before God). All three are accomplished “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” — trinitarian to the root.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in vv. 9–10 describes the Corinthian street — not foreign or distant behaviour but the lives many of the congregation had lived and from which the gospel had extracted them. Paul is not writing to people who need to be warned away from exotic sins; he is reminding them of who they used to be, so they understand what they now are. Now: The church in every generation contains people whose past is on the list in vv. 9–10. The three words of v. 11 — washed, sanctified, justified — are the most liberating words any of them will ever hear about that past. It was real; the transformation is realer.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that wrongdoers will not inherit God’s kingdom? Do not be deceived. Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who have sex with men, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.

Do not be deceived. The Corinthians thought that because they were spiritual, behaviour did not matter. Paul says it does.

Ten kinds of wrongdoing. A typical list (compare Galatians 5:19–21). Sexual sins (immorality, adultery, homosexual practice), religious sin (idolatry), and sins of money and the tongue (theft, greed, drunkenness, slander, swindling). Notice that the greedy and the slanderers stand beside the sexually immoral. No one can point the finger.

The two words. Malakoi (literally “soft ones”), used of the passive partner in male same-sex relations, and arsenokoitai, a compound of “male” and “bed” that seems to come from the Greek of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, which forbid a man lying with a male. The ESV joins them as “men who practice homosexuality”.

Christians differ here. Some modern interpreters argue that Paul meant only exploitative forms such as pederasty, prostitution or master-slave abuse, not committed same-sex partnerships, which they say were unknown to him. The historic view of the whole church, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, is that these words refer to same-sex sexual activity as such. Verdict: the historic view is right. Arsenokoitai echoes Leviticus, which forbids the act itself, not only abusive forms; Paul elsewhere grounds his teaching in creation, male and female (Romans 1:26–27; Genesis 1:27; 2:24); and committed same-sex relationships were known in the ancient world.

Said with care. Paul describes ongoing practice, not temptation. A believer who experiences same-sex attraction and resists it is in the same position as any Christian fighting temptation. And verse 11 follows at once: “such were some of you”. The church must be a place where people of every past, and every present struggle, find both truth and welcome.

On a Tuesday. Look down the list for your own sin before you look for anyone else’s. Greed and slander are as likely in church as anywhere.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the two Greek terms behind “men who practice homosexuality” refer to the passive and active partners in homosexual acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were made holy, you were declared righteous in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.

Such were some of you. The Corinthian church included former idolaters, thieves, drunkards, the sexually immoral and those who had practised homosexuality. The gospel had changed them. Past tense: “were”.

Three verbs. All passive, all God’s action, all decisive:

Washed: cleansed from sin. Many link this to baptism (Acts 22:16), the outward sign; the reality is the Spirit’s cleansing: “the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).

Sanctified: set apart as God’s holy people (1:2).

Justified: declared righteous before God (Romans 5:1).

The order. Sanctified is listed before justified, but Paul is not giving a sequence. All three happen in union with Christ. Elsewhere, justification is the ground on which sanctification grows.

The Trinity. The name of the Lord Jesus, the Spirit, our God. The whole Trinity works in salvation.

On a Tuesday. If you are haunted by your past, read this verse aloud. “Such were” you. Now you are washed.

For worship. Thank God by name for each of the three verbs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–20 — Flee Sexual Immorality: The Body as Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul takes up slogans the Corinthians were using. “Everything is permitted for me”, they said; yes, but not everything is helpful, and Paul will not be mastered by anything. “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food”, they said, meaning that the body’s appetites, including sex, do not matter; God will do away with both. But the body is not meant for sexual immorality. It is meant for the Lord, and the Lord for the body, and God, who raised the Lord, will raise us too. Believers’ bodies are members of Christ; should they unite them with a prostitute? Never. Whoever joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her, for Scripture says the two become one flesh, but whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him. So they must flee sexual immorality. Other sins are outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Their body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, who lives in them, given by God. They do not belong to themselves; they were bought at a price, so they must honour God with their bodies.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection and the Significance of the Body

Paul’s argument for sexual ethics is grounded in resurrection theology: “God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power” (v. 14). The body is not a temporary shell to be discarded but the vehicle of the self that God will raise — the same body, transformed. This is why what we do with the body matters eternally. The body-soul dualism that dismisses bodily sins as theologically insignificant — a common Gnostic error in the ancient world — is precisely what Paul is refuting. The resurrection of the body is the theological foundation of a robust, embodied Christian ethics.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Visiting a prostitute in Corinth was a normal feature of social life — not perceived as transgression but as participation in the city’s religious and social fabric. The Corinthian with a “strong” theology might have regarded it as religiously meaningless (the idol is nothing) and biologically natural. Paul’s counter-argument changes the frame entirely: it is not religiously meaningless because the Holy Spirit inhabits the believer’s body; the body is not yours to give away because it was bought with a price. Now: The sexual ethics of any age are shaped by whatever account it gives of the body. Paul’s account — the body as Spirit-indwelt, resurrection-destined, cross-purchased — is the most exalted account of human physicality in any worldview.

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I am allowed to do anything,” you say. But not everything is good for you. “I am allowed to do anything.” But I will not let anything master me.

A slogan. Probably a Corinthian catchphrase, perhaps twisting Paul’s own teaching on freedom from the law. Paul quotes it and corrects it twice.

Not helpful. Freedom must be guided by what builds up (10:23).

Not dominated. A play on words in Greek: “all things are in my power (exestin), but I will not be overpowered (exousiasthēsomai) by anything”. So-called freedom can become slavery: to sex, drink, food, screens.

On a Tuesday. Ask of any habit not only “Is it allowed?” but “Is it good for me?” and “Does it control me?”
verseByVerse.note: The words in quotation marks are probably slogans used at Corinth, which Paul quotes and then corrects.

verseByVerse.quote: “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”—and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will do away with both,” you say. But the body is not meant for sexual immorality. It is meant for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.

Another slogan. The Corinthians argued that sex is like eating: a natural appetite of the body, morally neutral, and the body will perish anyway. Many Greeks thought the body unimportant compared with the soul.

Paul’s answer. Food and stomach will pass away. But the body is not like the stomach: it is for the Lord, and will be raised (v. 14). What we do with our bodies matters to God.

On a Tuesday. Our culture says sex is just a physical appetite. The Bible says your body belongs to the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God raised the Lord from the dead, and he will raise us also by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are parts of Christ’s body? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!

Resurrection. The body has a future. That is why it matters now.

Members of Christ. Not only the church as a whole but each believer’s physical body belongs to Christ.

Prostitutes. Prostitution was common and legal in Corinth, often linked with banquets and, in Greek tradition, with temples. The ancient geographer Strabo claimed the temple of Aphrodite on the Acrocorinth once had a thousand temple prostitutes, though that referred to old Greek Corinth before 146 BC and may be exaggerated. Either way, Roman Corinth had a reputation for sexual licence.

Never! Mē genoito: Paul’s strongest denial.

A textual note. Manuscripts vary on whether God “will raise”, “raises” or “raised” us. “Will raise” is best attested and fits the future resurrection.

On a Tuesday. When tempted, picture whose body you are using.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know that anyone who unites himself with a prostitute becomes one body with her? For Scripture says, “The two will become one flesh.” But whoever is united with the Lord is one spirit with him.

One flesh. Genesis 2:24, God’s design for marriage. Paul says sex creates a real union even outside marriage. It is never “just physical”.

One spirit with the Lord. The believer’s union with Christ is deeper still. To join yourself to a prostitute contradicts your union with Christ.

On a Tuesday. Sex is not casual because God made it to bind two people together for life. Treat it with that seriousness, and with gratitude in marriage.

parallels.desc: they shall become one flesh

verseByVerse.quote: Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Run from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.

Flee. Do not argue with it or manage it. Run, like Joseph, who “left his garment in her hand and fled” (Genesis 39:12).

Against his own body. What does Paul mean? Other sins also involve the body (drunkenness, gluttony). Possibly another Corinthian slogan: “every sin is outside the body”, which Paul rejects. Or: sexual sin uniquely gives the body to another in a union meant only for marriage, damaging the person himself. “He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself” (Proverbs 6:32).

On a Tuesday. Practical flight: install filters, avoid being alone with someone you are attracted to, tell a friend, get out of the situation. Do not trust your willpower.

parallels.desc: Joseph fled

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who lives in you, whom you received from God? You do not belong to yourselves, for you were bought at a price. So honour God with your bodies.

Temple. In 3:16 the church is the temple; here, each believer’s body. The Spirit lives in you as God’s glory filled the temple.

Not your own. The opposite of the modern slogan “my body, my choice”.

Bought with a price. The language of the slave market. A slave was bought and belonged to his new master. We were redeemed “with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19).

Glorify God in your body. In sexual purity, but also in how we eat, rest, work and care for our health. The body is a place of worship.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “and in your spirit, which are God’s”. The earliest end with “in your body”. The addition softens Paul’s focus on the body.

For worship. The Heidelberg Catechism begins: “That I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, in life and in death, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ.” Pray it this week.
verseByVerse.note: “Bought with a price” uses the language of the slave market.

7.title: Marriage, Celibacy, and the Calling of God
7.overview:
From chapter 7 Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. The first concerns sex and marriage. Some in Corinth had swung to the opposite extreme from the immorality of chapter 6: they said it was better for a man not to touch a woman at all, even in marriage, and perhaps that believers should divorce unbelieving spouses or not marry. Roman society, by contrast, pressed people to marry: the emperor Augustus had passed laws penalising the unmarried. Paul steers between both pressures.

Married couples should not deny each other sexually, except briefly by agreement for prayer. Singleness is good and Paul himself prefers it, but it is a gift, and those without it should marry. Believers should not divorce, as Jesus taught; a believer married to an unbeliever should stay if the unbeliever is willing, but is not bound if the unbeliever leaves. In general, each person should serve God in the situation in which he was called, whether circumcised or not, slave or free, though a slave who can gain freedom should take it. Because the time is short and the world in its present form is passing away, and because of a present crisis, Paul advises the unmarried to consider staying single, so as to serve the Lord without divided concerns. But marriage is no sin, and a widow may remarry, only to a believer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the questions in their letter, beginning with the claim that it is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman. Because sexual immorality is a real danger, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Husband and wife owe each other sexual intimacy; neither has sole rights over their own body, for each belongs to the other. They should not deprive each other except by mutual agreement for a limited time of prayer, and then come together again, so that Satan does not exploit their lack of self-control. Paul says this as a concession, not a command. He wishes everyone could be single as he is, but each person has his own gift from God. To the unmarried and widows he says it is good to stay single as he does, but if they cannot control themselves they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn with desire.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Goodness of Marriage and the Gift of Celibacy

Reformed theology has always resisted the Catholic elevation of celibacy above marriage as the spiritually superior state. The Reformers read 1 Corinthians 7 as affirming both callings as genuine gifts of God, neither intrinsically superior. Luther’s own marriage was a theological act — a public demonstration that marriage is not a second-class spiritual status. Paul’s careful handling of both callings in vv. 7–9 supports this reading: celibacy is a charisma, a grace-gift, as is marriage. Neither is commanded; both are honoured.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian ascetics who were advocating celibacy within marriage may have been influenced by the same Gnostic-adjacent body-negativity that produced the “food for the stomach” argument in chapter 6 — but in the opposite direction: if the body is spiritually inferior, why give it what it desires? Paul’s answer refuses both the libertine and the ascetic extremes. Now: The Christian tradition has tended to err in one direction or the other in every generation: either treating sexuality as a dangerous force to be suppressed, or (more recently) treating it as a sovereign identity that cannot be questioned. Paul’s account makes it neither: a good gift, shaped by covenant obligation, eschatologically relativised.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now about the things you wrote to me. “It is good for a man not to touch a woman,” you say. But because there is so much sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.

Their letter. “Now concerning” introduces each of their questions (7:1, 25; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1, 12).

A slogan. The ESV puts the words in quotation marks as the Corinthians’ own view. Some ascetic believers apparently held that sex, even in marriage, was unspiritual.

Paul’s answer. Marriage, with its sexual union, is God’s good gift and a protection against immorality. “It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18).

Is celibacy holier? Through much of church history celibacy was regarded as a higher calling, and Roman Catholic teaching still requires it of most priests. The Reformers rejected this: “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4); Paul warns against those “who forbid marriage” (1 Timothy 4:3). Verdict: marriage and singleness are both honourable callings; neither is holier in itself, and church leaders may marry (9:5; 1 Timothy 3:2).

What it does not mean. Not that marriage is merely a remedy for lust. Paul is answering a specific question. Elsewhere he describes marriage as a picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:22–33).

On a Tuesday. If you are married, thank God for your spouse, body and soul. If single, thank God that your life is no less holy.
verseByVerse.note: From here Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. The ESV notes that “to have sexual relations” is literally “to touch.” The quoted saying was probably a slogan of some at Corinth.

parallels.desc: it is not good that the man should be alone

verseByVerse.quote: The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The husband should give his wife what is due to her as a wife, and the wife likewise to her husband. For the wife does not have sole authority over her own body; her husband shares it. In the same way the husband does not have sole authority over his own body; his wife shares it.

Mutuality. Remarkable for its time. In the Roman world a husband’s rights over his wife were taken for granted; few writers spoke of the wife’s rights over the husband. Paul makes the obligations exactly equal.

What it does not mean. This verse can never justify forcing a spouse. It describes self-giving, not demanding. Love “does not insist on its own way” (13:5).

A textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the KJV (“render unto the wife due benevolence”), have “the goodwill that is owed”; the earliest read “what is owed”. The meaning is the same.

On a Tuesday. Married couples: ask not “What am I getting?” but “What do I owe my spouse?” in love, kindness and intimacy.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not deprive each other, except perhaps by mutual agreement for a set time, so that you can give yourselves to prayer. Then come together again, so that Satan does not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

Three conditions. Abstinence in marriage must be by agreement, for a limited time, and for prayer.

Satan. He exploits prolonged denial.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (KJV “to fasting and prayer”) add “fasting and”. The earliest have only “prayer”.

On a Tuesday. Spiritual zeal that neglects your spouse is not spirituality. Talk with your spouse about how you serve God together.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say this as a concession, not as a command. I wish everyone were as I am. But each person has his own gift from God: one has this gift, another has that.

A concession. Probably referring to the permission to abstain briefly (v. 5), or to marriage itself as allowed rather than commanded.

As I am. Unmarried, at least at this time. Paul may have been a widower; as a Pharisee and member of the council he would probably have been married (Acts 26:10), but we do not know.

A gift. Charisma. Singleness is a gift for some; marriage is a gift for others. Jesus spoke of those who “have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12).

On a Tuesday. If you are single, your singleness may be a gift for a season or for life. Use it for the Lord. And churches: do not treat single people as incomplete.

verseByVerse.quote: To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the unmarried and to widows I say: it is good for them to stay unmarried, as I am. But if they cannot control themselves, they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn with passion.

Countercultural. Augustus’s marriage laws penalised Roman citizens who did not marry or remarry. Paul says singleness is good.

To burn. With sexual desire, not in hell.

On a Tuesday. If you are single and struggling with desire, marriage is a good and right desire. Pray for a godly spouse and seek one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To married believers Paul passes on the Lord’s own command: a wife should not separate from her husband, and if she does she must remain unmarried or be reconciled; and a husband must not divorce his wife. To others, in cases Jesus did not address, Paul gives his own apostolic instruction. A believer married to an unbeliever who is willing to stay should not divorce. The unbelieving spouse is made holy through the believer, and so are their children. But if the unbeliever leaves, let it be so; the believer is not bound in such cases, for God has called us to peace. And who knows whether the believer may yet save the unbelieving spouse?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Command and Apostolic Judgment

Paul’s careful distinction in vv. 10 and 12 (“not I, but the Lord” vs. “I, not the Lord”) is a fascinating window into apostolic hermeneutics. It does not mean that vv. 12–16 are less authoritative Scripture — Paul is writing under inspiration. It means that vv. 10–11 apply a dominical teaching directly, while vv. 12–16 extend the principle to a situation Jesus did not address. Both are authoritative; they are transparent about their different relationship to the dominical tradition.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Divorce was common and easy in the Roman world, and Corinth’s fluid social culture made marriage instability familiar. The question of what to do in a mixed marriage — especially if the unbeliever wanted out — was live and urgent for many in the community. Now: The “Pauline privilege” continues to be one of the most practically significant and debated passages in NT ethics, applied to situations ranging from desertion to abuse. The governing principle — God has called you to peace — is a pastoral starting point, not a blank cheque.

verseByVerse.quote: To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the married I give this command, not I but the Lord: a wife must not separate from her husband. But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife.

The Lord’s command. Jesus’ teaching: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (Mark 10:9).

Separate and divorce. In Roman law either partner could end a marriage simply by leaving; no court was needed. So “separate” here effectively means divorce.

Is divorce ever allowed? Christians hold three main views.

Never, or no remarriage while the spouse lives (Roman Catholic teaching, and some Protestants).

Divorce and remarriage permitted for adultery (Matthew 19:9, “except for sexual immorality”) and for desertion by an unbeliever (v. 15). This is the historic Reformed view (Westminster Confession 24.5–6).

Broader grounds, such as abuse or other serious breaches of the marriage covenant.

Verdict: the Reformed view, with this pastoral note. Many Reformed pastors today recognise that persistent abuse is a form of covenant-breaking akin to desertion. In every case, a person in danger should separate for safety at once, and involve the authorities and the church. Paul’s command here is for ordinary marriages, not a requirement to stay in harm’s way.

On a Tuesday. If your marriage is struggling, do not reach for divorce. Seek help early: a pastor, a Christian counsellor, honest friends. Reconciliation is Paul’s goal.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites Jesus’ own teaching on divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the rest I say, I and not the Lord: if any believer has a wife who is not a believer, and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her. And if a woman has a husband who is not a believer, and he is willing to live with her, she must not divorce him.

I, not the Lord. Not that Paul’s words are less inspired, but that Jesus did not address this situation during his ministry. Paul now speaks with apostolic authority (v. 40; 14:37).

Mixed marriages. When one partner converted, the marriage became “mixed”. Some Corinthians apparently thought the believer should leave. Paul says no.

On a Tuesday. If you became a Christian after marriage and your spouse has not, stay faithful and loving. Your marriage is still holy to God.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had not addressed marriages where one partner became a believer; Paul applies his authority as an apostle.

verseByVerse.quote: For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the unbelieving husband is made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy through her believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is they are holy.

Made holy. Not saved (v. 16 shows that), but set apart in a special relationship to God’s people. The believer is not defiled by the marriage; rather the unbelieving partner and the home come under the influence of God’s grace.

Your children are holy. Paedobaptists see here evidence that children of believers belong to the covenant and should be baptised. Credobaptists note that the unbelieving spouse is also called “holy”, yet no one would baptise him; so the holiness is not the status that baptism signifies. Verdict: the verse speaks of the privileged setting of a believer’s family, not of a right to baptism. Credobaptists and paedobaptists can agree that such children are richly blessed and should be raised in the faith.

On a Tuesday. Your faith matters for your family. Pray for your spouse and children, and let your home be a place where they see Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “Made holy” does not mean saved, but set within the sphere of God’s blessing through the believing partner.

verseByVerse.quote: But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if the unbelieving partner leaves, let them go. In such cases the believing brother or sister is not bound. God has called you to live in peace.

Not enslaved. The believer is free. Most Protestants, following the Reformers, take this to include freedom to remarry. Roman Catholic canon law has a similar provision, the “Pauline privilege”.

Peace. The believer should not fight to keep an unwilling partner, nor live in endless conflict.

A textual note. Manuscripts are divided between “God has called you” and “God has called us”. The meaning is unaffected.

On a Tuesday. If you have been deserted by an unbelieving spouse, you are not guilty, and you are not bound for life. Seek pastoral counsel about the future.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God has called us to peace.”

verseByVerse.quote: For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?

Two readings. Either a note of hope (“Perhaps you will win them, so stay”) or of realism (“You cannot be sure of winning them, so do not force them to stay”). Verdict: both fit Paul, but in context (after v. 15) the realistic reading is likely: do not cling to a departing spouse in the hope of converting them. Yet hope remains where the unbeliever stays: wives may win their husbands “without a word by the conduct of their wives” (1 Peter 3:1).

On a Tuesday. If your spouse is not a believer, pray for them daily and love them practically. Leave the outcome with God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Live as You Were Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul states a general rule he teaches in every church: each person should live the life the Lord assigned and in which God called him. If a man was circumcised when called, he should not try to undo it; if uncircumcised, he should not seek circumcision. Neither counts for anything; what counts is keeping God’s commands. Each should remain in the situation in which he was called. A slave who was called should not let it trouble him, though if he can gain his freedom he should take it. For a slave called by the Lord is the Lord’s freed person, and a free person called is Christ’s slave. They were bought at a price, so they must not become slaves of human beings. Each should remain with God in the condition in which he was called.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Relativisation of Social Status by the Gospel

Paul’s refrain — remain as you are — is not social conservatism but theological prioritisation. The gospel relativises every earthly status by subjecting it to a higher identity: in Christ. This does not mean social structures are indifferent (Paul does not say slavery is good), but that the gospel’s transformative work operates from the inside out, transforming the meaning of every condition before changing the condition itself. This is the seed from which the ultimate abolition of slavery grew in Christian history: not immediate political revolution but the recognition that the slave is Christ’s freedman, which eventually made the institution of slavery theologically intolerable.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: First-century Christianity attracted people across the entire social spectrum, from Lydia the merchant to Onesimus the slave. The question of whether conversion required a change of social status was real and practically urgent. Paul’s answer guards against two errors: treating social change as spiritually necessary (legalism applied to status), and treating social change as spiritually forbidden (quietism about injustice). Now: The principle “remain as you are” guards against the modern Christian anxiety that effectiveness for God requires a different job, a different social location, a different cultural context. You were placed where you are by Providence; bloom there.

verseByVerse.quote: Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches. Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, each person should live the life the Lord has assigned to them, the life to which God called them. This is the rule I lay down in all the churches. Was someone already circumcised when he was called? He should not try to undo it. Was someone uncircumcised when called? He should not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. What matters is keeping God’s commands.

The principle. Becoming a Christian does not require changing your social position, marriage, ethnicity or job (unless it is sinful). You can serve God where you are.

Undoing circumcision. Some Jews who wanted to fit into Greek society, where men exercised naked in the gymnasium, had surgery to disguise their circumcision. The Jewish books of Maccabees mention it with horror. Paul says a Jewish believer should not hide his Jewishness, nor a Gentile become Jewish.

Keeping the commandments. Not the ceremonial law, which Paul has just set aside, but God’s moral will. Faith that works through love (Galatians 5:6).

On a Tuesday. You do not need a “Christian job” to serve God. A plumber, a nurse, an accountant or a homemaker can honour God where they were called.
verseByVerse.note: Some Jews under Greek influence had surgery to hide their circumcision.

verseByVerse.quote: Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each person should remain in the situation they were in when God called them. Were you a slave when you were called? Do not let it trouble you. But if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity.

Slavery in Corinth. Perhaps a third of the population of Roman cities were slaves, and many others were freed slaves. Roman slavery was not based on race; slaves could be educated, run businesses, and often bought their freedom with savings or were freed by their owners (manumission). Corinth itself had been resettled largely by freedmen.

Take freedom, or stay as you are? The Greek of the last sentence is ambiguous. It can mean “if you can become free, use that opportunity” or “even if you can become free, make use of your present condition instead”. Verdict: the first is more likely. Paul says “do not become slaves of men” (v. 23), and in Philemon he hints that Onesimus should be freed. Paul does not endorse slavery; he lists “enslavers” among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). His point is that a slave’s standing before God is not affected by his legal status.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a hard work situation you cannot change, serve Christ there with dignity. If a better opportunity comes, you are free to take it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the second sentence can also be read “make use of your present condition instead.” Slaves could sometimes buy or be granted their freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men. So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For anyone who was a slave when called by the Lord is the Lord’s freed person. Likewise, anyone who was free when called is Christ’s slave. You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Friends, each of you should remain before God in the situation in which you were called.

A freedman of the Lord. A freed slave in Rome still owed loyalty to his former master, now his patron. The Christian slave is spiritually free, and Christ is his patron.

A slave of Christ. The free person now belongs to Christ.

Bought with a price. As in 6:20. Christ paid for you, so do not hand your conscience over to any human master.

With God. The key phrase: whatever your situation, you are “with God” in it.

On a Tuesday. Whether you are the boss or the junior, you are Christ’s. That frees the junior from despair and the boss from pride.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–40 — The Unmarried, the Betrothed, and the Widows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the question of those who have never married, Paul has no command from the Lord, but gives his judgement as one the Lord has made trustworthy. Because of the present crisis, he thinks it good for people to stay as they are. Those who are married should not seek to separate; those who are free should not look for a wife. But marrying is no sin, though married people will face hardship, and Paul wants to spare them. The time is short. From now on, married people should live without being absorbed in marriage, mourners as if not mourning, the joyful as if not rejoicing, buyers as if they owned nothing, users of the world as if not engrossed in it, because the world in its present form is passing away. Paul wants them free from anxiety. The unmarried can focus on the Lord’s affairs and how to please him; the married must also think about the world and how to please their spouse, so their interests are divided. He says this for their benefit, not to restrict them, but so that they may serve the Lord with undivided devotion. A man engaged to a woman may marry her if he feels he should; it is no sin. But one who has firmly decided not to marry does well too. Marriage is good, but staying single is better in present circumstances. A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives, but if he dies she is free to marry anyone she wishes, provided he belongs to the Lord. Paul thinks she will be happier if she stays as she is, and he believes he too has God’s Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Eschatological Relativisation and Christian Freedom

Paul’s “as if not” framework is one of the most pastorally liberating texts in the NT for the believer under pressure. It is not an ascetic refusal of the world’s goods but an insistence that no good and no loss in this age has the last word. Marriage, mourning, rejoicing, buying — all are real; none are final. The person who holds them “as if not” is not less engaged with life but more free in it, because their ultimate security is not invested in any of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s counsel to the betrothed (“do not seek a wife”, v. 27) and to the widow (“she is happier if she remains as she is”, v. 40) was given “in view of the present distress” — the compressed time between the first and second coming, with its attendant pressures. He is not issuing universal commands but pastorally calibrated counsel. Now: The eschatological urgency has not diminished — we are closer to the end than Paul’s Corinth was. The counsel to hold earthly goods and relationships lightly, in undivided devotion to the Lord, is not less relevant but more.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now about those who have never married: I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgement as someone who, by the Lord’s mercy, is trustworthy. I think that, because of the present crisis, it is good for a person to remain as they are.

Betrothed. Literally “virgins”: young unmarried people, probably engaged couples.

My judgment. Paul distinguishes a command of the Lord from his apostolic counsel. Both are inspired Scripture, but here he gives advice, not a rule.

The present distress. What was it?

A local crisis: there is evidence of severe grain shortages in Corinth around AD 51, when inscriptions honour a city official for supplying grain during famine.

Persecution, or the general pressure of the last days between Christ’s first and second comings (v. 29).

Verdict: possibly both. The advice is tied to a time of crisis, which is why it is not a permanent preference for singleness over marriage.

On a Tuesday. Christians facing war, persecution or hardship may wisely delay marriage. In ordinary times, marriage is a good path for most.
verseByVerse.note: The “present distress” may refer to famine, persecution or the pressures of the last days.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you married? Do not seek a divorce. Are you unmarried? Do not look for a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned; and if an unmarried woman marries, she has not sinned. Those who marry, however, will face many troubles in this life, and I want to spare you that.

Bound to a wife. Or engaged. Do not break the commitment.

Not sinned. Paul is emphatic. Marriage is not second-best spiritually.

Worldly troubles. Literally “trouble in the flesh”: the hardships of family life in a time of crisis, such as caring for children in famine or persecution.

On a Tuesday. If you are engaged or married, do not feel guilty for it. If single, do not feel pressured.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods, and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What I mean, friends, is this: the time has been shortened. From now on, those who have wives should live as if they had none; those who mourn as if they did not; those who rejoice as if they did not; those who buy as if they owned nothing; and those who use the things of the world as if not fully absorbed in them. For this world in its present form is passing away.

The time is short. Synestalmenos: compressed, like a sail being furled. Christ’s resurrection has started the last days; history is heading to its end.

As though not. Not that husbands should neglect wives (v. 3 forbids that), or that we should not grieve or rejoice. But none of these things is ultimate. Hold them loosely.

Passing away. Schēma: the outward form, like scenery in a play being changed. “The world is passing away along with its desires” (1 John 2:17).

On a Tuesday. Enjoy your marriage, your house, your hobbies. But do not let any of them become your god. They are scenery, not the play.

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I want you to be free from worries. An unmarried man is concerned about the Lord’s affairs, how he can please the Lord. But a married man is concerned about the affairs of this world, how he can please his wife.

Anxieties. Not sinful anxiety, but the legitimate cares of life.

Married men’s concerns. Paul assumes it is right for a husband to try to please his wife. It is a godly duty, but it divides attention.

On a Tuesday. If you are single, use the freedom you have for Christ’s work. If married, pleasing your spouse is part of pleasing the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his interests are divided. The unmarried woman, or the woman never married, is concerned about the Lord’s affairs, to be holy in body and spirit. But a married woman is concerned about the affairs of this world, how she can please her husband. I am saying this for your own good, not to put a restriction on you, but so that you may live in a right way, in undivided devotion to the Lord.

Divided. A married Christian has two good loyalties. A single Christian can give more time to ministry.

Holy in body and spirit. Devoted wholly to the Lord.

Not a noose. Literally “not to throw a lasso over you”. Paul is giving advice, not imposing rules.

On a Tuesday. Single women in church history, such as Amy Carmichael in India and Gladys Aylward in China, gave their lives to mission in ways a married life might not have allowed. Honour the single people in your church.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin. But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone thinks he is not acting properly towards the woman he is engaged to, if his passions are strong and he feels he ought to marry, he should do as he wishes. He is not sinning; they should marry. But if a man has settled the matter in his own mind, under no compulsion and with control over his own will, and has decided not to marry the woman, he too does the right thing. So the one who marries his fiancée does well, and the one who does not marry does even better.

Who is “anyone”? Three interpretations:

An engaged man deciding whether to marry his fiancée (ESV, most modern versions).

A father deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage (KJV and older versions; the verb in v. 38 can mean “give in marriage”).

A “spiritual marriage”, where a couple lived together without sex; there is evidence of this practice later in church history, but little for Paul’s day.

Verdict: the engaged man fits best, since “his passions are strong” describes the man himself. The point is the same either way: marriage is good, and so is a free, uncompelled choice of singleness.

On a Tuesday. If you are engaged and unsure, pray together, take advice, and do not drift. Either decision can honour God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “betrothed” is literally “virgin,” and that the passage can also be read of a father deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord.

Bound. Marriage is for life (Romans 7:2, “a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives”).

Free after death. Remarriage after a spouse’s death is entirely right. Some early Christians frowned on it; Paul does not.

Only in the Lord. To a fellow believer (2 Corinthians 6:14).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (KJV “bound by the law”) add “by the law”. The earliest lack it.

On a Tuesday. If you are a widow or widower considering remarriage, you are free. Choose a fellow believer, and seek wise counsel.
verseByVerse.note: “Only in the Lord” means to a fellow believer.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet in my opinion she is happier if she stays as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

Happier. Makariōtera: more blessed. Again, advice for a time of crisis.

I think I have the Spirit. Not uncertainty about his inspiration, but gentle irony towards the Corinthians who claimed to be spiritual (14:37). Paul has the Spirit too, more than they.

For worship. Whether married, widowed or single, thank God for your situation as a calling from him, and offer it back to him.
