This is my rule in all the churches.<sup>18</sup>Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision.<sup>19</sup>For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.<sup>20</sup>Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called.<sup>21</sup>Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)<sup>22</sup>For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ.<sup>23</sup>You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men.<sup>24</sup>So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.<sup>25</sup>Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy.<sup>26</sup>I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.<sup>27</sup>Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.<sup>28</sup>But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.<sup>29</sup>This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none,<sup>30</sup>and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods,<sup>31</sup>and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.<sup>32</sup>I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord.<sup>33</sup>But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,<sup>34</sup>and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband.<sup>35</sup>I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.<sup>36</sup>If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin.<sup>37</sup>But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well.<sup>38</sup>So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better.<sup>39</sup>A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.<sup>40</sup>Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

8.title: Knowledge, Idols, and Love for the Weak
8.overview:
The next question from the Corinthians’ letter is about food offered to idols. Some background makes it vivid. In a Greek or Roman city, most meat came from animals sacrificed at temples: part was burned for the god, part went to the priests, and much of the rest was eaten at banquets in the temple dining rooms or sold in the meat market (the macellum, whose inscription has been found in Corinth). Temples were also the restaurants and party venues of the city; papyrus invitations survive asking guests to dine “at the table of the lord Sarapis”. Excavations at Corinth’s temple of Asclepius found dining rooms with couches. For a Christian, refusing every such meal could mean cutting yourself off from trade guilds, family celebrations and civic life.

Some Corinthian believers, proud of their knowledge, argued that idols are nothing and there is only one God, so they could eat anywhere. Paul agrees with their theology, and gives one of the most important statements of Christian belief: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. But knowledge without love puffs people up. Not every believer has that confidence; some, long used to idols, still feel that eating such food is worship, and if they follow the example of the “strong” against their conscience, they are damaged. A believer for whom Christ died must not be ruined by another’s freedom. So Paul would rather never eat meat again than cause a brother to fall. (Chapter 10 will add that actually taking part in idol feasts is forbidden.)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On food sacrificed to idols, Paul quotes the Corinthians’ claim that “we all have knowledge”, and warns that knowledge inflates people, while love builds them up. Anyone who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he should; but whoever loves God is known by him. So, about eating such food: they say an idol is nothing in the world and there is no God but one. Paul agrees. Though there are many so-called gods and lords in heaven and on earth, for believers there is one God, the Father, from whom all things come and for whom we live, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things come and through whom we live.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Christological Shema and the One Lordship

The confessional statement of vv. 5–6 is a watershed in NT christology. Paul takes the foundational monotheistic confession of Israel — “the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deut 6:4) — and distributes it between the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. God the Father receives the title “one God” with the phrase “from whom are all things and for whom we exist”; Jesus Christ receives the title “one Lord” with the phrase “through whom are all things and through whom we exist.” Both titles draw on the divine prerogative of creation. This is not bitheism or subordinationism; it is the Shema expanded to include the Son within the identity of the one God of Israel — which is exactly what Nicaea later defended.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The “strong” at Corinth were the theologically sophisticated — probably a mix of those with a Jewish background (who knew the idol was nothing) and educated Gentiles who had absorbed the Stoic critique of popular religion. Their knowledge was real. Their pride was realer. Now: The Reformed tradition is not immune to the Corinthian disease of knowledge-pride. The person who has worked through the doctrines of grace and arrived at the Reformation’s conclusions is in real danger of making theological correctness a platform for contempt of those still confused. Paul’s question applies: have you been known by God? (v. 3). That is the only knowledge that ultimately matters.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now about food sacrificed to idols. We know that, as you say, “we all have knowledge.” But knowledge puffs up, while love builds up. Anyone who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know.

Idol food. Meat or other food offered in pagan worship. Christians met it in three places: at banquets in temples, in the market, and at friends’ dinner tables (10:25–28).

“We all have knowledge.” A Corinthian slogan. The “strong” claimed superior knowledge as the basis of their freedom.

Puffs up, builds up. Physioi and oikodomei. Knowledge alone inflates like a balloon; love builds like a house. Paul is not against knowledge, but knowledge used without love becomes pride.

Not yet known as he ought. True knowledge includes knowing how little we know, and how to use what we know in love.

A textual note. The earliest papyrus lacks some words in verses 2–3 (“anything” in v. 2, “God” and “by him” in v. 3), giving a shorter text: “if anyone loves, he is known”. Most scholars think the longer text, found in nearly all manuscripts, is original.

On a Tuesday. If you know more theology than others in your church, ask whether it has made you more loving or more superior.
verseByVerse.note: Much of the meat sold in the market had first been offered in a pagan temple; temples also had dining rooms used for banquets and celebrations. The quoted phrases are probably Corinthian slogans.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But anyone who loves God is known by God.

Known by God. The surprise: Paul does not say “knows God” but “is known by God”. What matters most is not our knowledge of God but his knowledge of us: his loving, choosing knowledge (Galatians 4:9, “now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God”; compare Amos 3:2).

For worship. Thank God that your security rests not on how much you know, but on his knowing and loving you.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.” For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, about eating food offered to idols: we know, as you say, that “an idol is nothing in the world” and that “there is no God but one.” For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”...

An idol is nothing. True: the gods represented by idols do not exist as gods. “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but do not speak” (Psalm 115:4–5).

No God but one. Israel’s confession, the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

So-called gods. Corinth had temples to Apollo, Aphrodite, Poseidon, Asclepius, Demeter, Isis and Sarapis, and the cult of the emperors, the “lords”.

What it does not mean. Not that idolatry is harmless. Paul will say in 10:20 that behind idols stand demons. The gods are not real, but the spiritual powers exploiting idol worship are.

On a Tuesday. Our culture has its own “gods” and “lords”: money, sex, career, celebrity, nation. They have no true divine power, but they can still enslave.

parallels.desc: the LORD our God, the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
...yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we live; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we live.

The Shema reworked. One of the most important verses in the New Testament. Paul takes Israel’s confession, “The LORD our God, the LORD is one”, and divides it: “God” is applied to the Father, and “Lord” (the Greek word for the divine name, YHWH) is applied to Jesus Christ. Jesus is included within the one God of Israel’s confession.

Creator. All things are “from” the Father and “through” the Son. Jesus is not part of creation; he is the agent of creation (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16, “all things were created through him and for him”).

Does this make Jesus less than God? Arians in the fourth century, and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, argue that “one God, the Father” means Jesus is not truly God. Verdict: the opposite. Paul places Jesus inside the Shema as the one Lord, and gives him the role of Creator that belongs to God alone. The church’s Nicene Creed (325, 381) echoes this verse: “one God, the Father Almighty … and one Lord, Jesus Christ … through whom all things were made.” Father and Son are distinct persons, one God.

Through whom we exist. Christ is not only creator but redeemer: we live through him.

For worship. Recite the Nicene Creed’s opening lines, and notice how they come from this verse.
verseByVerse.note: Paul expands Israel’s confession “the LORD is one” to include Jesus Christ as the one Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The Weak Brother and the Limits of Freedom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But not everyone has this knowledge. Some, used to idols until recently, still think of the food as offered to an idol when they eat it, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not bring us closer to God; we are no worse off if we do not eat and no better off if we do. But they must be careful that their freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak. If someone with a weak conscience sees a knowledgeable believer eating in an idol’s temple, he may be encouraged to eat idol food himself, and so the weak believer, a brother for whom Christ died, is destroyed by the other’s knowledge. Sinning against fellow believers in this way, wounding their weak consciences, is sinning against Christ. So if food makes a brother fall, Paul will never eat meat again, so as not to make him fall.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Weak Brother and the Limits of Christian Freedom

The category of “weak brother” in Paul is not a permanent spiritual classification but a pastoral description of someone whose conscience is not yet formed to the level of theological maturity the gospel makes possible. The strong are not forbidden to exercise their freedom; they are required to consider the effect of their freedom on those still developing. This is not a silencing of the theologically mature but a school in cruciform love: the pattern of Christ, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Cor 8:9), is the paradigm for the voluntary limitation of legitimate freedom in love for the weak.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific situation — food offered to idols in a pagan temple context — is culturally remote for most Western Christians. But the principle is not: the more mature members of any community regularly face the question of how to use their freedom in ways that do not damage those who are less free. Now: The contemporary applications range from alcohol (where an alcoholic is in the room) to entertainment choices (where a recovering addict might be triggered) to musical styles in worship (where real spiritual associations exist for some). The principle is constant: love for the weak sibling takes precedence over the exercise of genuine freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But not everyone has this knowledge. Some people are so used to idols that, even now, when they eat such food they think of it as offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not bring us near to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.

The weak. Recent converts from paganism, for whom idol food was bound up with their old religion. Eating it felt like worshipping again.

Defiled conscience. Not that the food defiles, but that acting against conscience does (Romans 14:23, “whatever does not proceed from faith is sin”).

Food does not commend us. Neither eating nor abstaining makes us more spiritual. Possibly another Corinthian slogan, which Paul accepts.

A textual note. Some later manuscripts (KJV “with conscience of the idol”) read “conscience” instead of “being accustomed”. The earliest read “through being accustomed to the idol”. The two Greek words look alike.

On a Tuesday. A former alcoholic may feel that any drink is a step back. A believer from a Hindu or Buddhist background may be troubled by eating food offered at a shrine. Be sensitive to such consciences.

verseByVerse.quote: But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But be careful that this freedom of yours does not become a stumbling block to the weak. For if someone with a weak conscience sees you, with all your knowledge, reclining at a meal in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols?

This right. Exousia: freedom, authority. The strong believed they had the right to eat. Paul does not deny it here, but limits it by love.

In an idol’s temple. The dining rooms of temples were used for weddings, birthdays and guild dinners. Couches were arranged around the walls, and diners reclined.

Encouraged. Literally “built up”, ironic: the strong think they are building up the weak by showing them freedom; in fact they are building them up to sin.

How do chapters 8 and 10 fit? In chapter 10 Paul forbids taking part in idol feasts altogether, because it means fellowship with demons (10:14–22). Some think the chapters conflict. Verdict: Paul argues in stages. Here he meets the strong on their own ground and shows that even if eating were harmless, love would forbid it. In chapter 10 he shows it is not harmless at all. Market meat eaten at home is a different matter (10:25–27).

On a Tuesday. Your freedom is real, but others are watching. Before using it, ask who might follow you into something they cannot handle.

verseByVerse.quote: And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So this weak believer is ruined by your knowledge, the brother or sister for whom Christ died. When you sin against your brothers and sisters in this way and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.

Destroyed. Apollytai: ruined, perishing. Strong language. The weak believer may be drawn back into idolatry and lose his way.

Can a true believer be lost? Arminian Christians see here proof that someone for whom Christ died can perish. Reformed Christians, who hold that Christ’s death secures the salvation of those for whom he died, read it as describing the real damage done to a believer’s faith and conscience, and as a warning that God uses to keep his people from apostasy (Romans 14:15). Verdict: the warning is real, and the strong are responsible for what they do; but Scripture elsewhere promises that God keeps those who are truly his (1:8–9; John 10:28). Paul is speaking of the tendency of the act, not of God’s final decree.

The brother for whom Christ died. The most powerful argument. Christ gave his life for this person; will you not give up a meal?

Against Christ. As Jesus said to Saul, “why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). To wound a believer is to wound Christ. “As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).

On a Tuesday. Before posting a mocking comment about a fellow believer’s scruples, remember Christ died for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother or sister to fall into sin, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not make them fall.

Paul’s resolve. He will give up any freedom, permanently if necessary, rather than harm another believer. “It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble” (Romans 14:21).

Who is the weaker brother? Not anyone who disapproves of something you do. The weak brother is someone who might be led to act against his own conscience by your example. Paul did not give way to legalists who wanted to impose rules on others (Galatians 2:3–5). Love limits freedom for the vulnerable, but does not surrender the gospel’s freedom to those who would bind consciences.

On a Tuesday. At a dinner with a friend who is struggling with alcohol, do not order wine. At home with your family, you are free.

For worship. Thank Christ, who gave up far more than meat for you.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up.<sup>2</sup>If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.<sup>3</sup>But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.<sup>4</sup>Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.”<sup>5</sup>For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—<sup>6</sup>yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.<sup>7</sup>However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.<sup>8</sup>Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.<sup>9</sup>But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.<sup>10</sup>For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?<sup>11</sup>And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died.<sup>12</sup>Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.

9.title: Rights Surrendered: The Apostle as Slave to All
9.overview:
Chapter 9 can look like a digression from idol food, but it is Paul’s example. He has just said he would give up meat rather than harm a brother. Now he shows that he lives that way. As an apostle he has every right to financial support: to food and drink, to bring a wife on his travels like Peter and the Lord’s brothers, and to be paid like a soldier, a farmer or a shepherd. The law of Moses says the same, the temple priests lived from the offerings, and Jesus himself commanded that preachers of the gospel should live by it. Yet Paul has used none of these rights in Corinth, because he would rather die than give anyone a reason to say he preached for money.

His freedom is spent in serving others. He has made himself everyone’s slave to win as many as possible: to Jews he lived as a Jew, to Gentiles as one outside the Mosaic law (though never outside God’s law, since he is under Christ’s law), to the weak as weak. He does it all for the gospel. Then Paul turns to the Isthmian Games, held every two years just outside Corinth. Athletes train with fierce self-control for a wreath that withers. Christians run for a crown that lasts, so Paul disciplines his body, lest after preaching to others he himself should be disqualified.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks whether he is not free, whether he is not an apostle who has seen Jesus the Lord, and whether the Corinthians themselves are not the result of his work in the Lord. Even if others doubt his apostleship, the Corinthian church is the seal that proves it. To his critics he offers this defence. He and Barnabas have the right to be fed, the right to take a believing wife with them like the other apostles, the Lord’s brothers and Peter, and the right not to work for a living. No soldier pays his own wages, no one plants a vineyard without eating its grapes, no shepherd goes without milk. The law of Moses says not to muzzle an ox while it threshes, and that was written for our sake, so that workers can expect a share of the harvest. If Paul has sown spiritual seed among them, it is not too much to reap material support. Others enjoy this right; Paul more so. Yet he has not used it, but puts up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ. Those who serve in the temple eat from its offerings, and in the same way the Lord has commanded that those who preach the gospel should get their living from it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Right of Ministers to Financial Support

Paul’s argument from Deuteronomy 25:4 (“You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain”) follows a characteristic pattern in his hermeneutics: the OT command for the benefit of animals carries an “how much more” application to human ministers of the gospel. The principle that the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7, quoted by Paul in 1 Tim 5:18) is embedded in the creation order and confirmed by the Lord’s own command. The Reformed tradition has always insisted on adequate financial support for ordained ministry as a matter of justice, not charity — grounded precisely in passages like this.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The travelling sophist in Corinth charged fees for his teaching; the apostle who did not was, paradoxically, suspected of being less legitimate — not worth paying. Paul’s refusal to accept payment actually undermined his status in the eyes of some Corinthians, which is why he defends the right even while refusing to exercise it. Now: The principle cuts in two directions: congregations should support their ministers generously; ministers should never let financial considerations drive their preaching agenda. The apostle who can preach without anxiety about whether his congregation will like what they hear is the freest preacher in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not the result of my work in the Lord? Even if others do not accept me as an apostle, surely you do, for you are the seal that proves my apostleship in the Lord.

Free. Linking back to chapter 8: Paul has freedom, as the strong claim to.

Seen the Lord. A requirement for apostleship: witness of the risen Christ (Acts 1:22, “a witness to his resurrection”; 15:8). Paul saw him on the Damascus road. This is one reason there are no apostles in this sense today.

The seal. A seal pressed in wax authenticated a document. The church at Corinth is Paul’s authentication.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) reverse the first two questions: “Am I not an apostle? am I not free?” The earliest begin with “free”, which fits the link with chapter 8.

On a Tuesday. The best evidence of a ministry is changed people.
verseByVerse.note: An apostle had to have seen the risen Lord. A seal authenticated a document.

verseByVerse.quote: This is my defense to those who would examine me. Do we not have the right to eat and drink?
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is my defence to those who sit in judgement on me. Do we not have the right to food and drink?

Defence. Apologia, a courtroom term. Some in Corinth questioned Paul’s apostleship because he did not take support, as a “real” apostle or philosopher would.

Eat and drink. At the church’s expense.

On a Tuesday. It is right for churches to provide for those who serve them.

verseByVerse.quote: Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do we not have the right to take a believing wife with us on our travels, as the other apostles do, and the Lord’s brothers, and Peter? Or is it only Barnabas and I who must work for a living?

A believing wife. The apostles were mostly married, and their wives travelled with them, supported by the churches. Peter was married: Jesus healed “Simon’s mother-in-law” (Mark 1:30).

Married ministers. This verse shows the apostles were not required to be celibate. Clerical celibacy developed later; the Reformers restored the freedom to marry.

The brothers of the Lord. James, Joses, Judas and Simon (Mark 6:3). Who were they?

Jesus’ half-brothers, sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus (the Helvidian view, held by most Protestants today).

Sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage (Epiphanius; the Orthodox view).

Cousins (Jerome; the Roman Catholic view, to preserve Mary’s perpetual virginity).

Verdict: the first is the most natural reading of “brothers” and of Matthew 1:25 (“knew her not until she had given birth”). But it should be held charitably: Luther, Calvin and many Reformers themselves believed in Mary’s perpetual virginity.

Barnabas. Paul’s partner on the first missionary journey (Acts 13–14), who also supported himself.

On a Tuesday. Pray for pastors’ and missionaries’ spouses, who carry much of the cost of ministry.
verseByVerse.note: Peter (Cephas) was married, and his wife travelled with him. The Lord’s brothers included James and Jude.

verseByVerse.quote: Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its grapes? Who looks after a flock and does not drink any of its milk?

Three pictures. Soldier, farmer, shepherd. Each expects to live from his work. Roman soldiers were paid a salary and given rations.

On a Tuesday. If your church pays its pastor poorly while expecting full-time service, these questions apply.

verseByVerse.quote: Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Am I saying this only from a human point of view? Does the law not say the same? For it is written in the law of Moses: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” Is it oxen God is concerned about? Or is he not speaking entirely for our sake? Yes, it was written for us, because the ploughman should plough in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing the harvest.

Deuteronomy 25:4. “You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain.” Oxen walked round the threshing floor, trampling the sheaves; the law let them eat as they worked.

Is God concerned for oxen? Of course he is (Psalm 104:14; Jonah 4:11). Paul is not denying it, but saying the law’s purpose reaches further: if even an ox may eat from its work, how much more a human worker.

Allegory? Some have taken Paul as allegorising, ignoring the literal sense. Verdict: he is drawing out the principle behind the law, arguing from the lesser to the greater, as Jewish teachers did. The surrounding laws in Deuteronomy 24–25 concern fair treatment of workers and the poor.

On a Tuesday. Old Testament laws that seem obscure often carry principles for today. Ask what the law shows about God’s character.
verseByVerse.note: Oxen threshing grain walked over it on the threshing floor; the law let them eat as they worked.

parallels.desc: you shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much to reap a material harvest from you? If others have this right of support from you, do we not have it even more? But we have not used this right. Instead, we put up with anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.

Spiritual and material. Spiritual gifts are worth more than money; supporting those who bring them is a small return (Romans 15:27; Galatians 6:6, “Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches”).

Others. Probably Apollos, Peter or the visiting teachers, who did accept support.

Endure anything. Paul accepted hardship, hunger and manual labour rather than give anyone an excuse to dismiss the gospel as a money-making scheme. Travelling teachers were often suspected of greed.

On a Tuesday. Is there a right you could give up, so that someone listens to the gospel?

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that those who work in the temple get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in what is offered on the altar? In the same way, the Lord has commanded that those who preach the gospel should get their living from the gospel.

The temple. In Israel the priests and Levites received portions of the sacrifices and the tithes (Numbers 18:8–31). Pagan priests did the same.

The Lord commanded. Jesus: “the laborer deserves his wages” (Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10). One of the few places Paul quotes a teaching of Jesus.

Paid ministry. Some movements (some Brethren groups, Quakers) have been wary of paid ministers. Verdict: Paul is clear that a paid ministry is the Lord’s command and right. He chose to forgo it in specific circumstances, but defends it as the norm.

On a Tuesday. Giving to support your pastor is not charity; it is obedience to the Lord.

parallels.desc: the priests’ portion

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Becoming All Things to All People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul has not used any of these rights, and he is not writing to get them now; he would rather die than let anyone empty his boast. Preaching itself gives him no ground for boasting, because he is under compulsion; woe to him if he does not preach. If he did it willingly he would have a reward; but since he is entrusted with it as a duty, his reward is this: to offer the gospel free of charge and not use his rights. Though free from everyone, he has made himself everyone’s slave to win more people. To Jews he became like a Jew, to those under the law like one under it (though not under it himself), to those without the law like one without it (though not free from God’s law, being bound by Christ’s law), to the weak he became weak. He has become all things to all people so that by every possible means he might save some, and he does it all for the gospel, so as to share in its blessings.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missional Identification and the Integrity of the Gospel

Paul’s “all things to all people” has been both one of the most misused and most important principles in Christian mission. Misused, it becomes a pretext for theological drift — adjusting the content of the gospel to make it more acceptable. Properly understood, it describes the willingness to adjust the container — cultural form, communicative register, social entry point — while keeping the content constant. Keller’s ministry in Manhattan was an extended application of this principle: enter the cultural world of the highly educated secular professional, learn to speak their language, earn the right to challenge their assumptions — and preach the same crucified Christ that Paul preached in Corinth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s concrete examples — becoming as a Jew, as under the law, as outside the law, as weak — map onto the social divisions within his own missionary world. He was not fixed in one cultural mode but radically adaptable in form while immovable in content. The Damascus road encounter made him a prisoner of the message; everything else was negotiable. Now: Contextualisation is the ongoing challenge of every missionary enterprise. The line between appropriate adaptation and compromising capitulation is real and requires constant discernment; but the failure to contextualise — treating one’s own cultural form of Christianity as the gospel itself — is at least as dangerous as over-adaptation.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have not used any of these rights, and I am not writing this in the hope that you will do these things for me. I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of this boast. For when I preach the gospel, I have nothing to boast about, since I am under compulsion to preach. How terrible for me if I do not preach the gospel!

Rather die. Paul’s refusal of support was not a minor preference but a matter of deep principle.

Necessity. Paul did not choose to be an apostle; Christ laid it on him (Acts 9:15–16; 26:16–18). Like Jeremiah, who said God’s word was “in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9).

Woe. Not fear of punishment, but the inner compulsion of a calling.

On a Tuesday. Is there something God has clearly called you to that you are avoiding? Paul’s “woe” is worth hearing.

parallels.desc: a burning fire shut up in my bones

verseByVerse.quote: For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward, but if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship. What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I preach voluntarily, I have a reward. If not voluntarily, I am still carrying out a trust committed to me. What, then, is my reward? Just this: that in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge, and so not make full use of my rights in the gospel.

A stewardship. Paul is like a slave-steward given a task; he cannot claim wages for doing his duty (Luke 17:10).

His reward. Paradoxically, the reward is the joy of giving the gospel away freely. The satisfaction of offering grace as grace.

On a Tuesday. The deepest reward of service is often the service itself: the joy of giving without return.
verseByVerse.note: A steward was a household manager, entrusted with his master’s goods.

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law) that I might win those under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though I am free and belong to no one, I have made myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible. To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win Jews. To those under the law I became like someone under the law, though I myself am not under the law, to win those under the law.

Free yet a slave. Luther’s famous summary in The Freedom of a Christian: “A Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none. A Christian is a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.”

As a Jew. Paul kept Jewish customs among Jews: he circumcised Timothy “because of the Jews” (Acts 16:3), took a Nazirite vow (Acts 18:18; 21:23–26), and kept festivals.

Not under the law. Paul knew that in Christ he was free from the Mosaic law as a covenant. He kept its customs as a matter of love, not of obligation for salvation. When others demanded circumcision for Gentiles, Titus “was not forced to be circumcised” (Galatians 2:3).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) omit the words “though not being myself under the law”. The earliest include them, and they are clearly original; scribes may have dropped them by accident.

On a Tuesday. Adapt to the people you want to reach: their food, customs and way of speaking. But never adapt the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: To those outside the law I became as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ) that I might win those outside the law. To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To those without the law I became like someone without the law, though I am not free from God’s law but am under Christ’s law, to win those without the law. To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people, so that by all possible means I might save some.

Outside the law. Among Gentiles Paul ate their food and did not keep Jewish customs (Galatians 2:12–14).

The law of Christ. Paul is not lawless. He is bound by Christ’s commands, summed up in love (Galatians 6:2, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ”). The moral law remains, now as Christ’s law.

The weak. The weak in conscience of chapter 8. Paul gave up his freedom for their sake.

All things to all people. Not compromising truth or morals, but flexibility in everything non-essential.

Contextualisation and its limits. Missionaries like Hudson Taylor, who wore Chinese dress and grew a queue (pigtail), followed this principle. The limit is sin and the gospel itself: Paul never became an idolater to reach idolaters.

On a Tuesday. A Christian in a secular workplace can join colleagues for lunch, learn their interests and speak their language, without joining in gossip or dishonesty.

verseByVerse.quote: I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do all this for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings.

For the gospel. The motive behind everything.

Share with them. Paul wants to be a fellow partaker of the gospel’s blessings with those he reaches. He is not above the gospel; he needs it too.

For worship. Thank God for those who adapted their lives to reach you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–27 — The Discipline of the Athlete
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the athletic games. In a race all the runners run, but only one wins the prize, so they should run to win. Every competitor trains with strict self-discipline, and they do it for a wreath that will wither; believers do it for a crown that will last for ever. So Paul does not run aimlessly or box like someone throwing punches at the air. He disciplines his body and makes it his servant, so that after preaching to others he himself will not be disqualified.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance and Effort: The Perseverance of the Saints

The warning of v. 27 — “lest I myself should be disqualified” — has been debated in relation to the doctrine of perseverance. Reformed theology does not take this as a threat to genuine believers’ final security but as the description of the means by which that security is maintained: the God who sovereignly keeps his people does so through their own disciplined effort, not instead of it. The warning is the mechanism of perseverance: those who are genuinely elect will take the warning seriously, run hard, and thereby demonstrate and maintain their calling.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians lived in the shadow of the Isthmian Games and would have immediately understood the competitive imagery. Paul makes the comparison in order to shame them slightly: the athletes prepare with greater earnestness for a temporary prize than the Corinthians apply to an eternal one. Now: The contemporary church has, in many quarters, lost the language of spiritual discipline entirely — afraid that any emphasis on effort sounds like works-righteousness. Paul’s athletic imagery corrects this: grace produces effort; the free gift of the gospel generates the runner’s willingness to run hard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that in a race all the runners compete, but only one wins the prize? Run in such a way that you win it. Everyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline. They do it to receive a wreath that will wither, but we do it for a crown that will never wither.

The Isthmian Games. Held every two years at Isthmia, near Corinth, in honour of Poseidon; second only to the Olympics. Paul was probably in Corinth for the games of AD 51, perhaps making and repairing tents for the crowds.

Self-control. Athletes trained for months under strict rules of diet and exercise. Competitors at Olympia swore an oath that they had trained for ten months.

The prize. At Isthmia, a wreath of pine or of withered celery. Glory, but brief.

Imperishable. The crown of righteousness and eternal life (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4).

Only one wins? Paul is not saying Christians compete against each other, with only one saved. The point is the effort: run as hard as the winner runs.

On a Tuesday. People train for a marathon or a career with amazing discipline. What discipline do you bring to prayer, Bible reading and holiness?
verseByVerse.note: The Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympics, were held near Corinth every two years. Winners received a wreath of pine or dried celery.

verseByVerse.quote: So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I do not run aimlessly. I do not box like someone punching the air. No, I beat my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified.

Not aimlessly. A runner who knows where the finishing line is.

Not beating the air. Shadow-boxing, or wild punches that miss. Real blows aimed at a real opponent.

Discipline my body. Hypōpiazō: literally “give a black eye to”. Vivid boxing language. Not self-harm or asceticism (Colossians 2:23), but bringing desires under control.

Disqualified. Adokimos: failing the test, rejected. What does Paul fear?

Some (Arminian readers) see the possibility of losing salvation.

Others see the loss of reward or of usefulness in ministry.

Verdict: in 2 Corinthians 13:5–7 adokimos describes those not truly in the faith, so Paul is not speaking merely of a lesser reward. He knows that a preacher who does not practise what he preaches shows he was never genuine. But this fear is a means of perseverance, not a sign of insecurity. The man who wrote this also wrote that nothing can separate us from God’s love (Romans 8:38–39).

On a Tuesday. Pastors and teachers can preach holiness and live carelessly. Many famous leaders have fallen. Keep watch over your own life, with accountability.

For worship. Thank God for the imperishable crown, and ask for grace to run today.

10.title: Israel’s Warning, the Lord’s Table, and the Glory of God
10.overview:
Paul completes his answer about idol food. The strong in Corinth felt secure: they were baptised, they shared the Lord’s Supper, they knew idols were nothing. Paul warns them with Israel’s story. The whole generation that left Egypt enjoyed God’s privileges: led by the cloud, brought through the sea, fed with manna, given water from the rock, which Paul says was Christ himself. Yet most of them died in the wilderness, because they fell into idolatry, sexual immorality, testing God and grumbling. Their story was written as a warning for us. Whoever thinks he stands should watch out, though God is faithful and will always provide a way through temptation.

So: flee idolatry. At the Lord’s Supper believers share in Christ’s blood and body and are made one body. Israel’s sacrifices likewise bound worshippers to the altar. Idols are nothing, but behind pagan sacrifice stand demons, and believers cannot share both the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Then Paul gives practical rules. Food bought in the market may be eaten without asking questions, for the earth belongs to the Lord. At an unbeliever’s dinner, eat what is served, unless someone points out that it was sacrificed, and then abstain for the sake of that person’s conscience. In everything, eating or drinking, do all to the glory of God, and seek the good of others so that they may be saved.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds them of Israel in the exodus. All the people were under the cloud and all passed through the sea; all were, as it were, baptised into Moses in the cloud and the sea; all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink, from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ. Yet God was displeased with most of them, and their bodies were scattered in the wilderness. These things are examples to warn us not to crave evil as they did: not to be idolaters, as when the people sat down to feast and rose up to revel; not to commit sexual immorality, as when twenty-three thousand died in one day; not to put Christ to the test, as some did and were killed by snakes; and not to grumble, as some did and were destroyed by the destroying angel. These events happened to them as examples and were written down to warn us, on whom the climax of the ages has come. So anyone who thinks he is standing firm should take care not to fall. Every temptation they face is the common lot of humanity, and God is faithful: he will not let them be tested beyond what they can bear, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, so that they can endure it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Existent Christ and the Typology of the Wilderness

Paul’s identification of the rock in the wilderness as Christ (v. 4) is a claim that the Son of God was the agent of God’s sustaining grace before the incarnation — the “Angel of the LORD” tradition of the OT now understood christologically. This is christological pre-existence applied to redemptive history: the same Christ who died on the cross was present and active in the wilderness, providing the spiritual sustenance that Israel squandered. Reformed typology has always read the OT this way: Christ is not absent from the old covenant; he is present as promise, type, and mediator.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who were attending temple meals — eating idol food in an actual pagan temple — needed to hear that spiritual confidence is not the same as spiritual safety. Israel had more obvious privileges than any of them and still fell. Now: The sacramental Christian who trusts in regular communion and baptism as automatic guarantees of spiritual health — without the disciplined effort, the watchful sobriety, the dependency on God that Paul describes — is making exactly the Israelite mistake. The sacraments are genuine means of grace, not magic shields.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that our ancestors were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea. All of them were baptised into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.

Our fathers. To mostly Gentile believers, Paul calls the Israelites “our fathers”. The church is the continuation of Israel’s story.

The cloud and the sea. “The LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud” (Exodus 13:21), and they crossed the Red Sea on dry ground (Exodus 14).

Baptised into Moses. A picture: as Christians are baptised into Christ, Israel was united to Moses, their leader, through the cloud above and the water around them.

All. Five times in four verses. Every Israelite had these privileges.

What it does not mean. Not that baptism or the sacraments automatically save. That is the very error Paul is warning against: the Corinthians assumed their baptism and the Lord’s Supper made them safe whatever they did.

A textual note. Manuscripts differ between a passive form, “were baptised”, and a middle form, “had themselves baptised”. The meaning is similar.

On a Tuesday. Being baptised, a church member or raised in a Christian home does not guarantee you are right with God. Trust Christ, and walk with him.

parallels.desc: the pillar of cloud
through the sea on dry ground

verseByVerse.quote: and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that went with them, and that rock was Christ.

Spiritual food. Manna from heaven (Exodus 16). “Spiritual” because given by God’s Spirit and pointing to Christ, the true bread from heaven (John 6:31–35).

Spiritual drink. Water from the rock, at the beginning (“you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it”, Exodus 17:6) and near the end (Numbers 20:11) of the wilderness years.

The rock that followed. Later Jewish tradition told of a rock or well that rolled along after Israel through the desert, giving water. Paul may allude to it, but he gives it a deeper meaning: the real source of Israel’s supply was Christ, present with his people.

The rock was Christ. God is often called “the Rock” in the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15). Paul says Christ was with Israel in the wilderness, before his incarnation. A clear witness to his eternal existence and deity.

On a Tuesday. When you feel spiritually dry, remember: Christ is the rock who gives water. Go to him in prayer and in his word.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition told of a rock that followed Israel through the wilderness; Paul says the true source of their water was Christ.

parallels.desc: bread from heaven
water from the rock

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet God was not pleased with most of them, and their bodies were scattered across the wilderness.

Most of them. Of the adults who left Egypt, only Joshua and Caleb entered the promised land (Numbers 14:29–30).

Overthrown. Literally “strewn”, their corpses laid low in the desert.

The lesson. Privileges do not guarantee perseverance. A generation that saw the greatest miracles in history died in unbelief.

On a Tuesday. Spiritual experiences, revivals and blessings in the past are no substitute for faith today.

parallels.desc: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things happened as examples for us, to keep us from craving evil things as they did.

Examples. Typoi: types, patterns. Israel’s history is not just ancient record but a warning pattern for the church.

Desire evil. At Kibroth-hattaavah, “the graves of craving”, the people longed for the meat of Egypt (Numbers 11:4–34). Craving is the root of the sins that follow.

On a Tuesday. What are you craving? Unchecked desire is how falls begin.

parallels.desc: the graves of craving

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be idolaters as some of them were. As Scripture says, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and got up to indulge in revelry.”

The golden calf. Exodus 32:6. While Moses was on the mountain, the people made a calf, sacrificed to it, held a feast and “rose up to play”, a phrase suggesting dancing and sexual revelry.

Why this example. It exactly matches the Corinthian situation: eating and drinking at a feast connected with idols.

On a Tuesday. Idolatry often looks like a party. Watch where celebrations lead you.

parallels.desc: they sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play

verseByVerse.quote: We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We must not commit sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand of them died in a single day.

Baal of Peor. Numbers 25. Israelite men joined Moabite women in sexual immorality and in sacrifices to their god. A plague followed.

23,000 or 24,000? Numbers 25:9 says “those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand”. Is this a contradiction? Several explanations: Paul says “in a single day”, perhaps distinguishing those who died that day from the total; both may be round numbers; or Paul may be recalling the number loosely. Verdict: not a genuine contradiction. The differing totals measure different things, and ancient writers often rounded. Belief in Scripture’s truthfulness does not require modern statistical precision.

The link with Corinth. Idol feasts and sexual immorality went together, then and in Corinth (6:12–20).

On a Tuesday. Sexual sin was a fatal temptation for God’s people in the wilderness, and still is. Take it seriously.
verseByVerse.note: Numbers gives 24,000 as the total who died in the plague; Paul speaks of those who fell in a single day.

parallels.desc: Israel and the Moabite women

verseByVerse.quote: We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were killed by snakes.

The bronze serpent. Numbers 21:4–9. The people complained against God and Moses about the food, and “the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people”. Testing God means demanding that he prove himself, or seeing how far we can go.

Christ in the wilderness. Paul says Israel tested Christ: again he was present with them.

A textual note. Manuscripts read “Christ” (the earliest papyrus and many others), “the Lord” (ESV note) or “God”. “Christ” is probably original; scribes may have changed it because it seemed strange to speak of Christ in the time of Moses.

On a Tuesday. Going to a pagan feast to prove your freedom was testing Christ. Doing something risky to see whether God will protect you is the same sin.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Lord.”

parallels.desc: fiery serpents among the people

verseByVerse.quote: nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And do not grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the destroying angel.

Grumbling. Probably the rebellion of Korah and the people’s complaint afterwards (Numbers 16:41–49), or the complaint after the spies’ report (Numbers 14).

The Destroyer. The angel of judgement, as at the Passover (Exodus 12:23).

On a Tuesday. Grumbling against God and his leaders is serious. Turn complaints into prayer.

parallels.desc: the destroyer

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These things happened to them as examples, and they were written down as warnings for us, on whom the culmination of the ages has come.

For our instruction. “Whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction” (Romans 15:4). The Old Testament is Christian Scripture.

The end of the ages. The climax of history, begun with Christ’s first coming. We live in the last days (Hebrews 1:2).

On a Tuesday. Read Exodus and Numbers this year, asking what they warn and teach you.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So anyone who thinks they are standing firm should be careful that they do not fall.

Overconfidence. The strong in Corinth felt safe. Pride comes before a fall (Proverbs 16:18).

What it does not mean. Not that believers should live in fear of losing salvation. The next verse promises God’s faithfulness. But it does mean no one is beyond temptation. “Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart” (Hebrews 3:12).

On a Tuesday. The sins you think you could never commit are the ones to watch most carefully.

verseByVerse.quote: No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No temptation has come upon you except what is common to everyone. And God is faithful; he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, he will also provide a way out, so that you can endure it.

Common to man. You are not uniquely tested. Others have faced the same and stood.

God is faithful. As in 1:9. Your safety rests on him.

Not beyond your ability. God sets limits on temptation, as he did with Satan’s testing of Job (Job 1:12).

The way of escape. Literally “the way out”, like a pass through mountains. Not removal of the trial, but a way to endure it. For the Corinthians, the way out of idol feasts was simple: do not go (v. 14).

What it does not mean. Not that God never allows suffering beyond our strength (2 Corinthians 1:8). The promise concerns temptation to sin: God will always make it possible not to sin.

On a Tuesday. When temptation comes, look for the exit God provides: leave the room, close the app, call a friend. It is there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — The Lord’s Table and the Demons’ Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So, dear friends, they must run from idolatry. Paul appeals to their good sense to judge what he says. The cup of blessing believers bless is a sharing in Christ’s blood, and the bread they break is a sharing in Christ’s body; because there is one loaf, they who are many are one body, for they all share the one loaf. Look at Israel: those who eat the sacrifices share in the altar. Paul does not mean that idol food or idols are anything in themselves. He means that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons, not to God, and he does not want them to be partners with demons. They cannot drink the Lord’s cup and the cup of demons, or share the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Are they trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy? Do they think they are stronger than he is?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as Participation

Paul’s use of koinōnia in vv. 16–17 — the cup of blessing is a koinōnia in the blood of Christ; the bread is a koinōnia in the body of Christ — is the most precise language of eucharistic participation in the NT. It does not specify the mode of Christ’s presence, but it insists on its reality: something genuinely happens in the Supper that is a real sharing in what Christ accomplished. Reformed eucharistic theology (following Calvin rather than Zwingli) has insisted on this real spiritual presence: Christ is truly present in the Supper, giving himself to be received by faith.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Attending a civic dinner at a Corinthian temple was not optional for many members of the social elite; it was part of the patronage network on which their livelihood depended. Paul’s “flee idolatry” would have carried genuine social cost. Now: The situations where Christian participation in cultural or civic life involves implicit participation in what is spiritually incompatible are multiple and not always obvious. Paul’s principle — you cannot share in the Lord’s table and the demons’ table — is the test: what are you actually participating in when you participate in this?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my dear friends, run away from idolatry. I am speaking to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.

Flee. As with sexual immorality (6:18), not negotiate. The way of escape (v. 13) from idol feasts is not to attend.

Sensible people. A touch of irony to those who prided themselves on wisdom. Paul appeals to their reason.

On a Tuesday. John’s last words to his churches: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21). What do you need to run from?

verseByVerse.quote: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cup of blessing for which we give thanks, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body, for we all share the one loaf.

The cup of blessing. At a Jewish meal, and especially at Passover, a cup of wine was blessed with thanksgiving to God. Jesus took that cup at the Last Supper.

Participation. Koinōnia: sharing, communion, fellowship. In the Lord’s Supper believers share in Christ himself and his saving death.

How is Christ present? Christians hold four main views.

Transubstantiation (Roman Catholic): the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood in substance, though they look the same.

Sacramental union (Lutheran): Christ’s body and blood are truly present “in, with and under” the bread and wine.

Memorial (often linked with Zwingli): the Supper is chiefly a remembrance and a pledge of faith.

Spiritual real presence (Calvin and the Reformed): the bread and wine remain bread and wine, but by the Holy Spirit believers truly feed on Christ, who is in heaven, receiving his body and blood spiritually by faith (Westminster Confession 29.7).

Verdict: the Reformed view. “Participation” is stronger than mere memory; Christ is really given and received. But the bread is still called bread after the blessing (11:26–28), Christ’s body is in heaven (Acts 3:21), and Jesus said, “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all” (John 6:63). We are lifted to Christ by the Spirit through faith.

One body. Sharing one loaf makes the church one. The Supper is a meal of unity, which makes the Corinthian divisions at the table (11:17–22) all the worse.

For worship. At the next Lord’s Supper, remember that you are not only remembering Christ, but receiving him, and being bound to everyone who eats with you.
verseByVerse.note: “The cup of blessing” was the Jewish name for a cup of wine drunk with thanksgiving at a meal, including the Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the people of Israel: do not those who eat the sacrifices share in the altar? What am I saying, then? That food sacrificed to an idol is anything, or that an idol is anything?

Israel’s altar. In many Old Testament sacrifices (the fellowship or peace offerings), part was burned to God, part given to the priests, and the rest eaten by the worshippers (Leviticus 7:15; Deuteronomy 12:7). Eating was fellowship with God at his altar.

Not that idols are real. Paul has agreed: idols are nothing (8:4). But that is not the whole story.

On a Tuesday. Meals carry meaning. What we celebrate and with whom we celebrate it shows our loyalties.
verseByVerse.note: Worshippers ate part of many sacrifices, sharing a meal with God.

verseByVerse.quote: No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No, I mean that the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God, and I do not want you to be partners with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too. You cannot share in the Lord’s table and the table of demons.

Demons. Echoing Moses: “They sacrificed to demons that were not God” (Deuteronomy 32:17). The gods are not real, but demonic powers use idolatry to enslave people.

Participants. To eat at an idol’s feast is to share fellowship with what lies behind it.

The table. In pagan invitations, the meal was “at the table of the lord Sarapis”. Paul sets “the Lord’s table” against it. You cannot sit at both.

What it does not mean. Not that every object connected with another religion is demonic, or that Christians must fear the market (v. 25). The issue is active participation in worship of other gods.

On a Tuesday. Christians today sometimes meet this in a literal form: offerings at shrines, ancestral rites, occult practices. In the West it may be subtler. Do not share the table of anything that rivals Christ.

parallels.desc: they sacrificed to demons that were not God

verseByVerse.quote: Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are we trying to arouse the Lord’s jealousy? Are we stronger than he is?

Jealousy. Deuteronomy 32:21: Israel “made me jealous with what is no god”. God’s jealousy is the burning love of a husband who will not share his bride.

Stronger than he? Irony aimed at “the strong” (8:7–13). They think they can handle idol feasts. Can they handle God’s judgement?

For worship. Thank God that his love for you is jealous: he will not let you go to rivals without a fight.

parallels.desc: they have made me jealous with what is no god

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–33 — Do All to the Glory of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul quotes the slogan “everything is permitted” and answers that not everything is beneficial or builds others up. No one should seek his own good, but the good of others. They may eat anything sold in the meat market without asking questions for conscience’ sake, because, as the psalm says, the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord. If an unbeliever invites them to dinner and they want to go, they may eat whatever is served without asking. But if someone tells them it was offered in sacrifice, they should not eat it, for the sake of the person who told them and for conscience, his conscience, not theirs. Why should Paul’s freedom be judged by someone else’s conscience, and why be blamed for food he thanks God for? Whether they eat or drink or do anything else, they should do it all for God’s glory. They should give no cause for stumbling to Jews, Greeks or the church of God, just as Paul tries to please everyone in everything, seeking not his own benefit but that of many, so that they may be saved.
verseByVerse.theology:
Soli Deo Gloria Applied to Ordinary Life

The Reformation’s fifth great watchword — soli Deo gloria, to God alone be glory — finds its Pauline root in v. 31. Every meal, every conversation, every commercial transaction, every athletic effort is capable of being an act of worship when performed in the right spirit and with the right orientation. The Reformed conviction that all of life is worship is the systematic development of this verse. The “sacred/secular divide” is not merely unhelpful; by Paul’s logic it is theologically incoherent: all of life, including the most mundane, is lived before the face of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The practical guidelines of vv. 25–28 gave the Corinthians actionable wisdom for the specific daily situations they faced. The principle of “ask no questions” at the market protected them from unnecessary scrupulosity; the principle of sensitivity at the dinner table protected the weak and the unbeliever. Both together are shaped by the glory of God, not by personal preference. Now: “Do all to the glory of God” is not a cliché but a practice — a habit of asking, in any situation: how can this moment, this act, this conversation, be a participation in the glorification of God?

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Everything is permissible,” you say. But not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible.” But not everything builds up. No one should look out for their own good, but for the good of others.

The slogan again. As in 6:12. Paul returns to the test of love.

Build up. The question is not “Am I allowed?” but “Will this strengthen others?”

His neighbour’s good. “Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up” (Romans 15:2).

On a Tuesday. Before choosing a film for a family evening, a joke at work or what to post online, ask: does it build up?

verseByVerse.quote: Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience, for “the earth is the Lord’s, and everything in it.”

The meat market. Makellon, from the Latin macellum. Corinth’s market had butchers’ shops. Some of the meat came from temples; some did not. Paul says do not ask.

Psalm 24:1. “The earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof.” Jews used this verse as a blessing before meals. All food belongs to God the Creator. “Everything created by God is good” (1 Timothy 4:4).

Freedom. A remarkable stance for a former Pharisee, who once kept strict food laws.

On a Tuesday. Do not torment yourself with scruples about every product you buy. Thank God for food and enjoy it.

parallels.desc: the earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof

verseByVerse.quote: If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—
verseByVerse.commentary:
If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat whatever is put in front of you without raising questions of conscience. But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who told you and for the sake of conscience.

Dinner with unbelievers. Paul assumes Christians will accept invitations from unbelievers. No withdrawal from society.

If someone says. Perhaps a fellow guest or the host, pointing out the food’s origin. Now eating would look like approving of idolatry, and would confuse the person who spoke.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) repeat at the end of verse 28 the quotation “for the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof”. The earliest lack it; it was copied from verse 26.

On a Tuesday. Accept invitations from non-Christian neighbours. Eat and enjoy. Only refuse when doing so is needed to bear witness.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I mean the other person’s conscience, not yours. For why should my freedom be judged by someone else’s conscience? If I take part with thanks, why am I blamed for food I have thanked God for?

His conscience. You abstain for the other person’s sake, not because your own conscience requires it.

Why judged? Paul defends Christian liberty. Others may not impose their scruples as a rule for everyone. Liberty is limited by love, not by others’ disapproval.

Thankfulness. Food received with thanks is sanctified (1 Timothy 4:4–5).

On a Tuesday. Hold your freedom gladly, but be willing to give it up for someone else’s good.

verseByVerse.quote: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.

The great principle. The whole debate about idol food comes down to this. Eating, drinking, working, resting, all of life is for God’s glory.

Ordinary life. The Reformers drew from this the dignity of every calling: a milkmaid or a farmer serves God as truly as a monk or priest.

Westminster. “Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever” (Shorter Catechism, Q. 1).

For worship. Pray before meals, not as a ritual, but as a reminder that this meal is for God’s glory too.

verseByVerse.quote: Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not cause anyone to stumble, whether Jews, Greeks or the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in every way. I am not seeking my own benefit but the benefit of many, so that they may be saved.

Three groups. Jews, Gentiles, the church: all humanity.

Please everyone. Not people-pleasing (Galatians 1:10), but considering others in everything (9:19–23).

That they may be saved. The goal of Christian freedom: not self-expression but others’ salvation.

On a Tuesday. Think of one person in your life who is not a Christian. What could you give up or do this week to help them towards Christ?

For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.<sup>5</sup>Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.<sup>6</sup>Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.<sup>7</sup>Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”<sup>8</sup>We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.<sup>9</sup>We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,<sup>10</sup>nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.<sup>11</sup>Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.<sup>12</sup>Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.<sup>13</sup>No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man.
