Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.<sup>13</sup>So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

14.title: Prophecy, Tongues, and the Order of Worship
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is the practical resolution of the gift discussion: having established the theological framework (ch. 12) and the supreme criterion (ch. 13), Paul now applies both to the specific question of tongues vs. prophecy in corporate worship. The governing principle, stated and restated throughout the chapter, is edification: “Let all things be done for building up” (v. 26). Every decision about worship — which gifts to use, in what order, in what manner — must be evaluated by this single criterion: does it build up the whole community?

By this criterion, prophecy (intelligible proclamation of the word of God that addresses the congregation) consistently outranks tongues (speaking in an uninterpreted language) in the corporate setting. This is not because tongues is a lesser gift in itself — Paul says he speaks in tongues more than all of them (v. 18) and does not forbid the practice (v. 39). It is because in a public gathering, intelligibility is a prerequisite for edification. The tongue-speaker who blesses God in an unknown language is genuinely worshipping; but the assembled community cannot say “Amen” to what they cannot understand. And a community that cannot say “Amen” together is not being built up together.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The command to pursue love at the beginning of chapter 14 connects directly back to chapter 13’s “still more excellent way.” Love is to be pursued (run after, chased); spiritual gifts are to be earnestly desired. The two are not in tension; they are in sequence. Love is the supreme orientation; within that orientation, the gifts are to be eagerly sought, particularly prophecy. Why prophecy above all? Because prophecy, in Paul’s usage, is the Spirit-given capacity to speak words that strengthen, encourage, and console the gathered community. This is the paradigm of a community-building gift: intelligible, directly edifying, addressed to everyone present.

The contrast with tongues is introduced immediately: the tongue-speaker speaks to God (genuine worship, real communication with the divine), but no one understands unless there is interpretation; the prophet speaks to people (genuine proclamation, real communication with the community). Both are genuine; but in the corporate setting, the second does what the first cannot do alone. “The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets” (v. 5) — the qualifier is important: interpreted tongues can function like prophecy, and is equally valuable.
verseByVerse.theology:
Intelligibility as a Prerequisite for Edification

Paul’s governing principle for corporate worship — intelligibility — has deep theological roots. The God who speaks is a God who communicates; the Word became flesh precisely to be heard and understood. Worship that renders the word of God inaccessible to the gathered community is, at a structural level, working against the grain of the incarnation. The Reformers’ insistence on vernacular worship (against the Latin Mass) was an application of precisely this principle: if the people cannot understand what is being said and done, they cannot be edified.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian preference for tongues in corporate worship was driven by the same status-seeking that produced the faction fights: tongues was the impressive gift, the spectacular performance. Paul’s preference for prophecy is a preference for the communal over the spectacular, the edifying over the impressive. Now: The principle of intelligibility has applications beyond tongues: jargon-laden sermons, inaccessible liturgy, and culturally opaque worship practices all fail the same criterion. Does the person who attends understand what is happening? Are they being built up?

verseByVerse.quote: Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy. For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy.

Two commands, and it matters that they are both here. After a chapter saying that the gifts without love are worth nothing, the obvious inference would be to stop caring about the gifts. Paul heads that off in his first sentence. Love is not an alternative to gifts; it is the way gifts are to be used.

Both verbs are strong. Pursue is a hunting word — chase it down, run after it. Earnestly desire is the verb behind our word zeal. So the Christian is to be zealous about both, and there is a definite order: love first, gifts within it.

Then the whole chapter’s argument in one word: especially that you may prophesy. That is a startling preference to put to this church, and it will take the rest of the chapter to justify. But the reason is simple enough to state now, and it will not change: prophecy can be understood by the people in the room.

For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.

Before going further, the reader deserves an honest account of what tongues actually is, because the chapter assumes a knowledge we no longer have.

The Greek word is simply “tongue” — the same word used for a language. At Pentecost the gift produced recognisable human languages: visitors from fifteen regions each heard the wonders of God in his own dialect (Acts 2:6–11). What happens in Corinth is plainly different in its effect, because here no one understands him, and a separate gift of interpretation is required. Paul himself speaks of various kinds of tongues (12:10) and once, in passing, of the tongues of men and of angels (13:1), which suggests the category was broader than one thing.

So what can be said with confidence? Four things, and they are enough. It is genuine speech, given by the Spirit. It is addressed to God, not to the congregation — which is why Paul will describe it as praying, singing and giving thanks (vv. 14–16) rather than as teaching. It is unintelligible to hearers unless interpreted. And it utters mysteries — not riddles, but the things of God that he has revealed and that still exceed us.

What were these tongues? Some think they were ecstatic speech or a heavenly language; others, that they were real human languages, as at Pentecost. The second is the more likely: Luke uses the same words for the gift in Acts 2, where every hearer recognized his own language, and Paul’s insistence on interpretation (vv. 13, 27) makes best sense if there was a real language to interpret. And since the sign gifts belonged to the apostolic foundation (13:8–10), there is no warrant for a private prayer language today. Paul’s private use of tongues was the gift itself, not a separate devotional practice for later believers.

What cannot be said is that it is the badge of a real Christian, or the proof of an advanced one. That was settled two chapters ago: not all speak with tongues (12:30), and the mark of the Spirit is the confession that Jesus is Lord (12:3). Corinth had made a distinction out of a distribution, and the whole chapter is a patient dismantling of it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.

Here is the contrast that governs the chapter. Tongues speaks to God; prophecy speaks to people. Both are real, both are given by the Spirit, and only one of them does anything for the person in the next seat.

And notice how Paul defines prophecy. He does not define it by its source, or by how it feels, or by whether it predicts anything. He defines it by its effect, and he names three effects. That is a remarkable way to identify a gift, and it gives the church a usable test: look at what happened to the people who heard it.

Upbuilding is the builder’s word again — the congregation is a structure going up, and this speech adds a course of stone. Encouragement translates a word close to the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit, the one called alongside: it means coming up beside someone and putting strength into him, whether by urging or by comfort. And consolation is the plain word for what you say to the grieving.

Stand those three next to the popular idea of prophecy and the difference is striking. Prophecy as most people imagine it is dramatic, predictive, and slightly alarming. Prophecy as Paul describes it leaves a congregation stronger, braver and comforted. A word that leaves people frightened, confused, or impressed with the speaker has not passed this test, whatever it claimed about its source.

This is also why prophecy is not preaching, though the two overlap. Preaching expounds a text that is already given. Prophecy in this chapter is something said into a particular room on a particular day, which must then be weighed by the others (v. 29) — a thing no one would ever say about Scripture. So whatever else must be settled about this gift, it is subject to Scripture and never an addition to it.

What is not in dispute is that these three effects are wanted, and that any Christian may aim at them. Even a believer entirely certain that the gift itself has ceased may take verse 3 as a description of what his conversation after the service ought to do. Somebody in the room this Sunday needs to be built up, somebody needs courage, and somebody needs consoling — and the words that do it are the nearest thing to this verse that most of us will ever handle (cf. 1 Thess 5:11; Heb 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church. Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church.

Read the first half slowly, because it is easily heard as a sneer and it is not one. Paul is not saying the tongue-speaker is being selfish. He is stating a fact about what the gift does: it strengthens the person exercising it. That is a genuine good, and Paul will shortly say he does it himself more than any of them (v. 18).

The problem is not the gift. It is the setting. Corinth had taken something that builds up the individual and made it the centrepiece of the gathering, and the gathering exists for a different purpose.

Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. Nobody expecting a crackdown expects that sentence. Paul’s wish for the whole church is that they should all have the gift they are abusing. He is not trying to remove anything. He is trying to reorder it — which is the harder and better kind of correction, and much rarer in churches than either enthusiasm or suppression.

The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.

And there is the qualifier that shows exactly where the ranking comes from. Interpreted tongues is no longer inferior to prophecy, because interpreted tongues does what prophecy does — the room understands and is built up. So the greatness Paul is measuring is not intrinsic to the gift at all. It is entirely a question of how many people benefit. The same gift moves up or down the scale depending on whether anyone else in the room can follow it.

That principle reaches a great deal further than tongues, and it is worth applying to things nobody would call a spiritual gift. The sermon full of allusions the congregation cannot catch. The prayer meeting conducted in a register that a newcomer could not join. The music pitched where only the musicians can sing it. In every case the activity may be excellent, and the same question decides the matter: is anyone else being built by this, or only the one doing it?

There is also a quiet permission here for private devotion, and it should not be lost in the corporate argument. Paul never tells the tongue-speaker to stop; he tells him where. At verse 28 he will say plainly: if no interpreter is present, keep silent in church and speak to yourself and to God. That is not a demotion. It is a place.

parallels.desc: would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul deploys three analogies to make the case for intelligibility: musical instruments (a flute or harp playing indistinct notes produces no music, v. 7), military signals (a bugle giving an uncertain sound produces no army response, v. 8), and language itself (if I do not know the meaning of a language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, v. 11). All three make the same point: the content of a communication is only as effective as the recipient’s capacity to receive it. Uninterpreted tongues in a corporate meeting fails on all three counts: it produces no music (no shared worship), no battle readiness (no community mobilised for mission), and no genuine communication (speaker and hearer are mutually foreign).

Paul’s personal testimony in vv. 18–19 is striking: “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.” Five to ten thousand: the ratio expresses the absolute priority of intelligibility in corporate worship. Paul is not disparaging his own practice of tongues; he values it greatly. But he refuses to import into corporate worship what belongs in personal devotion.

Between the analogies and the five-to-ten-thousand ratio lie two passages that carry the section’s pastoral weight. In vv. 13–15 Paul refuses the choice most Christians think they have to make: I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also. Spirit and mind together, not one without the other.

And in vv. 16–17 the whole argument comes down to one word: Amen. A prayer the room cannot say Amen to has left the room out, however sincere it was.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Corporate Criterion and the Nature of Worship

Paul’s insistence on intelligibility in corporate worship reflects a deep theological conviction about the nature of Christian assembly: it is not a private spiritual experience shared simultaneously by many individuals but a genuinely corporate event in which the whole body is built up together. Worship is not merely my encounter with God in the presence of other people; it is our encounter with God as a body. This corporate dimension requires intelligibility: I cannot say “Amen” to what I cannot understand, and a community of “Amens” is the sign that the body is genuinely worshipping together.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian tongues-enthusiasts were essentially importing an individual spiritual practice into the corporate meeting without consideration for the community’s ability to participate. Paul’s five-to-ten-thousand ratio is not a rule to be calculated but a principle to be embodied: always ask, in corporate worship, whether what is done can be received and responded to by the whole community. Now: The principle applies to any element of worship that prioritises the experience of some over the edification of all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?

Paul puts himself in the frame, which is his habitual courtesy in this letter. He does not say “when you speak in tongues you are useless.” He says: suppose I turn up and do it — what good would that do you?

The idea of benefit is the key, and it is not new: the same question — what is helpful, whose advantage is served — governed the argument about idol meat (10:23, 33), and it governs this one. Paul is not asking whether an activity is spiritual, permitted, or sincere. He is asking whether anyone is better off.

Then four things he could bring instead, and they are not four synonyms. Revelation is something disclosed by God; knowledge is grasp of the truth; prophecy is that truth spoken into this room now; teaching is the patient explanation that makes it hold. Between them they describe how the word of God actually reaches a congregation, and every one of them has this in common: the hearer understands.

Behind the whole argument lies something about the character of God, and it is worth saying because it settles more than this chapter. Our God speaks. He is not the mute idol of 12:2. He made the world by speaking, he gave a book, and when he came in person he came as the Word. Everything about him leans toward being understood. A form of worship that makes God’s truth inaccessible to the people present is not merely inconvenient; it is running against the grain of who he is.

That conviction did real work in history. It is why the Reformers fought for services in the language of the people, and why Tyndale vowed that a boy driving the plough would one day know more of the Scriptures than the learned cleric he was arguing with. A Latin liturgy in an English village fails this verse exactly as an uninterpreted tongue in Corinth failed it: the words may be true, reverent, and beautiful, and the man in the back row goes home with nothing.

The same test can be turned on things that are nobody’s fault. A preacher who quotes Greek without translating it, a prayer packed with phrases a person would only know from having grown up in church, a hymn whose language was ordinary in 1780 and is now a puzzle — none of these is done with any bad intent, and each of them leaves somebody in the building outside the conversation. The remedy is small and unglamorous: explain the word, give the reference, say what you mean.

And notice that Paul is asking about benefit, not about interest. A congregation can find a sermon interesting and go home with nothing to do, nothing to believe more firmly, and nobody comforted. Interest is not the test. Somebody stronger by the end is the test.

verseByVerse.quote: If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played? And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played? And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?

Two pictures, and Paul chose them well.

The first is a flute or a harp producing sound without distinction — notes that do not resolve into a tune. Everyone has heard it. An orchestra tuning up is a wonderful noise and nobody hums it on the way home. There is nothing wrong with any individual sound; what is missing is the shape that makes sound into music. Paul says that is what uninterpreted tongues does to a service.

The second is sharper, because it has consequences. A bugle in a camp was not decoration; it was command. Different calls meant advance, retreat, stand to. And an army only marches if the call is distinct. A bugler who blows something ambiguous does not produce a slightly confused response; he produces a camp of men looking at each other while the enemy comes over the ridge.

The change of image is the point. The flute makes indistinctness a matter of aesthetics; the bugle makes it a matter of survival. Paul is telling a church that treats the question of clarity as a matter of taste that it is in fact a matter of readiness. A congregation that cannot make out what is being said cannot obey it.

Which lands on anyone who speaks to God’s people, and it lands as a duty rather than a style preference. Clarity is not a gift some preachers happen to have. It is the whole job. A sermon that is admired and not understood has failed in the way the bugle failed, and nobody in the congregation will be able to say what they are supposed to do on Monday.

It is worth adding that the instrument is not blamed for having no mind of its own — Paul calls these lifeless things. The people in the church are not lifeless. They can choose to be distinct, and this chapter tells them to (cf. Num 10:9; Neh 8:8).

The trumpet image was not a figure of speech to Israel. God gave Moses two silver trumpets with a fixed code of signals: both blown together summoned the whole congregation, one alone summoned the chiefs, an alarm meant the camps on the east should set out (Num 10:1–7). Lives were arranged around the certainty that the same sound meant the same thing every time.

Which is why muddled teaching is a more serious failure than it feels. A congregation that cannot tell what its Bible requires does not become mildly less informed; it becomes an army that will not move. And the people most damaged are always the ones with the least background — the new believer, the visitor, the man who came in troubled and needed one clear sentence and was given a beautiful fog.
verseByVerse.note: A trumpet sounded signals to soldiers in battle.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning, but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air.

There is the phrase that sums up the whole chapter, and it is more desolate than it first sounds. Speaking into the air. Not speaking nonsense, and not speaking wickedly. Speaking real words that reach nobody — sound going out into an empty room and simply dispersing.

Paul then presses the point with the most ordinary observation imaginable. There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning, but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.

Notice the concession he makes first, because it is generous and deliberate: every language in the world means something. He is not saying that tongues is gibberish. Every one of those languages is a real language, full of poetry and law and love and grief, to somebody. The problem is never with the language. It is with the gap.

The word for foreigner is barbaros — and its origin is a small joke at the Greeks’ expense. It is onomatopoeic: to a Greek ear, foreign speech sounded like “bar-bar-bar,” so a foreigner was a bar-bar-ian, a person who made noises. Anyone who has stood in a market or a hospital corridor in a country whose language he does not have knows the feeling exactly: surrounded by meaning, cut out of all of it, reduced to guessing at faces.

And now put that feeling in a church. That is Paul’s argument. The gift that Corinth prized most highly was producing, in the person sitting three feet away, the loneliness of a stranger in a foreign country — and producing it in the one place on earth where nobody is supposed to be a foreigner. This is the church Paul has already told that Jews and Greeks, slaves and free were baptised into one body (12:13). Now they had invented a new way to be strangers to each other, and they were proud of it.

The application is not confined to tongues, and it is worth putting bluntly to a congregation that would never dream of the Corinthian error. Any church can manufacture barbarians. It happens through unexplained jargon, through in-jokes and shared history, through a way of praying that outsiders cannot join, through assuming everyone knows where the book is kept and what the notice means. None of it is malicious. All of it says the same thing to the person standing at the back: you are not from here.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.

One verse, and it is a model of how to correct people without crushing them.

Look at what Paul affirms before he redirects. Since you are eager — he takes their eagerness as given, and he does not condemn it. He could easily have said: your appetite for spiritual experience is the whole problem, calm down. Many pastors would. Instead he treats their hunger as the raw material and simply turns it round: you want the Spirit’s manifestations, so excel at the thing his manifestations are for.

That is worth learning as a way of handling zeal. Misdirected enthusiasm in a church is a great deal easier to work with than no enthusiasm at all, and it is usually killed by the wrong kind of correction. Paul does not want less eagerness. He wants it pointed at the congregation.

Strive to excel — the verb means to abound, to overflow, to have more than enough. Paul takes the Corinthian instinct to outdo one another and does not abolish it either. He gives it a new field. If you must compete, compete at this: who can do the most good to the people in this room.

Which is an almost comic reversal when you think about the church it was written to. Here is a congregation ranking itself by gifts, and the apostle proposes a different league table — and the people at the top of it will be the ones nobody has been counting. The member who has quietly rebuilt the confidence of a family going through a bad year is winning this competition. He does not know there is one.

Here is the test, and it can be applied to any activity in a church. Not “was it spiritual?” Not “did I feel God in it?” Simply: who is stronger because of it? If the honest answer is nobody, the thing may still be innocent, but it has not yet been what this verse is asking for.

There is a warning in the verse for the opposite temperament too, and it should be said, because in most sober congregations there are more of these people than there are Corinthians. Some Christians are eager for nothing at all. They have never wanted a manifestation of the Spirit, never asked God for anything they could not arrange themselves, and mistake their flatness for maturity. Paul does not commend that. He does not say “stop being eager”; he says “be eager about the right thing,” which assumes the eagerness is there to be redirected.

So the verse asks two questions rather than one. Am I eager? And is my eagerness pointed at the people around me? A church that cannot answer the first has a problem this chapter never addresses, because the Corinthians never had it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful. What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful. What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.

The instruction is practical: if you have the one gift, ask God for the other, so that what you are doing can be shared.

Then a phrase that has been made to carry a great deal: my mind is unfruitful. It does not mean the speaker has left his mind behind, or that he is in a trance and not responsible. Paul’s own next sentence rules that out, because he says I will — four times. This is a man deciding what to do, which is not a description of anyone overwhelmed. Unfruitful means it is not bearing fruit for others: the mind is not producing anything the congregation can pick up.

And then the resolution, which is neither of the two answers people usually reach for. I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also. Both. Not a choice. Paul refuses the two great mistakes about worship in a single sentence.

The first mistake is to want the spirit without the mind — worship as pure experience, where thinking is felt to interrupt the feeling, where the aim of a service is a state and doctrine is an obstacle to it. The second is to want the mind without the spirit — worship as instruction only, correct and cold, where a congregation could sing about the blood of Christ with the expressions of people reading a timetable, and where any warmth is suspected of being manipulation.

Both are amputations, and both are common, and each is usually adopted as a reaction against the other. Paul will not have either. And notice that he applies the rule to singing as well as praying, which is where most Christians meet it. Singing with the mind means actually thinking the words — and anyone who has arrived at the end of a hymn with no memory of the middle verse knows how possible it is to sing with neither.

There is a simple discipline in it. Before the service, read the words of what you are about to sing. During the prayers, mean the Amen. Afterwards, ask what was said. That is praying with the mind, and it does not cost a Christian one degree of warmth — the opposite, in fact, since nobody has ever been moved by something he did not take in (cf. Ps 47:7; Col 3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying? For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying? For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.

Paul brings the argument down to one word, and it is a word every congregation says without thinking about it.

Amen is Hebrew, and the church took it over from the synagogue without translating it, which is itself a small marvel — the same syllables have been said by God’s people for three thousand years. It means something firm, reliable, sure. When one person prays aloud and the congregation says Amen, they are not being polite. They are signing the prayer. It becomes theirs. Nehemiah records the whole assembly answering Amen, Amen, lifting their hands, and bowing their heads to the ground (Neh 8:6).

So the outsider who cannot say Amen has not merely missed a nice moment. He has been excluded from the congregation’s prayer — present at it, unable to join it. And Paul’s word for him, outsider, means someone occupying the position of the uninitiated: the enquirer, the newcomer, the person who came because a friend asked him. The one guest in the building who most needed to be included has been quietly left out by the thing everyone else found most exciting.

Then the fairness of verse 17, which keeps the whole rebuke honest: you may be giving thanks well enough. Paul concedes the point completely. The thanksgiving is real, it is directed to God, and God has heard it. Nothing about it is fake. But the other person is not being built up — and in a gathering of the church, that is decisive.

This is the sentence to carry out of the chapter, because it applies to a hundred things that are not tongues. It is possible to do something in a church service that is entirely genuine, entirely God-directed, entirely sincere — and still wrong, because of who else was in the room. Sincerity is not the criterion Paul uses anywhere in these three chapters. The criterion is always the person next to you.

Here is a test with immediate application. Think of the last time you took part audibly in a gathering — a prayer, a reading, a comment in a study, a testimony. Could a nervous newcomer with no church background have said Amen to it, and known what he was agreeing to? If not, the fault was not his.
verseByVerse.note: “Amen” (“so be it”) was the congregation’s response to prayer and thanksgiving.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.

This is the verse that stops the argument from being a caricature, and it should be allowed its full force before anything is built on it.

Paul speaks in tongues. Not occasionally, and not reluctantly — more than all of you, said to the congregation in the New Testament most famous for the gift. And his attitude to it is not tolerance but gratitude: I thank God. Whatever a reader concludes about the gift today, he is not entitled to a lower view of it than the man who wrote this chapter of restrictions. Every rule in this chapter comes from someone who prized the thing he was regulating.

It also tells us, all but certainly, where he did it. He has just spent seventeen verses saying it does not belong in the assembly without interpretation, so this was chiefly private, in his own praying, and by his own account there was a great deal of it. The apostle who travelled constantly, was beaten, imprisoned and shipwrecked, and carried the anxiety of all the churches, had a private prayer life more extensive than that of a whole congregation.

Nevertheless, in church. Two words that divide the whole question. Paul is not weighing tongues against prophecy in the abstract; he is asking what belongs in a public gathering. The same activity can be excellent in one setting and out of place in another, and the distinction is not hypocrisy but wisdom.

Then the ratio, and it is a deliberate absurdity: five against ten thousand. Two thousand to one. He is not proposing a calculation. He is saying that in the assembly, comprehensible speech and incomprehensible speech are not on the same scale at all — that five intelligible words which teach somebody outweigh an entire evening of the other.

Five words is worth sitting with. It is one sentence: Christ died for our sins (15:3) is exactly five. Paul is saying that a single plain sentence, understood by a struggling believer, is of more value in a church than a display that lasts all night. Any Christian can manage five words. That is the point of choosing such a small number.

And note the aim attached to them: in order to instruct others. Paul is not praising brevity for its own sake, and this verse is no charter for the person who thinks sermons should be shorter. He is praising speech that lands somewhere. The measure is not length but transfer — whether something that was in one head is now in another.

There is real freedom in this for anyone who has ever felt they had nothing to offer in a church. You do not need ten thousand words. You do not need a platform, a gift you can name, or a way with an audience. Five plain words that instruct one person are, on the apostle’s own scale, worth more than the most impressive thing that happened in Corinth that year.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now introduces a typological argument from Isaiah 28:11–12: “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” God’s judgment on unbelieving Israel took the form of foreign languages — the speech of the Assyrian conquerors that Israel could not understand, signalling divine abandonment. Paul applies this: tongues in the church is a sign for unbelievers, not believers — but a sign of judgment, not of welcome. Prophecy, by contrast, is a sign for believers (it builds them up) and can also convict and welcome the unbeliever who walks in.

The scenario of vv. 23–25 makes the pastoral point concrete: if the whole church is speaking in tongues and an unbeliever walks in, they will say “you are out of your minds.” But if all prophesy, the unbeliever is convicted, judged, the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and he falls on his face and worships God. This is the result Paul wants: genuine encounter with the living God mediated through intelligible proclamation. Tongues in a corporate meeting, without interpretation, produces the opposite: it signals disorder, not the presence of God.

The section opens with the rebuke that sets its tone: do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature (v. 20). A church that thought itself advanced is told it has been judging like a child.
verseByVerse.theology:
Worship and Witness

Paul’s concern for the unbeliever who might walk in to the church meeting is a significant ecclesiological statement: corporate worship is not only for the already-converted. The community that worships in such a way that the outsider can be addressed, convicted, and drawn to worship is doing something the tongues-heavy meeting cannot do. This does not make evangelism the primary purpose of corporate worship — the primary purpose is the glorification of God — but it recognises that intelligible worship of the living God is inherently missionary in its effect.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian meetings were apparently chaotic — multiple tongues-speakers simultaneously, no interpretation, no order. Paul’s Isaiah citation turns their spiritual pride upside down: the tongues without interpretation is a sign associated with divine judgment, not divine favour. Now: The church that makes its corporate worship impenetrable to the outsider — whether through uninterpreted ecstatic experience, impenetrable theological jargon, or cultural inscrutability — is failing the unbeliever who walks through the door. The word of God should be the thing that disturbs, not the incomprehensibility of the proceedings.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature. In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature.

A beautifully turned rebuke. Corinth thought of itself as spiritually advanced, and Paul tells them they are behaving like toddlers — drawn to whatever is loudest and shiniest, which is exactly how a small child assesses value. And he adds the one respect in which he does want them childish: in evil, be infants. Be the sort of person who has to have wickedness explained to him.

Then the hardest argument in the chapter. In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.

The quotation is from Isaiah 28, and the setting must be known or the argument makes no sense. Isaiah is preaching to the drunken leadership of Israel, and they mock him — his plain speech sounds to them like baby-talk, a string of nonsense syllables. Very well, says God: if my clear word through a prophet is only babble to you, you shall have a message you genuinely cannot understand. He means the Assyrian army, whose foreign speech would soon be heard in their streets. Unintelligible language was the judgment. It was the sound of God having stopped speaking to them in words they could follow.

That unlocks verse 22, which otherwise seems to contradict what comes next. When Paul says tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, he does not mean tongues is a good way to reach them. He means it functions as the sign it functioned as in Isaiah: a mark of people who are outside, hearing sounds that carry nothing to them. It is a sign of judgment, not of welcome. And prophecy is a sign for believers in the opposite way — the mark of a God who is present with his people and speaking to them in words they understand.

Which is why the next verse can say that unbelievers walking into a room full of tongues will conclude the church is mad. That is not a contradiction of verse 22; it is the demonstration of it. The sign does exactly what Isaiah said such a sign does: it leaves the outsider outside.

And there is a sobering thing here for any church, quite apart from tongues. The most frightening judgment God ever brings on a people is not fire. It is unintelligibility — a famine of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11), a pulpit full of noise, a religion that has stopped saying anything. That can happen to a congregation without anybody deciding it, and the people inside are usually the last to notice.
verseByVerse.note: “The Law” here means the Scriptures. In Isaiah, foreign speech — the Assyrian invaders — was a sign of judgment on those who refused to listen.

parallels.desc: by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people

verseByVerse.quote: If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds?

Paul asks them to picture their own meeting through the door. Someone has come — perhaps a neighbour, perhaps a husband who finally agreed to come once. He steps in, and every person in the room is speaking words he cannot understand, all at the same time. What does he conclude?

The Greek says he will think they are raving. Not that the doctrine is false; he has not heard any doctrine. He will simply decide that these people are unhinged, and he will go home, and he will not come back. And here is the sting: he was never given the chance to reject Christ. He rejected a room.

That deserves to be said plainly, because the objection is always available that the world finds the gospel foolish anyway. It does — Paul said so at 1:23. But there is a difference between the offence of the cross and the offence of a shambles, and this chapter exists to say that a church may not confuse the two. If people are put off, let it be by Christ crucified, and not by the fact that nobody explained anything.

But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all.

The second scenario, and everything is different. Notice that it is not one gifted speaker doing the work. All prophesy — the whole congregation is speaking words that build up, encourage and console. And the visitor is convicted by all, which is a courtroom word, and called to account by all, which is another.

Nobody has cross-examined him. Nobody has singled him out; the whole point is that the congregation is talking about God to each other, and the truth spoken plainly begins doing its own work on a man who came in only to keep somebody company. He came to observe and finds himself on trial — which is what always happens when the word of God is intelligible in a room (cf. Heb 4:12–13).

It is worth noticing how ordinary the mechanism is. Nothing in these two verses requires a special word of knowledge about the visitor. It requires a congregation in which people are plainly saying true things about God to one another, and a man who happens to be in the room while they do it. The conviction is the word’s own work, not the speaker’s insight.

Which is a comfort to anyone who has ever felt that evangelism requires a technique he does not have. The most effective thing a congregation can do for the friend it has finally persuaded to come is not to arrange something special for him. It is to be, on that particular Sunday, a body of people who genuinely mean what they are saying — and to say it in words he can follow.

verseByVerse.quote: the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.

This is what Paul wants a church service to do, and it is worth stopping over, because it is far more ambitious than most of us expect on a Sunday morning.

The secrets of his heart are disclosed. Not published — disclosed, made plain, brought into the light. And disclosed to whom? Chiefly to himself. Anyone who has sat under plain preaching and had the sensation of being described knows exactly what this means. Nothing supernatural has to be assumed about the speaker. The word of God has a way of walking into a man’s private rooms and turning on the lights, and the effect is that he stops listening to what is being said about people in general and starts hearing about himself.

Then falling on his face. Not nodding. Not thoughtfully agreeing. This is the posture of a man who has met something and lost his footing — the posture of Ezekiel by the river, of John on Patmos, of every person in Scripture who found himself unexpectedly in the presence of God.

And then the sentence that Paul wants said about a congregation: God is really among you. It is not the sentence anyone expects him to want. It is not “these people are warm,” or “that was a fine argument,” or “they made me feel welcome.” Every one of those is good and none of them is this. He wants the visitor to walk out having concluded that God was in the building.

Here is what a church can take from it, practically. The thing most likely to convert the person who visits is not the excellence of the arrangements, the quality of the music, or the skill of the welcome, though all of them help and none should be neglected. It is a congregation talking plainly about a God who is actually there. Corinth thought the way to impress an outsider was to show him something extraordinary. Paul says the way is to say something true, and let God be extraordinary.

And what he came for was not a religious experience. He came for that man — the one at the back, on his face, saying the only sentence that matters. There has never been a service anywhere that God attended reluctantly.

The words the visitor speaks are not new, either. God is really among you is what the Old Testament promised would one day be said by outsiders about Israel — foreigners falling down and confessing that God was there and nowhere else (Isa 45:14), ten men from every nation taking hold of the robe of a Jew and saying they had heard God was with him (Zech 8:23). Paul takes those promises and lays them on a house church in a Greek port. The nations coming in has begun, and it is happening in an ordinary room, one man at a time.

parallels.desc: God is with you only
we have heard that God is with you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Orderly Worship and Final Rules
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter’s practical climax: “What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.” The snapshot of the Corinthian meeting is lively and participatory — not a one-man performance but a multi-voiced gathering where each person brings a contribution. Paul affirms this participatory dynamic; he does not suppress it. But he channels it through the criterion of edification and the principle of order.

The specific rules: tongue-speakers two or at most three, in turn, with interpretation; prophets two or three, with the others weighing what is said; women to be silent in the weighing of prophets. The rule for women in vv. 34–35 is one of the most contested in the NT. The most natural reading in context is that Paul is restricting women from the public evaluation of prophets — a specific speech act in the context of ordered judgment, not a general prohibition on women speaking. Verse 37 grounding the whole in the Lord’s command ensures Paul is not merely offering preference but apostolic authority.

The chapter closes with the summary of everything: “all things should be done decently and in order.” Order in worship is not a cultural preference; it is a theological statement about the character of the God being worshipped: “God is not a God of confusion but of peace” (v. 33). The orderliness of Christian worship reflects the orderliness of the God from whose own ordered life (Father, Son, Spirit in eternal communion) the community draws its life.

Two verses near the end govern how the whole chapter should be held. Verse 36 names what was really wrong at Corinth — not tongues but independence: Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached? The gospel arrived there from somewhere else, carried by people who had received it themselves.

And verse 39 closes the chapter with a command, not a ban: earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.
verseByVerse.theology:
God as the Ground of Ordered Worship

The theological ground for orderly worship — “God is not a God of confusion but of peace” — is a direct application of the doctrine of God to liturgical practice. The triune God is the most perfectly ordered being there is: the three persons in eternal, loving, ordered communion. Worship that is chaotic and disorderly is, at a deep level, a misrepresentation of the God being worshipped. Conversely, worship that is ordered, intelligible, and participatory is an enacted icon of the divine order. The Reformers understood this: the liturgical reforms of Geneva and Zurich were not mere preference but a theological conviction that worship should reflect the character of the God it addresses.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian meeting was apparently chaotic: multiple simultaneous tongues, no weighing of prophecies, a general air of competitive spiritual display. Paul’s practical rules — two or three, in turn, with evaluation — are not bureaucratic restrictions but pastoral wisdom about how a community can actually benefit from the gifts God has given it. Now: “Decently and in order” is the guiding principle for every aspect of church life, from Sunday worship to congregational meetings to pastoral care. Order is not the suppression of the Spirit; it is the condition in which the Spirit’s gifts can be received and used by the whole community.

verseByVerse.quote: What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.

Paul stops arguing and describes, and the description is one of the most interesting sentences in the New Testament about what a church meeting looked like.

Each one has. People arrived with something. One had a psalm to sing, another a piece of teaching, another something God had shown him, another a tongue, another the interpretation of it. It is a room of contributors, not an audience. Whatever else was wrong at Corinth — and the list has been long — nobody was there as a spectator.

And Paul does not put a stop to it. That is the thing to notice, given everything he has just said about their disorder. He could have written: from now on, one man speaks and the rest listen. Instead he regulates what he finds, and the regulation is a single clause: let all things be done for building up.

Which raises the honest question of what a church service should look like now, because most churches today are far more like a lecture with music than like this room. Two things can be said without pretending to more than the text gives.

The first is that the binding instruction here is not the format but the criterion. Paul lays down no order of service, no timings, no minimum number of contributions. He insists on one thing: that everything done should build people up. A church may meet that standard in many shapes, and the New Testament plainly leaves room for teaching to be central, since it lists teachers before most other gifts (12:28).

The second is that the picture is nonetheless a rebuke to passivity, and most of us need the rebuke more than we need the format. Whatever the Sunday structure, the question “what am I bringing?” is a fair one to put to any Christian on the way in. It need not be a platform contribution. It may be a conversation prepared for a person you know is struggling, a burden carried into the prayers, an invitation to lunch. The instinct of verse 26 is that believers come to a gathering with something in their hands, and that instinct survives every difference of tradition.

Because the phrase governing all of it is the one that has governed the whole chapter, and it is measured on other people. Not “let all things be done sincerely,” or “reverently,” or “with excellence.” For building up.

verseByVerse.quote: If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.

The rules, and they are strikingly specific for a man who has just affirmed the gift so warmly.

Three limits. A maximum number: two, or at the outside three, in one meeting — which implies that Corinth had been running many more. An order: each in turn, which implies they had been speaking over one another. And a condition: interpretation, without which the whole thing stops.

Notice what these rules assume. If a person can be told to wait his turn, then he is able to wait his turn — which Paul will say outright at verse 32. The Spirit does not seize people and make them speak against their will, and no one in that congregation could plead that he had no choice. That single assumption quietly settles a great deal, then and since. Any claim to a spiritual experience that cannot be paused when the elder raises his hand has already been answered by this verse.

And notice the tone of the last clause, because it is easy to hear as a dismissal and is not one. Let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God. The tongue-speaker without an interpreter is not told his gift is bogus, or that he should stop using it, or that he should be ashamed of it. He is told where it belongs. Between him and God, in his own praying, it stands exactly as it was. What it may not do is take up the congregation’s time producing nothing for anybody.

That is a model for how a church should handle a great many things that are good in themselves and unsuited to the assembly. A believer’s hobby-horse doctrine, his particular burden, his favourite emphasis, the experience that changed his life — none of these need be denied to be given their proper place. The question is never “is this real?” The question is “is this the room?”

And there is an implied instruction to the church as well as to the speaker. If interpretation is what makes tongues useful, a congregation should want interpreters and pray for them (v. 13). Paul’s rules are not designed to reduce the gift to a minimum. They are designed to make it useful.

There is a further thing hidden in the numbers, and it applies far beyond tongues. Two or three, and no more — even of a good thing, even of a thing the Spirit gave. Paul assumes that a congregation’s time is finite and that not everything genuine can be fitted into it. Somebody with something real to offer will have to go home without offering it, and that is not a tragedy; it is what happens in a room with other people in it.

That restraint is a form of love, and it is one of the harder ones. It means holding back something you were looking forward to, because the meeting has already had enough of that kind of thing. The person who can do that has understood the chapter better than anyone who merely agrees with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged.

Prophecy gets the same numerical limit as tongues, and then something tongues did not get: let the others weigh what is said.

The verb means to sift, to judge, to discriminate. Prophecy in the Corinthian assembly was to be examined by the congregation. That one instruction settles more about the nature of this gift than any definition could, and it must be held onto firmly, because it is where a great deal of harm has been done in the church.

Nobody weighs Scripture. Nobody sifted Isaiah to see how much of him to keep. If a prophecy in this room is to be tested by the people listening, then this gift is not on the same footing as the written Word of God, and a man who claims to speak for God in a way that places him beyond examination has misunderstood what he is claiming. Thus says the Lord, said in a manner that forbids questioning, is precisely what this verse rules out.

So how is it weighed? Four questions do most of the work. Does it agree with Scripture? — and anything that does not is finished at once, whatever accompanied it. Does it exalt Christ, or the speaker? Does it build up, encourage and console, which is what Paul said prophecy does (v. 3)? And what is the speaker like — is this a person whose life commends what he says? The Bible never asks anyone to accept a spiritual claim without examination, and the Berean Jews are commended precisely for checking an apostle against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11; 1 Thess 5:21; 1 Jn 4:1).

Then the courtesy of verse 30: if something is given to a person sitting down, the one on his feet stops. That is a small rule with a large implication. It means no one has the floor by right. Even a genuine speaker from God may be interrupted, and the mark of a man who is truly hearing from God is that he does not mind sitting down.

Is there prophecy today? The gift of prophecy, like tongues, belonged to the apostolic foundation of the church (Eph 2:20), and with the completion of Scripture it has ceased. That does not make this passage useless. When someone says, “The Lord told me,” the church still has to weigh it, and the tests are the ones Paul’s instruction implies: does it agree with Scripture, does it exalt Christ, and does it build up? An impression may be sincere and even wise, but it is never a word that binds anyone’s conscience.

So that all may learn and all be encouraged. There is the purpose again, and both halves matter. Learning without encouragement produces a congregation that is informed and flat. Encouragement without learning produces one that is cheerful and hollow. Paul asks for both from the same activity, which is a high standard and the right one.

parallels.desc: test everything

verseByVerse.quote: and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints.

Two of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone who has to lead a church.

The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. That is the answer to the one defence the Corinthians could still have offered, and it is the defence that has been offered ever since: “I could not help it. The Spirit came on me. Are you telling me to quench the Spirit?”

Paul’s answer is that the prophet is in charge of his own mouth. The spiritual impulse is under the control of the person who has it. This has to be true, or Paul’s rules would be unenforceable: you cannot tell a man to wait his turn if he genuinely cannot.

And it exposes something important about how the Holy Spirit works, over against every counterfeit. The pagan oracle was possessed; the priestess at Delphi was taken over, and her loss of control was the proof of the god’s presence. The Holy Spirit does not do that. He never overrides a person; he restores him to himself. Self-control is the last item in the fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:23), and a spiritual experience that removes it is not evidence of more of the Spirit but of something else altogether. The man out of whom Jesus cast the legion was found sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind (Lk 8:35). That is the Holy Spirit’s signature.

Then the theological ground: God is not a God of confusion but of peace. Paul does not settle the question of order by taste, or by temperament, or by what is customary. He settles it by the character of God. Worship is meant to be a true statement about the one being worshipped, and a congregation in uproar is making a false one.

But the guard must be set here too, because this sentence has been used to smother things it was never aimed at. Peace is not the same as quiet, and order is not the same as predictability. A church can be so orderly that nothing whatever happens in it — where no one would ever weep, or stay behind, or say anything that was not on the sheet. That congregation has not obeyed this verse; it has merely avoided the problem the verse addresses. Paul is regulating a fire, not a filing cabinet, and he will end the chapter by forbidding them to put the fire out (v. 39).

The last clause — as in all the churches of the saints — reminds Corinth that it is not the only congregation in the world, and that its practice is not its own invention to make. It is an unglamorous point and a healthy one. A church that does something no other church anywhere does should at least ask itself why.

verseByVerse.quote: the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.

Few passages in the Bible are harder, and the reader who has been waiting since chapter 11 for this to be faced deserves it faced rather than hurried.

The difficulty is not the culture. It is Paul. Three chapters ago, in this same letter, he regulated the way women should be dressed when they pray and prophesy in the assembly (11:5) — and he did not object to their doing it. A man does not lay down guidance for how women should pray aloud in church and then, three chapters later, forbid them to open their mouths. Whatever this passage means, it cannot mean the flat opposite of what he wrote a few pages earlier, and any reading that produces that result has gone wrong somewhere.

Four readings are on the table. Some have taken it as a universal ban on women speaking in church; that founders on 11:5, and also on the fact that Christians who hold it do not actually apply it — the women in such congregations sing, confess, and answer.

Some have suggested the two verses were not written by Paul at all, noting that a few manuscripts place them after verse 40. That displacement is real and worth knowing, but every manuscript we possess contains the verses somewhere, so they cannot simply be removed. They are part of the text.

Some read verses 34 and 35 as a Corinthian slogan that Paul quotes in order to demolish it in verse 36 — Or was it from you that the word of God came? It is an ingenious reading and it has the merit of taking verse 36 seriously, but the letter gives no signal that a quotation has begun, and verse 37 calls what he is writing the Lord’s command.

The reading that fits the passage best takes it from its own context. Look where these verses sit: in the middle of the paragraph about prophecy being weighed by the congregation (v. 29). That weighing was a public, judicial act — the assembly sitting in judgment on what had been said, testing a claim to speak for God. And notice what verse 35 regulates: asking questions. The instruction is not addressed to praying or prophesying at all; it is addressed to the cross-examination and the questioning that went with it. Wives are told not to take part in publicly weighing the prophecies, and to bring their questions home rather than conducting them across the room during the meeting.

Read that way, the two passages agree completely. A woman may pray and prophesy in the assembly (11:5). She is not to exercise the congregation’s governing judgment over the church’s teaching, which belongs with the same ordering Paul roots in creation elsewhere (1 Tim 2:12). And the practical setting fits the ancient room, where the sexes often sat apart, where most women had far less schooling than the men, and where an honest question called across a courtyard could stop the meeting.

Which law does Paul mean by as the Law also says? No single verse is quoted. Most likely he means the order of creation in Genesis 2, which he cites elsewhere for the same principle (11:8–9; 1 Tim 2:13) and which stands in the Law in the sense of the five books of Moses.

What does this mean for a church today? The restriction concerns the authoritative teaching and judging of doctrine in the gathered church, which Paul elsewhere reserves to men (1 Tim 2:12). It does not forbid women to pray aloud, read Scripture, sing, give testimony, teach other women and children (Titus 2:3–5), or speak in a members’ meeting. And since prophecy has ceased, the part women once played in praying and prophesying (11:5) is now their full share in the church’s prayer and praise.

And women with no husband to ask? Paul’s point is to keep the meeting orderly, not to keep women from learning. A single woman, a widow or a wife whose husband does not believe should be taught by the elders and by other mature believers, as every member should.

Two things should be said before leaving it, and they matter more than the exegesis to most people who will read this. The first is that nothing here is a verdict on the worth, intelligence or spirituality of women. The same apostle wrote that in Christ there is neither male nor female (Gal 3:28), greeted Junia as a fellow prisoner well known to the apostles (Rom 16:7), and honoured Priscilla, Phoebe, Euodia and Syntyche for their labour alongside him (Rom 16:1–4; Phil 4:2–3). The second is that this passage has been used to shame women into silence far beyond anything Paul wrote, and that misuse has done real damage. A congregation where women are afraid to speak at all has not obeyed this text; it has ignored chapter 11.
verseByVerse.note: Paul has already assumed that women pray and prophesy in worship (11:5). Interpreters differ on what speaking is forbidden here; many take it as the public judging of prophecies just mentioned (v. 29).

verseByVerse.quote: Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?

Two questions, dripping with irony, and they are the sting in the tail of the whole chapter. This verse is often skipped in the argument about the two before it, and it should not be, because it tells us what Paul thought the Corinthians’ real problem was.

It was not tongues. It was independence.

Behind every fault in this letter lies a congregation that had come to believe it was the centre of things — that its practices were its own to invent, its judgments its own to make, and its founder’s instructions a matter for consideration. Paul asks the two questions that puncture it. Did the gospel start here? Are you the only place it has got to? Both answers are humiliating and both are obvious. The word of God came to Corinth from somewhere else, brought by a man who had received it himself, and it had already reached a great many other cities where the churches did not do what Corinth was doing.

The link with verse 33 is exact. As in all the churches of the saints — and now, are you the only ones? Paul is placing this congregation back among its peers. Whatever they had concluded about worship, they had concluded it alone, and that alone was a warning sign.

Which is a useful thing to hold up to any church, and it is not an argument for mere conformity. Truth is not decided by counting congregations, and there have been moments when one church was right and the rest were wrong. But novelty is worth examining, and a church that finds itself doing something no other body of Christians anywhere has thought necessary should at least ask whether the Spirit really has told it alone. The same Spirit is at work in the church in the next town, and in the churches of the last twenty centuries.

There is a humility in this for individuals too. The believer convinced that he has seen something in Scripture that the whole church has missed is occasionally right and is usually a man who has been reading alone for too long. Paul’s questions are worth asking of any private certainty: did this begin with me, and am I the only one it has reached?

And there is a warmer thing in the verse than the sarcasm suggests. The word of God came to Corinth. It arrived. Somebody carried it across the Aegean to a city with a bad reputation and no interest in it, and a synagogue ruler named Crispus, with his household and many other Corinthians, heard it and believed (Acts 18:8). Nobody in that congregation had generated a word of it. They were the beneficiaries of a long chain of people who had received something and passed it on.

That is true of every Christian who has ever lived. Whatever any of us knows about God reached us because it was handed over. There is no self-made believer, and a congregation that remembers how the word got there is a great deal harder to make arrogant.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord. If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord. If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.

Paul now supplies the test he knew would be needed, because he could predict exactly who would object to this chapter. It would be the people most confident of their own spirituality.

So he sets a trap and states it openly. Do you consider yourself a prophet? Do you consider yourself spiritual? Then here is how that claim is checked: you will recognise that what I am writing is the Lord’s command. Any spirituality that arrives at a different conclusion from apostolic instruction has failed at the only point where it could ever have been tested.

Notice how large a claim that is about this letter. Paul does not present these chapters as his best judgment, his temperament, or a policy for a difficult congregation. He calls them a command of the Lord. That is the apostolic authority the whole New Testament rests on: not that these men were wise, but that they were sent, and that what they wrote to the churches carries the weight of the one who sent them (cf. 2 Pet 3:15–16).

Then verse 38, which is short and cold. If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized. The manuscripts vary slightly here between he is not recognized and “let him not be recognized,” and the difference is small, because either way the man is outside the circle he was claiming to lead. He wanted to be acknowledged as a prophet. He is not acknowledged at all — and the passive voice leaves open by whom, which is the most uncomfortable thing about the sentence.

The principle has a long reach and it is worth having, because it settles the commonest form of spiritual manipulation. Whenever anyone claims an authority, an insight or an experience that places him above correction from Scripture, this verse answers him. The claim is self-refuting. A genuine work of the Spirit will always submit to the Word the Spirit gave; the test is not whether a man sounds spiritual, but what he does when the Bible contradicts him.

The test works on ordinary Christians as well as on leaders, and it is easy enough to run on yourself. Everyone has a place where Scripture cuts across something he wants — a grudge, a habit, a plan, an opinion held for thirty years. The question is what happens in that moment. A man who reaches for a reason why the passage does not quite apply to his own case has just learned something about the real source of his convictions, whatever else he believes about the Bible.

And there is mercy in Paul’s verb. He says the spiritual man should acknowledge this — should come to see it, the way one recognises a face. He does not say he will agree at once, or without a struggle, or without wanting to argue first. Recognition can take a while, and often does.

verseByVerse.quote: So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order.

The chapter ends with two commands and a governing principle, and the balance of them is the whole point.

Earnestly desire to prophesy. The same verb he opened with. After a whole chapter of regulation, Paul does not want a subdued church. He wants them hungry for the gift that builds people up.

And do not forbid speaking in tongues. That is a command, and it is placed exactly where a lesser writer would have put a ban. Paul has spent the chapter restricting the practice of tongues in the assembly — two or three, in turn, interpretation required, otherwise silence — and he closes by forbidding the church to forbid it. He knows perfectly well what happens when a congregation is corrected about an excess: it swings, and the next generation treats the thing as an embarrassment.

Even for those who conclude, as is argued here, that the sign gifts belonged to the apostolic foundation, that sentence should temper the way the conviction is held. The instinct to shut down anything that cannot be controlled is not a Christian virtue, and it is not what this apostle did with a church that had abused almost every gift it had. He regulated, and then he protected.

But all things should be done decently and in order. The last word, and it is a phrase from the drawing room and the parade ground: with dignity, and in formation. It is a sentence often quoted by people who want a quiet church, and it will not quite serve that purpose, because verse 39 stands in front of it. Order is what Paul wants around the fire, not instead of it.

And that is the balance the whole chapter has been holding: a church that is neither chaotic nor cold, where the Spirit’s gifts are wanted and not feared, where what happens can be understood by a stranger at the back, and where every single thing is measured by whether anybody was built up. Corinth had the fire and no grate. Many congregations since have had a beautiful grate and no fire.

How does a church that believes tongues have ceased obey do not forbid speaking in tongues? By recognising that Paul was protecting a gift then active, and by holding the conclusion that it has ceased with humility rather than scorn. In practice, elders should test any claim to tongues by Paul’s own rules in this chapter: speakers in turn, never more than two or three, always with interpretation, and silence otherwise (vv. 27–28). And earnestly desire to prophesy is obeyed today by longing for the clear, Spirit-given proclamation of the word that builds the church up.

Underneath it all is the God of verse 33 — not a God of confusion but of peace, whose own life is perfect order and perfect love at once, who has never had to choose between liveliness and dignity, and who gave gifts to men so that a room full of ordinary people might be built up into something that will last after every tongue has fallen silent (cf. Eph 4:11–13).

When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. 15.title: The Resurrection of the Dead
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the theological climax of the entire letter — and one of the most important chapters in the New Testament. Everything else in 1 Corinthians has been application; this is foundation. The resurrection of Christ from the dead is not an appendix to the gospel; it is the gospel. And the resurrection of the body is not a peripheral eschatological detail; it is the goal toward which all of creation is moving.

Some at Corinth were denying the resurrection of the dead — not necessarily the resurrection of Christ (which they apparently accepted as historical) but the future bodily resurrection of believers. Paul treats this as the most catastrophic doctrinal error possible: “if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain” (v. 14). The resurrection is the structural load-bearing wall of the entire Christian building. Remove it and nothing stands.

Paul’s response moves in three great movements: the historical certainty of Christ’s resurrection, established by testimony (vv. 1–11); the logical and theological necessity of the resurrection for the whole Christian faith (vv. 12–34); and the nature of the resurrection body, answering the philosophical objections about how the dead are raised (vv. 35–58).
