The chapter ends with one of the most electrifying doxologies in Scripture: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Resurrection of Christ: The Apostolic Testimony
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul begins with the most important word in this chapter: “I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received.” Of first importance — of primary significance: not first in a sequence of equally important things but first because everything else depends on it. The resurrection of Christ is not one doctrine among many; it is the doctrine from which all others derive their force. And Paul has both received it (from the tradition, from the Lord himself) and delivered it (to the Corinthians, faithfully, without alteration).

The content of the tradition is the gospel in miniature: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures; he was buried (confirming the reality of the death); he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures; he appeared to Peter, then to the Twelve, then to more than five hundred brothers, then to James, then to all the apostles, then to Paul himself. The list of appearances is a legal brief — evidence gathered from multiple witnesses, most of whom are still alive and can be questioned. Paul is not asking for faith without evidence; he is pointing to the evidence and asking for faith proportionate to it.

Paul’s self-description in vv. 9–10 is the most concentrated theological autobiography in his letters: the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle because he persecuted the church of God; yet what he is, he is by the grace of God, and the grace was not in vain — he worked harder than all of them, yet not he but the grace of God that was with him. The paradox of grace and effort, of unworthiness and productivity, of receiving and working, is compressed into two verses that describe every genuine Christian life.

The opening two verses set the terms. Four verbs describe the gospel’s whole relation to a believer: it was preached, it was received, it is what they stand in, and it is what they are being saved by. Then the clause that unsettles some readers — if you hold fast… unless you believed in vain. Paul is not threatening a believer with loss; he raises the possibility that a profession was empty from the start.

And verse 11 closes the section by putting the whole apostolic company on one footing: whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Foundation of Salvation

Paul’s phrase “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” is among the earliest creedal formulations we possess, pre-dating the letter (Paul received it). The resurrection “in accordance with the Scriptures” grounds both events in OT prophecy — Psalm 16:10, Isaiah 53, Hosea 6:2 being the primary candidates. The conjunction of death and resurrection is crucial: the resurrection is not an isolated miracle but the divine vindication of the atoning death. Without the resurrection, the death has no declared meaning; without the death, the resurrection has no redemptive content. Together they constitute the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Greek philosophical tradition was deeply ambivalent about bodily resurrection. The famous scene in Acts 17:32 — when Paul mentions the resurrection, some mock and some are interested — captures the standard Hellenistic reaction. The Platonic tradition prized the release of the soul from the body; the idea of the body being raised was not an upgrade but a retrogression to the bodily existence the soul was trying to escape. Paul’s case for the resurrection runs directly against this deeply embedded cultural instinct. Now: The modern version of the Greek objection is not philosophical but scientific: dead bodies do not rise. Paul’s answer is the same: the evidence of the witnesses. The question is not whether bodies normally rise but whether this specific body, on this specific morning, was raised by the God who created bodies in the first place.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand, and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fourteen chapters of correction are behind him — factions, immorality, lawsuits, marriage, idol meat, head coverings, the Supper, the gifts. Now Paul turns to the thing all of it rests on, and his tone changes completely.

Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand, and by which you are being saved.

Four verbs, and together they are a small map of the Christian life. The gospel was preached — it came from outside, as news; nobody worked it out. It was received — taken, as a gift is taken, which is the only posture available to a man being given something. It is what they stand in — the present tense of it, the ground under their feet, and Paul chooses that verb for a congregation that had been standing on its gifts, its wisdom and its teachers. And it is what they are being saved by, which is a present continuous: salvation is not only something that happened to them at a meeting years ago but something still going on.

Then the clause that stops some readers cold: if you hold fast to the word I preached to you — unless you believed in vain.

It sounds, at first hearing, as though everything is conditional, and a Christian troubled about his own perseverance can be badly frightened by it. So read what Paul actually says. He does not say “you will lose what you have if you slip.” He raises the possibility that some of them believed in vain — that is, believed to no purpose, without effect, a profession that never had anything living in it. That is a different thing from a believer falling out of God’s hand, which this apostle elsewhere says is impossible (Rom 8:38–39).

Holding fast, in the New Testament, is never the cause of being kept; it is the evidence of it. The people God keeps are the people who keep going, and he keeps them by making them keep going. So this clause is not a threat held over a frightened Christian; it is a question put to a comfortable one. And it has a searching form: not “do you remember believing?” but “are you still holding on?” The mark of a real faith is not the vividness of its beginning but the fact that it is still there (cf. Col 1:23; Heb 3:14).

There is one more thing in the opening line that is easy to walk past. I would remind you. Paul is not about to tell this church anything new. Everything in this chapter, the longest and greatest in the letter, is material they already had and had stopped standing on.

That is worth knowing, because Christians commonly assume that what they need is more information. The Corinthians were drowning in information; they had been taught by Paul for eighteen months (Acts 18:11) and by Apollos after him. What they needed was for somebody to walk them back to the first thing and make them look at it again.

Most of the Christian life is like that. Very little of what steadies a believer in a hard year is new to him. It is the old thing, remembered at the right moment, by someone who troubled to say it again.
verseByVerse.note: Some at Corinth were denying the future resurrection of the body; most Greeks thought the body was left behind at death.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures.

Two words in that sentence are worth more than they look. Received and delivered are the standard vocabulary for handing on a fixed tradition, word for word, without adjustment — the same pair he used of the Lord’s Supper at 11:23. Paul is not composing here. He is reciting something he was given.

And that matters more for the historical question than almost anything else in the New Testament. Paul is writing about twenty-five years after the crucifixion. But he did not invent this formula; he received it — which means it was already in circulation and already fixed when he was taught it, and he was taught it at his conversion or shortly after, within a very few years of the event. This is not a legend that grew over generations. It is a summary that was being recited by Christians while the people who buried Jesus were still middle-aged.

Now the clauses, and each is load-bearing.

Christ died for our sins. Not merely died. The little word for carries substitution: in our place, on our account. A death without that word is a tragedy; with it, it is an exchange.

In accordance with the Scriptures. The phrase appears twice, once for the death and once for the rising, and it means this was not an emergency. Isaiah had described a servant pierced for our transgressions, who would see his offspring and prolong his days after making his soul an offering for guilt (Isa 53:5, 10). The psalmist had said God would not let his Holy One see corruption (Ps 16:10), which Peter preached at Pentecost (Acts 2:27). Hosea had spoken of God raising his people up on the third day (Hos 6:2), and Jesus himself pointed to Jonah in the fish (Matt 12:40). The plan is older than the crime.

He was buried. The oddest item on the list, and the one people skip. Why include it in a summary this compressed? Two reasons. It settles that he was actually dead — there was a body, and men carried it, and it was heavy. And it puts the claim in a place where it could be checked: a burial means a tomb, and a tomb has an address, and Jerusalem is a small city.

He was raised on the third day. Note the passive. Not “he rose,” though that is also true, but he was raised — the Father acting on the Son. The resurrection is the Father’s answer to the cross, and his verdict on it.

The third day is counted the way the ancient world counted, where any part of a day was a day. Jesus died on Friday afternoon, lay in the tomb through Saturday, and rose early on Sunday: Friday, Saturday, Sunday. The three days and three nights of the Jonah sign (Matt 12:40) is the same span in a common Jewish idiom, not a stopwatch.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 3–5 are an early summary of the faith that Paul had received — within a few years of the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.

The witness list begins, and it begins with a scandal.

Cephas is Peter, and the last thing the reader knows about Peter is that he stood by a fire in a courtyard and swore three times that he had never met the man. His denial is recorded in all four Gospels. And he is first on the list.

Luke preserves the same detail: when the two from Emmaus got back to Jerusalem, the others told them the Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon (Lk 24:34). Nobody records what was said in that meeting, which is a mercy; some conversations are not for publication. But the fact of it is here, in one of the earliest Christian creeds we possess: the first apostle the risen Christ went to was the man who had denied him.

Then the twelve — and a careful reader stops, because at that point there were not twelve. Judas was dead. Thomas was absent from the first appearance. So the number is wrong, and someone will say so.

The answer is that the Twelve had become a title rather than a headcount. It was the name of the group, the way a committee keeps its name when a seat is empty and a regiment keeps its number after a bad year. John uses it the same way, calling Thomas one of the twelve on an occasion when the room held ten (Jn 20:24).

And here is what to notice about that. A man polishing a story does not leave a countable discrepancy in the second line of his creed. He writes the eleven, which is what Luke writes when he is being precise (Lk 24:33), and nobody ever raises the question. The rough edge is the mark of a formula that was in use among people who were there and knew perfectly well what it meant.

Two men, then, at the head of the evidence: a denier, and a group with a hole in it where a traitor used to be. That is who heads the list of the risen Christ's witnesses. He did not go to the Sanhedrin, or to Pilate, or to the crowd. He went back to his friends, and the first name on the list is the one who had let him down worst (cf. Jn 21:15–17).

The angel at the tomb had already signalled it. Go, tell his disciples and Peter (Mk 16:7) — and those two extra words are the gospel in miniature. Peter had disqualified himself and would have said so. Somebody made sure his name was spoken separately, in case he assumed the message was for the others and not for him.

Which is the shape of this chapter’s comfort for anyone who has failed badly enough to believe he has forfeited his place. The risen Christ does not begin with the loyal. He begins with the man who has to be told twice that he is still wanted, and he goes and finds him first.
verseByVerse.note: Cephas is Peter. “The twelve” was the title of the group even when only eleven were present.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.

Two more entries, and both are doing work that is easy to miss.

The appearance to more than five hundred at once is recorded nowhere else in the New Testament, which is itself striking — Paul knows more than the Gospels chose to write down. But the clause to weigh is the parenthesis: most of whom are still alive.

That is not a devotional remark. It is an invitation, and its tone is almost brisk. The letter is going to a port city with constant traffic to Palestine. Paul is saying: several hundred people saw this at the same time, they are not hard to find, and you may go and ask them. A man inventing a story does not name a crowd of living witnesses and mention that they can be interviewed. He locates his miracle somewhere quieter.

Then James, and this one is quietly devastating. This is James the brother of the Lord, who ended up leading the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13–21; Gal 2:9) and was killed for it. And the Gospels record, without embarrassment, what he thought before that: not even his brothers believed in him (Jn 7:5). His family had at one point gone out to seize Jesus, saying he was out of his mind (Mk 3:21).

Consider what it takes to change a brother’s mind. Nobody in the world is harder to convince that a man is the Son of God than the man who grew up in the same house, ate at the same table, and watched him be an ordinary older brother for thirty years. Scepticism about a sibling is not a theory; it is a lifetime of evidence. James went from that to leading the mother church of Christianity and dying rather than take it back, and this verse is the whole explanation: then he appeared to James.

One thing the list does not contain is worth explaining, since a modern reader will notice it. The women are not here, though all four Gospels say the women found the tomb empty, and Matthew and John record that they were the first to see him (Matt 28:9; Jn 20:14–18). Paul is assembling something like a legal brief, and in that world a woman’s testimony carried little weight in a court — which is precisely why the fact that the Gospels kept the women in is such powerful evidence of honesty. Nobody constructing a case puts his least admissible witnesses at the front. They did it because that is what happened.
verseByVerse.note: Many of the five hundred could still be questioned when Paul wrote. James is the Lord’s brother, who had not believed during Jesus’ ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.

The word translated untimely born is blunt in Greek: it means a miscarriage, a birth that came violently and out of season. It may have been a name his opponents used for him — the runt, the one who arrived wrong — and if so, he has picked it up and put it in his own creed. Paul does that repeatedly. He takes the insult and keeps it.

Because it fits. The Twelve had three years of walking beside Jesus, being taught, being corrected, being prepared. Paul had none of it. He was on a road with warrants in his bag, travelling to arrest people, and the risen Christ intercepted him mid-journey. He was not raised into apostleship; he was seized into it.

Then the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. There is no performance in that sentence. Later he will call himself less than the least of all the saints (Eph 3:8) and, later still, the foremost of sinners (1 Tim 1:15) — and the striking thing is the direction of travel. The longer he walked with Christ, the smaller his estimate of himself became. That is the normal arithmetic of grace, and it runs the opposite way from the arithmetic of religion.

Notice what he never does, though. He does not say he is not an apostle. He never trades his commission for the comfort of self-abasement, because the commission was not his to resign; it was given. A Christian can hold two things at once here: an honest low estimate of himself, and a settled certainty about what God has said about him. Losing either produces a distortion — arrogance on one side, false humility on the other, and both of them are finally about the same subject.

And there is evidence in this verse as well as autobiography. Paul’s own conversion is one of the harder facts for a sceptic to place. Here is a trained, motivated, well-connected opponent, actively destroying the movement, with everything to gain by continuing — and he changes sides, loses his standing, and spends thirty years being beaten and imprisoned for the thing he was suppressing. Something happened on that road. He says he knows what it was.

And the persecution he names is not left in the abstract. Luke tells us what it looked like: witnesses laying their garments at his feet while a man was stoned to death (Acts 7:58); Saul ravaging the church, going house to house, dragging off men and women and committing them to prison (Acts 8:3); still breathing threats and murder as he set out for Damascus (Acts 9:1). There were widows in Jerusalem who knew his name.

That is the man who says he appeared also to me. Whatever else grace is, it is not a general kindliness. It is specific enough to walk out onto a road and stop a man who is on his way to arrest more of the family (cf. 1 Tim 1:13–16).
verseByVerse.note: “Untimely born” describes an abnormal birth — Paul’s sudden, late calling.

verseByVerse.quote: But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.

One of the most compressed sentences in Paul, and it holds together two things that people are forever pulling apart.

By the grace of God I am what I am. Nothing about him is self-made. Not the apostleship, not the conversion, not the endurance, and not the letters. Everything traces back to an unearned kindness that intercepted him when he was going the other way.

And then, immediately: I worked harder than any of them. Which sounds, on the face of it, like the boast he has just disowned — until the last clause takes it back without cancelling it: though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.

Do not resolve that tension by choosing a side; Paul refuses to. Grace is not an alternative to effort. Grace is what produces the effort. The man worked himself to exhaustion, and the working was itself the gift. It is the same grammar as work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Phil 2:12–13), and it is the answer to two opposite mistakes that Christians make with equal enthusiasm.

The first is the one that hears grace and concludes that effort is unspiritual — that a Christian should wait to be moved, that trying hard is a form of unbelief, that the disciplined believer is really relying on himself. Paul was the most exhausted man in the New Testament and he did not think so.

The second is the one that hears work and quietly begins keeping score — that measures itself against other Christians, is pleased with its own diligence, and would be offended to be told that all of it was a gift. Paul had a genuine claim to that comparison and he made it in the same breath as its cancellation.

Then verse 11 puts the whole apostolic company back on one footing: whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed. After all that autobiography, it does not matter which of them said it. The Corinthians had been dividing over exactly this — Paul, Apollos, Cephas — and here is the man himself waving the question away. The messenger is not the point. What was preached is the point, and it was the same from all of them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — If Christ Has Not Been Raised
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now deploys the logical consequences of denying the resurrection with a series of devastating conditional arguments. If the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised. If Christ has not been raised, then the preaching is empty, the faith is empty, the apostolic witness is false, no one’s sins have been forgiven, those who have died in Christ have perished, and Christians are, of all people, most to be pitied.

The argument is a reductio ad absurdum of the Corinthian position. The Corinthians apparently wanted to accept Christ’s resurrection as a unique event while denying the general resurrection of the dead. Paul shows that this is incoherent: the two stand or fall together, because Christ’s resurrection is of the same kind as the general resurrection, not a different kind of event. If the general resurrection is impossible, then Christ’s resurrection is impossible; and if Christ’s resurrection is impossible, then everything the Corinthians claim to believe has no foundation.

“You are still in your sins” (v. 17) — this is the pastoral heart of the argument. The resurrection is not merely a fact about Jesus’s fate after death; it is the evidence that the atonement was accepted. If the Father accepted the Son’s sacrifice, the verdict is the resurrection. If there is no resurrection, there is no verdict; if there is no verdict, the atonement is unconfirmed; if the atonement is unconfirmed, sins are not forgiven.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Confirmation of the Atonement

Paul’s logic in v. 17 — “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” — grounds the significance of the resurrection in its relationship to the atonement. The death of Christ atones; the resurrection of Christ confirms and declares the atonement accepted. This is why Romans 4:25 says Christ “was raised for our justification”: the resurrection is the Father’s “yes” to the Son’s atoning sacrifice. Without the resurrection, Good Friday is a tragedy; with the resurrection, Good Friday is the pivot of history.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian denial of bodily resurrection was probably influenced by Platonic body-soul dualism: if the soul is what matters, and it survives death, why would God re-attach it to a body? Paul’s argument is that this misunderstands both what salvation means (the redemption of the whole person, body and soul) and what happened to Christ (his body was raised, not merely his spirit). Now: The contemporary version of the Corinthian position often appears in Christian thinking that treats the soul’s going to heaven as the whole story and the resurrection as an afterthought. Paul’s insistence is that the resurrection body is the destination, and the intermediate state (soul in God’s presence before the resurrection) is the waiting room.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?

At last the actual problem. Some in Corinth were denying the resurrection of the dead — not, apparently, the resurrection of Jesus, which they seem to have accepted, but the idea that the rest of us will be raised bodily.

It helps to know why that felt reasonable to them, because it was not stupidity. Educated Greeks had a settled view of the body, and it was low. The soul was the real self; the body was its container and, for many, its prison. There was a well-worn play on words for it — sōma sēma, the body is a tomb. On that view, death is not the enemy but the release: the soul finally gets out. Immortality of the soul, yes, gladly. But God putting you back into a body? That is not salvation; that is being re-arrested.

So the Corinthian denial was not an attack on Christianity as they understood it. It was an attempt to keep the parts of it they liked and file the rest under the crude expectations of Jewish converts.

Paul’s reply is to show that the thing they wanted to keep cannot survive the thing they wanted to drop. But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. The reasoning is exact. Resurrection of the dead is the category. Christ’s resurrection is an instance of it. If the category is impossible in principle, no instance of it happened, including that one. You cannot say “such things do not occur, except once.”

And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain. The word means empty — hollow, with nothing inside. Not mistaken in a detail; containing nothing at all. An empty sermon and an empty faith, because faith is only ever as good as the thing it is resting on, and if the thing is not there the sincerity of the resting changes nothing.

That is worth sitting with, because it is the exact opposite of how faith is usually spoken about today. Christianity does not claim that believing is good for you. It stakes everything on an event, and it says so out loud, and it offers to be checked.

It is worth noticing what Paul does not do here, since it is what most of us would do. He does not tell the doubters that their faith can survive without the doctrine. He does not offer them a version of Christianity that keeps the ethics, the community and the comfort and quietly drops the miracle. There was an easier letter available to him and he did not write it.

That is a courtesy to the reader, though it does not always feel like one. A faith that can be adjusted to fit whatever a generation finds credible has no power to contradict that generation, and therefore nothing to offer it. Paul puts the whole weight on one load-bearing claim, and invites anyone who wishes to try to knock it down.

verseByVerse.quote: We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised.

Paul follows the logic down and it gets worse at every step. If there was no resurrection, then the apostles have not merely been mistaken. They have been going round the Mediterranean telling people that God did something he did not do — putting words in his mouth, attaching his name to a fiction. The Greek phrase means false witnesses against God.

Notice that Paul takes that possibility seriously enough to name it. He does not say the gospel is worth believing regardless. He says: if this did not happen, we are liars about the God we claim to serve, and we deserve whatever that means.

Then he arrives at the worst consequence, and it is not the one most people would have guessed. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.

Why should that follow? He died, after all. If the death is what pays for sin, why does the rising matter to the accounting?

Because a death, by itself, tells you nothing about whether it worked. Two men were crucified beside him and their deaths paid for nobody. What the cross needed was a verdict — some public act by which the Father declared that the sacrifice had been received and the debt cleared. That is what the resurrection is. Paul says it plainly elsewhere: Jesus was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Rom 4:25).

Think of it as a receipt. A man may pay an enormous debt and the payment does the work; but until the paper comes back stamped, the debtor has no way of knowing whether it went through. The empty tomb is the stamp. On Friday the price was paid. On Sunday the Father put it in writing, in a form that could be walked into and looked at.

Which turns this into a chapter about assurance and not only about the afterlife. The Christian troubled about whether his sins are really forgiven is being pointed, by this verse, away from his own feelings and toward a garden outside Jerusalem. The question is not whether you feel forgiven. It is whether the tomb is empty. If it is, the matter is settled, and it was settled without consulting you.

And notice how carefully Paul distinguishes two states that people confuse. He does not say that without the resurrection a Christian would feel unforgiven. He says you are still in your sins — a statement about the actual position, not the impression of it. Which cuts both ways, and the second way is the comfort. If the objective fact governs when the news is bad, it governs when the news is good. The believer who feels nothing on a grey Tuesday is not less forgiven than he was on the day he wept at the front of a church. The tomb did not become less empty overnight.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.

The argument stops being abstract. There were graves in Corinth with Christians in them — members of that congregation who had died in the few years since the church began, and whose families were still in the room when this letter was read out.

Fallen asleep is the New Testament’s habitual word for the death of a believer, and it is not a euphemism designed to avoid the subject. It says something: that this condition is temporary and that there will be a waking. But Paul now removes that, for the sake of the argument, and states the alternative without softening it. If there is no resurrection, they have perished. Gone. Not asleep — finished. Every one of those funerals was a final parting and the words said over the grave were false.

A word on asleep, because it is often misread. It describes how death looks from this side: the body lies down and will be woken. It does not mean the person is unconscious until the resurrection. Paul could say that to die is to depart and be with Christ (Phil 1:23), to be away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8), and Jesus promised the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). The believer who dies is with Christ, consciously, now. What waits for the last day is the body.

That is what the clever position in Corinth actually cost, and Paul makes them look at it. A doctrine can be discussed as an idea in a room full of healthy people. Take it to a graveside and you find out what it is.

If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.

Not “we are still better off.” Not “at least the ethics are good and the community is warm.” Paul says that if this life is all there is, the Christian has made the worst bargain of anyone alive, and deserves not respect but pity.

He had grounds for saying so. He had given up his standing, his safety, his prospects and his comfort; he would shortly list the beatings, the shipwrecks, the hunger and the sleepless nights (2 Cor 11:23–28). If there is no resurrection, that is not nobility. It is a man who threw his one life away on a rumour.

And the verse quietly indicts a kind of Christianity that is very common and very comfortable — the sort that values the faith for what it does now. It steadies a family, gives a shape to the week, provides friends and a moral framework and a sense of meaning. All of that is real, and Paul’s point is that a religion which delivers those things and nothing else is a pitiable arrangement, whatever its members say about it. This faith is not primarily a way to live. It is a claim that a dead man is alive, and everything else follows from that or falls with it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.” The “but in fact” is the most powerful turn in the chapter — possibly in the Bible. After the devastating catalogue of what follows if Christ is not raised, Paul turns the corner with the simplest assertion of the most important fact in history. He is raised. Firstfruits.

The firstfruits metaphor is drawn from the OT harvest liturgy: the first sheaf of grain, brought to the temple on the day after the Sabbath following Passover, was the pledge of the whole harvest to come. Christ’s resurrection is not an isolated miracle but the first instalment of a harvest that includes all who belong to him. His resurrection is not complete until theirs is complete; his rising is the beginning of a general rising in which all who are in him will participate.

The Adam/Christ typology of vv. 21–22 is one of the most compressed and profound theological arguments in the NT. As through one man (Adam) death came into the world and spread to all who are in him, so through one man (Christ) resurrection from the dead comes to those who are in him. The parallel is structural: two representative heads, two realms of existence, two destinies. Everyone is in one or the other — either in Adam (under death) or in Christ (under resurrection). The question is which solidarity defines you.

The section does not stop at Adam and Christ. Verses 23 to 28 lay out the sequence: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to him at his coming, then the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and authority and power. What is handed over is not a ruin salvaged from a fire but a completed kingdom.

At the centre of it stands verse 26, and it is the sentence a grieving Christian most needs: the last enemy to be destroyed is death. Not a doorway, not a natural transition, not a friend at the end of a long day — an enemy, and the one still standing when everything else has fallen. Scripture gives the mourner permission to hate it; the Lord himself wept on the way to a tomb he was about to open (John 11:35). And verses 27 and 28 apply Psalm 8 to Christ as the true human being, doing at last what Adam was made for, and end with the goal of everything: that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Adam/Christ Typology and the Scope of Redemption

The Adam/Christ typology here (cf. Rom 5:12–21) is the cornerstone of Paul’s understanding of both sin and salvation. Adam’s representative headship means that his sin brought death to all who are “in Adam” — which is every human being by natural birth. Christ’s representative headship means that his obedience, death, and resurrection bring life to all who are “in Christ” — which is every believer by the new birth. The scope is parallel but not identical: “in Christ shall all be made alive” refers to all who are in Christ, not to every human being universally. The typology demands that the domain of redemption be at least as real and significant as the domain of death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who had lost members to death needed to know that those deaths were not permanent losses but sleeps awaiting a harvest. The firstfruits language gave them a specific, liturgically resonant image: the resurrection of Christ is God’s pledge that the full harvest of resurrection is coming. Now: The Christian stands at the graveside of a believer with the same confidence: the firstfruits have already appeared; the rest of the harvest is as certain as the God who made the pledge. The resurrection is not a hope against hope but a certainty grounded in a historical event.

verseByVerse.quote: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

Two words in Greek, and they turn the whole chapter: but in fact. Paul has spent eight verses in a nightmare of his own construction — empty preaching, futile faith, unforgiven sin, dead friends gone for ever, a life thrown away. And then, without argument, he simply steps out of it. The corridor of horrors was hypothetical. He was never in any doubt about the way out.

The firstfruits. The image is agricultural and liturgical at once, and every Jewish reader knew it. On the day after the Sabbath following Passover, a single sheaf of the new barley was cut and brought to the priest and waved before the LORD (Lev 23:10–11). One sheaf, in a field still standing. It was not the harvest; it was the promise of the harvest. The rest was coming, and the sheaf in the priest’s hands was the proof.

Consider the timing of that ceremony, and then consider on which morning Jesus came out of the tomb.

What the image does is change the category of the resurrection completely. It is not a miracle that happened to one exceptional person — a stand-alone wonder, best admired from a distance. It is the first of a series. Nobody waves a sheaf over an empty field. The resurrection of Jesus is God’s public statement that the harvest of the dead has begun, and it therefore says something about every Christian grave that has ever been dug.

For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.

Paul’s way of thinking about the human race is one of representation. Two men stand at the head of two humanities, and what each did counts for everyone belonging to him. Adam sinned, and death entered and spread to all who are in him — which is everybody, by birth. Christ obeyed, died and rose, and life comes to all who are in him — which is everybody who belongs to him, by new birth.

The two alls must be read in their own halves of the sentence, and one clause controls both: in Adam, and in Christ. The verse is not teaching that every human being will finally be saved, since Paul spends the rest of his letters saying otherwise and this same chapter speaks of enemies still to be subdued. It is saying that whichever man you are joined to, his outcome is yours. Nobody is standing on his own.

Which is bad news read one way and the best news in the world read the other. You did not choose to be in Adam and you cannot argue your way out of it; the evidence is that you are going to die. But the same principle that ruins you is the principle that saves you, because being in Christ works exactly the same way — not by achievement, but by belonging (cf. Rom 5:17–19).
verseByVerse.note: The firstfruits were the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge of the whole harvest to come — at the time of the Passover festival.

verseByVerse.quote: But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.

Each in his own order is a military word — a rank, a division, troops moving in sequence. Paul is not being vague about the future; he is saying it has a shape and the shape has stages.

The first has happened. Christ, the firstfruits, is raised, and that is now a fixed point in history behind us rather than in front of us.

The second is still to come: at his coming, those who belong to Christ. And notice the definition of the group. Not those who achieved something, or understood something, or belonged to the right party in Corinth. Those who belong to Christ — the sole qualification is ownership, and it runs the right way round. They are his.

Then the end, and a picture that ought to be better known than it is. The Son delivers the kingdom to God the Father. The whole long campaign — the incarnation, the cross, the empty tomb, the two thousand years of the church, the resurrection of the dead — is a mission with a completion, and it ends with the Son handing the finished work to his Father.

And before that, destroying every rule and every authority and power. Paul uses words like these elsewhere for more than parliaments and armies; they cover the spiritual forces behind the visible ones, the powers he says the Christian actually wrestles with (Eph 6:12). Every one of them goes. Not reformed, not negotiated with, not accommodated. Abolished.

There is a steadiness in this for anyone reading the news. The powers that presently look permanent — the regimes, the ideologies, the interests that seem able to outlast any opposition, and the darker things that stand behind them — are on a list, and the list has a completion date. Nothing on it is going to survive the arrival of the King, and none of it will require a second campaign (cf. Col 2:15; Rev 11:15).

The verb at the centre of the sequence deserves a moment: he delivers the kingdom to God the Father. It is the language of a steward handing back an estate, or of a commander reporting to the one who sent him. And what is handed over is not a ruin salvaged from a fire. It is a kingdom — the whole thing, complete, every enemy dealt with and every subject alive.

Readers who know the debates about the millennium will want to know how this sequence fits them. Premillennial Christians, many of them careful students of Scripture, read the word Then as leaving room for an interval: Christ returns, raises his people, and reigns on earth for a thousand years before the end. They point to Revelation 20:4–6, where the saints came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years, and note that Paul’s word can mark a gap, since a long time has already passed between Christ’s resurrection and his coming. Amillennial Christians answer that Paul places the resurrection of believers at his coming and then the end, and the next verses say Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet, the last being death (vv. 25–26) — and death is defeated at the resurrection itself (vv. 54–55). That is why the amillennial reading is the more likely: Christ reigns now, and his coming brings the resurrection and the end together.

There is a quiet correction here for the way Christians often picture the end. It is not principally a rescue in which a remnant is snatched out of a world written off as a total loss. It is a campaign that finishes, a work that is completed, and a Son with something to present to his Father.

verseByVerse.quote: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.

Eight words that a great many people need and have never been given: the last enemy to be destroyed is death.

Look at what death is called. Not a doorway. Not a natural transition, not a part of the circle of life, not a friend who comes at the end of a long day. An enemy — and the last one standing, the one still on its feet after everything else has fallen.

That single word is worth more to a grieving Christian than a great deal of what is said at funerals. There is a way of speaking about death in religious circles that tries to make peace with it — that says it is only a change of address, that we should not be sad, that a believer ought to be serene. The Bible does not do this. The Bible calls death an enemy, and it gives the mourner permission to hate it.

The Lord himself did. On his way to the tomb of a friend he was about to raise, knowing exactly what would happen, Jesus wept (Jn 11:35) — and the word John uses of him a moment earlier suggests something closer to anger than sorrow, a snort of fury (Jn 11:33). He was not weeping about the outcome; he knew the outcome. He was standing in front of the thing itself, the enemy in a graveyard, doing to a family he loved what it does to everybody.

And be concrete about what it does, because vagueness here helps nobody. It takes a person who was in the room and makes the room empty. It ends the conversation in the middle. It takes a hand that has been held for fifty years and makes it cold in an hour. It leaves a chair, a coat, a handwriting, a voice on an old recording that is now unbearable to play. It is not tidy and it is not gentle and it does not care what anyone was in the middle of.

So the Christian is not asked to pretend. He is asked to believe that the enemy is on a schedule. The last enemy to be destroyed — not tamed, not made bearable, destroyed — and last, because everything else goes first and this is the one that has to be dealt with at the end.

The reigning Christ is at this moment putting his enemies under his feet, one after another, and he is working his way toward the grave. When he reaches it, it will not be a truce. There will come a day on which there is no death anywhere in the universe, and no one will ever again have to be told that someone has died.

parallels.desc: until I make your enemies your footstool

verseByVerse.quote: For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him.

The quotation is from Psalm 8, and the psalm is not, in the first place, about the Messiah. It is about human beings: what is man that you are mindful of him? — and yet God has crowned him with glory and put all things under his feet (Ps 8:4–6). It is creation’s job description for the human race, given in the garden and abandoned there. Adam was made to rule the world under God and instead handed it over.

Paul applies the psalm to Christ, and the logic is the one running through this whole chapter. Christ is the last Adam — the true human being, doing at last what humanity was made for. Psalm 8 has not been wrenched out of context; it has finally found a man it fits.

Then Paul stops to make a point so obvious it is almost comic, and yet it needs making: when Scripture says everything is put under him, that plainly does not include the One doing the putting. Nobody subjects himself to somebody else by an act of his own authority. The Father is not among the things subdued.

When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.

And here is a sentence that has troubled readers for centuries, because it appears to make the Son permanently lesser. It does not, and the reason is the same one that answered the same question at 11:3.

What is described here is not the Son’s nature but the completion of his mission. He was sent; he came; he obeyed; he died; he rose; he reigns; he subdues; and when the work is finished he presents it all to the Father and takes his place in the order he has occupied willingly from the beginning. The Son who is the exact imprint of his nature (Heb 1:3) does not become less divine by handing over a completed kingdom. He is doing what he has always done — and it is the same Son who said, in a garden, not my will, but yours, be done (Lk 22:42).

That God may be all in all. That is the end of the story, and it is worth refusing to leave it as a phrase. It means a universe with nothing left in it that is not filled with God — no corner where he is absent, no life he does not saturate, nothing between him and his people, and nobody anywhere having to go looking for him. Every place where a believer has felt God to be distant will have been abolished, along with distance itself.

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — The Logic of Resurrection Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now makes two arguments for the resurrection from the logic of Christian behaviour. First, an obscure and much-debated reference to baptism for the dead (v. 29): if the dead are not raised, why are people being baptised for them? Whatever the practice was, Paul uses it ad hominem — not endorsing it but pointing out that even by their own behaviour, the Corinthians reveal a belief in resurrection. Second, Paul’s own apostolic suffering: “I die every day!” (v. 31). If there is no resurrection, Paul’s life of constant danger, daily exposure to death, fighting with beasts at Ephesus — all of it is pointless self-destruction. If the dead are not raised, “let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” The Epicurean counsel of hedonism is the only rational alternative to resurrection hope.

The section closes with a proverb probably borrowed from the playwright Menander: bad company ruins good morals (v. 33). Then the sharpest words in the chapter: wake up from your drunken stupor… for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection and the Rational Grounds of Christian Ethics

Paul’s argument here anticipates the famous wager logic: if there is no resurrection, Christian ethics (self-denial, risk, suffering for others) is irrational. The person who lives as if the resurrection were true is either right (and has invested wisely) or wrong (and has lived a meaningful but ultimately futile life). The Epicurean is consistent: if there is no resurrection, maximise pleasure now. Paul’s whole life is a living argument for the resurrection: his willingness to face death daily makes no sense on any other hypothesis.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s reference to “fighting with beasts at Ephesus” may be literal (arena animals) or metaphorical (violent opponents); either way it describes the real mortal danger of apostolic ministry. The question is: for what purpose? If the dead are not raised, the purpose has no transcendent ground. Now: Every Christian who chooses a harder path for the sake of the gospel — the missionary in a dangerous field, the pastor who refuses to compromise his convictions, the layperson who sacrifices career advancement for integrity — is making an implicit resurrection bet. Their lives only make sense if the resurrection is true.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger every hour?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger every hour?

Verse 29 is the most obscure sentence in the letter, and dozens of explanations of it have been offered. It is worth being honest about that rather than pretending to a certainty nobody has.

Three readings are worth knowing. The plainest sense of the Greek is that some people at Corinth were being baptised as proxies for relatives or friends who had died unbaptised, in the hope that it would do the dead some good. Early writers such as Chrysostom knew of such a practice and condemned it, and it is still practised today by the Latter-day Saints on the strength of this verse. A second reading takes the small word for as meaning because of: people were coming to baptism because of the dead — moved to faith by the death of a believer whose hope had held to the end. A third takes it as baptism with one’s own coming death and resurrection in view.

The first is the most likely. It is what the words most naturally mean, and Paul’s distancing they fits a practice he reports without approving. If that is right, some Corinthians were doing something Scripture nowhere commands and Paul nowhere endorses, and the verse records their practice, not the church’s teaching.

What can be said with certainty is how Paul is using it, and that is the part that matters. He is not teaching it. Notice that he does not say you but they — he holds the practice at arm’s length, neither endorsing nor attacking it, and simply points out that whatever it is, it makes no sense at all unless the dead have a future. His argument is that the Corinthians’ own behaviour contradicts their stated theology.

That is worth noting as a method, because it is a fair one. People are often better than their opinions, and one honest way to answer a bad idea is to show the person that he does not actually live as though it were true. Nobody grieves as if the dead were nothing. Nobody attends a funeral and behaves like a man who thinks a machine has stopped.

Why are we in danger every hour? The second argument is Paul’s own life, and it will run to the end of verse 32. It is the same question turned on himself: what am I doing, if there is nothing after this?

Two things are worth carrying away from a verse this obscure. The first is that it is possible to hold a passage loosely without holding the Bible loosely. Not every sentence in Scripture yields its meaning, and saying so is honesty rather than doubt. The doctrine of the resurrection does not rest on verse 29; verse 29 is a supporting argument, and Paul’s own case runs perfectly well without our knowing what the practice was.

The second is a caution about the opposite error, which is real and does damage. A whole teaching has been built by one movement on this single obscure verse, against the plain sense of the rest of Scripture, which nowhere else suggests that anything can be done for the dead by the living. A doctrine erected on one difficult sentence, with nothing else in the Bible to support it, is a building on a very narrow footing.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of “baptized on behalf of the dead” is disputed; most likely some Corinthians were being baptized as proxies for the dead. Paul mentions the practice without approving it, only to show that it assumes a resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

I die every day is not a devotional phrase about self-denial. Paul is describing his working conditions. He lived where a violent end was a daily possibility, and he is saying that a man in that position needs a reason.

He swears to it, oddly, by my pride in you — he stakes the truthfulness of the claim on the one thing this difficult congregation would recognise as valuable: that he is proud of them. Even in the middle of an argument he tells them that.

I fought with beasts at Ephesus. Whether this is literal is disputed. A Roman citizen was not normally thrown to animals, and Luke does not record it; many take it as a vivid description of the mob and the opposition that nearly cost him his life in that city (Acts 19:23–41). Either way the sense is the same: he had been in a place where he did not expect to come out alive.

What do I gain? That is the honest question, and it deserves an honest answer. Nothing. If the dead are not raised, Paul has purchased absolutely nothing with his life, and he says so without flinching.

Then the quotation, which is from Isaiah 22:13 and is not a joke. Isaiah described a city under siege that ought to have been weeping and repenting, and instead threw a party — killing the oxen, drinking the wine, saying let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. It is the exact philosophy that the ancient world had already worked out and that ours has rediscovered: if this is all there is, get what you can before the lights go out.

And Paul does not sneer at it. That is the striking thing. He treats it as the rational position for a man with no resurrection. If death is the end, then a life of self-denial for other people’s benefit is not admirable, it is merely a waste, and the person eating and drinking has understood the situation better than the martyr has.

Which puts a sharp question to any Christian, and it is not one anyone can answer for somebody else. If you knew for certain there was nothing after death, what in your life would you change? Whatever comes to mind is the part of your life currently being funded by the resurrection. And if nothing comes to mind, that is worth sitting with too.
verseByVerse.note: Fighting with beasts at Ephesus is probably a picture of fierce human opposition; a Roman citizen could not normally be sent to the arena.

parallels.desc: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.

The proverb is probably a quotation from Menander, a Greek playwright, and it was probably a common saying by Paul’s day — the sort of line everybody knew without knowing where it came from. Paul is not shy about using it. He does the same at Athens with the poets (Acts 17:28) and in Titus with a Cretan (Titus 1:12). Truth is truth wherever it turns up, and an apostle is free to borrow a good sentence from a playwright.

But notice what the quotation is doing in an argument about the resurrection. It is a sentence about company, and that tells us something Paul assumes and we often do not: that people do not usually reason their way into a false belief. They drift into it, in company, over time.

That is worth taking seriously, because most Christians who abandon what they believed did not do it in a library. It happened gradually, through friendship, through the desire to be thought reasonable by people they admired, through a slow adjustment of what could comfortably be said aloud. Nobody sits down and decides to stop believing in the resurrection. He starts spending time where it is quietly assumed to be embarrassing, and after two years he finds he has moved.

Paul is not commanding a retreat from the world; he has already ruled that out in this letter (5:10). He is pointing at the particular company that is doing this particular damage — the confident deniers inside the church — and telling the congregation to stop finding them impressive.

Wake up from your drunken stupor. The verb is what you say to a man sleeping it off: sober up, come round. It is an extraordinary thing to say to a congregation that thought itself the most spiritually advanced in Greece. He does not tell them they are mistaken. He tells them they are not properly conscious.

For some have no knowledge of God. That is the diagnosis under the error. Behind the denial of the resurrection is not a difficulty with biology but an inadequate view of God — a God not big enough to raise the dead, which is to say not the God who made the world out of nothing. And Paul says he is telling them this to your shame, which is the second time in the letter he has used that phrase (6:5). A church full of knowledge, and some of its members do not know God.
verseByVerse.note: “Bad company ruins good morals” is a line from the Greek poet Menander.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The objection Paul now addresses is philosophical: “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” He calls the questioner a fool — not for asking but for assuming the objection is unanswerable. The answer comes in two parts: the seed analogy (vv. 36–44) and the Adam/Christ typology applied to the body (vv. 45–49).

The seed analogy is brilliant in its simplicity and precision. When you plant a seed, you do not plant the body that will grow; you plant a bare seed, and God gives it a body as he wills. The same is true of the resurrection: what is buried is the seed; what is raised is the fruit of that seed — the same organism, transformed. The continuity is real (it is the same seed that becomes the same plant); the transformation is radical (no one looking at a wheat seed would predict the wheat stalk). So with the resurrection body: continuous with the buried body (it is the same person raised), but transformed into a glory undreamt of by the buried condition.

The contrast of vv. 42–44 is fourfold: perishable/imperishable, dishonour/glory, weakness/power, natural body/spiritual body. Each contrast is between a condition appropriate to the present age (subject to entropy, subject to sin, subject to mortality) and a condition appropriate to the age to come (freed from all these). The “spiritual body” is not an immaterial ghost; it is a body animated and organised by the Holy Spirit, as the present body is animated and organised by the natural life principle (psychē). It is more physical than the present body, not less — fully embodied, fully alive, fully free from everything that degrades the present embodiment.

The section ends where it began, with Adam. The first man Adam became a living being; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit (v. 45). And verse 46 states the order God works in: it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.

Then the promise the whole section has been building to: just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven (v. 49).
verseByVerse.theology:
Continuity and Transformation in the Resurrection Body

The Reformed tradition has insisted, against all forms of Gnosticism and spiritual idealism, on the bodily nature of the resurrection. The creeds confess “the resurrection of the body” — not the survival of the soul. Paul’s seed analogy establishes both poles: continuity (the seed and the plant are the same organism in different stages) and transformation (the glory of the plant exceeds anything visible in the seed). The specific body that is buried — your body, with its particular history, its particular wounds, its particular scars — is the body that will be raised. This is why the bodily resurrection of Christ is the paradigm: the same body that was crucified was raised — still bearing the wounds (John 20:27), yet transformed into resurrection glory.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Greek objection to bodily resurrection was that the body is the problem, not the solution; the soul’s liberation from the body is the goal, not its resurrection. Paul refuses this framing entirely: the body is God’s creation, declared good, destined for resurrection. The problem is not embodiment but mortality, not physicality but corruption. The resurrection is the redemption of the body, not its abolition. Now: Every theology that treats the goal of salvation as the soul going to heaven (leaving the body behind) has the Corinthian problem. The goal is the new creation, the resurrection body, the renewed earth — the full embodied flourishing of redeemed humanity in the presence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.

Now the real objection, and Paul lets the sceptic put it in his own words, which is fair of him. It is not a stupid question. Bodies decay. Bodies burn. Bodies are lost at sea and eaten by animals and scattered so completely that not a molecule stays in place. The atoms that make up a man are borrowed and returned. Where exactly is the body that is going to be raised?

You foolish person is sharper in English than in Greek, and Paul is not calling him stupid for asking. The word describes someone reasoning without taking into account what he already knows — a man who has the answer in his own back garden and has not looked at it.

Because here is the answer: what you sow does not come to life unless it dies.

Every farmer in the ancient world, and every gardener since, has watched this happen and never found it strange. You take a hard dry seed and you bury it in the ground. That is a funeral. It goes into the dark, it is covered over, and if you dug it up a fortnight later you would find it soft and rotting and finished. And out of that comes a green shoot, and then a stalk taller than the seed ever was, carrying thirty seeds of its own.

The objection assumes that burial is the end of the story. The seed says otherwise, and it says it in every field the objector has ever walked past. Death is not the obstacle to the new life; in the only process any of us can actually observe, death is the doorway to it. The thing that looks like destruction is the mechanism.

And Jesus said exactly this about himself, days before it happened: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (Jn 12:24). He was talking about his own burial, and about a harvest that would include the man asking this question.

There is something worth noticing in Paul’s choice of evidence. He could have answered a question about the resurrection body from revelation — he had been caught up into the third heaven and had things he was not permitted to repeat (2 Cor 12:2–4). He answers it from a seed.

God has arranged the world so that the hardest thing a person has to believe is acted out every spring in front of him, in mud, by vegetables. That is not an accident. The resurrection is not an alien intrusion into a universe that runs on other principles; it is the principle the universe has been running on since the beginning, applied at last to the thing that matters most.

verseByVerse.quote: And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.

Paul presses the picture, and the two halves of it answer the two halves of the objection.

First: what you sow is not the body that is to be. Nobody who had never seen it happen would predict a wheat stalk from a wheat grain. Hold a seed in your hand: it is small, brown, dry, hard, and entirely unremarkable. There is nothing in its appearance that suggests a green stem, a head of grain, a field moving in the wind. If you had only ever seen the seed, you would consider the plant a wild story.

So the question with what kind of body do they come? has an answer, and part of the answer is: not one you could work out from looking at what goes into the ground. The resurrection body is not an improved corpse. It stands in the same relation to the buried body as harvest stands to seed-time.

Second: God gives it a body as he has chosen. That is where the question of molecules and dust and scattered atoms is quietly settled. The wheat plant is not built out of the material of the seed; the seed is spent, and the plant is made of soil and rain and air. Continuity is not a matter of the same particles being reassembled. It is a matter of the same God attending to the same person.

Which means that a Christian may lay to rest a body ruined by illness, or burned, or lost at sea, or long since gone to dust in a churchyard whose stones are unreadable, and none of it is an obstacle of any kind. The God who is going to do this made the original body out of the ground in the first place and has never been short of material. He is not searching for anything. He knows exactly where every one of his people is.

And note the last clause, which is a promise of particularity: to each kind of seed its own body. Not one generic glorified shape issued to everybody. Its own. Whatever else is uncertain, God is not planning to raise a crowd of interchangeable strangers.

That answers a fear people do not usually put into words: that whatever is raised will not really be me — that eternity means being absorbed into something general, a soul among souls, a light among lights. Every seed in a field goes into the ground as itself and comes up as itself. Barley does not come up wheat.

And the choosing is God’s, which is the last comfort in the verse. The body you will have was designed by the same person who designed this one, and he has had a very long time to think about it. He is not improvising at the graveside.

verseByVerse.quote: For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.

Paul now widens the lens, and the argument is doing something specific: it is dismantling the assumption that the word body can only mean one thing.

Look around, he says. A man’s flesh and a fish’s flesh are both flesh and they are not remotely alike; the bird that can live in the air and the fish that would drown in it are both embodied creatures. Then lift your eyes: there are bodies down here and bodies up there, and their glories are of different orders altogether. And even among the lights in the sky, no two are the same — the sun, the moon, and star differing from star.

The point is that God has never worked with one template. A God with this much range in what he has already made is not likely to be stuck for a design when he comes to raise the dead. The objector at verse 35 was assuming that a resurrection body would have to be the same sort of thing as the body he currently has, and that assumption is the whole of his difficulty.

There is also a note being sounded here that the Corinthians particularly needed, and Paul has been sounding it all letter. Star differs from star in glory. Difference is not a defect in God’s workmanship; it is his habit. He made a universe in which nothing is standardised — a church of eyes and ears and feet (12:17), and a sky in which no two lights are matched. A congregation that had been ranking one another by a single measure is being shown a night sky.

Some read star differs from star in glory as a ranking of believers in the resurrection. That is not Paul’s point here: he is answering the question With what kind of body do they come? (v. 35), and the illustration is about kinds, not ranks. Scripture does speak elsewhere of rewards that differ (3:12–15), but every raised believer will bear the image of the man of heaven (v. 49).

And there is something to be simply enjoyed in the passage, which too many commentaries hurry past. This is a tentmaker writing to a quarrelling church about a difficult doctrine, and he stops in the middle of it to look up. He notices fish and birds. He notices that the stars are not alike. The man who wrote the hardest arguments in the New Testament had his eyes open in the world, and thought God’s ordinary handiwork was worth putting into a sentence about the last day (cf. Ps 19:1; Job 38:31–33).

verseByVerse.quote: So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.

The comparisons stop and the promises begin. Four contrasts follow; here are the first three, and each one names something a reader has felt.

Sown perishable; raised imperishable. The present body is on a schedule of decay and everyone knows it. It began wearing out at about twenty-five. The knee goes, the eyes go, the name of somebody you have known for forty years will not come. Whatever is done to slow it — and there is nothing wrong with slowing it — the direction is fixed. The resurrection body will have no such direction. It will not be a body kept young by effort. It will be a body with nothing in it that can wear out.

Sown in dishonour; raised in glory. This is the honest one, and it should not be softened, because anyone who has sat with the dying knows exactly what Paul means. There is very little dignity available at the end. There is the indignity of being washed by strangers, of a body that will not obey, of a mind that says the wrong word, of a person who was formidable and is now frightened of the stairs. Death does not merely end a life; it humiliates it first. And into that Paul writes raised in glory — the same word used of the splendour of God himself. The body that was carried out of a ward with a sheet over it comes back radiant.

Sown in weakness; raised in power. Weakness is the daily one. It is not only the sickbed; it is the ordinary ceiling every person lives under — wanting to help and being too tired, wanting to stay and having to sleep, wanting to do the good thing and finding that the body will not carry the will that far. Every human being alive is limited by an instrument that cannot keep up with him. Raised in power means the instrument will be equal to the person at last.

And notice the verb governing all three: sown. Not disposed of, not lost, not stored. Sown — which is a thing done by a farmer, on purpose, with a harvest in mind. Christians have buried their dead for two thousand years in that word’s shadow. A grave, on Paul’s account, is not a full stop but a planting.

verseByVerse.quote: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.

The fourth contrast, and the one most often misunderstood, so it must be handled carefully.

Spiritual body does not mean a body made of spirit. It does not mean a ghost, a mist, a shining outline, or a soul that has escaped its container. The word does not describe what a thing is made of; it describes what animates and governs it. The natural body is a body run by ordinary created life — breath, blood, appetite, sleep. The spiritual body is a body wholly animated and directed by the Holy Spirit.

Which means the resurrection body is not less physical than the present one. If anything it is more so — more solid, more alive, more capable, because everything that currently drags at the body has been removed from it.

And we are not guessing, because one such body exists and was examined. The risen Christ was not a vision. He told them to touch him, and said that a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have (Lk 24:39). He ate a piece of grilled fish in front of them (Lk 24:42–43), which is a strange thing for a phantom to do, and which reads exactly like a man proving a point. And when Thomas needed evidence, he offered the wounds (Jn 20:27).

That last detail answers a question people carry and rarely ask. He kept the scars. The one resurrection body we have any information about is marked, permanently, by what was done to it. Glorification did not erase the history; it healed it and kept the record. Whatever that means for the rest of us, it means the risen life is not an amnesia.

Other questions crowd in here, and it is better to answer them plainly than to leave a reader guessing. Will we know one another? The disciples knew him — sometimes at once, sometimes after a moment, and always in the end — and Paul assumes throughout his letters that Christians will be reunited and will recognise each other (1 Thess 4:17–18; 2 Cor 4:14).
