What about a body wrecked by disease, or a mind lost to dementia, or a life lived with a disability? Verse 38 has already answered it: God gives it a body as he has chosen, and what is raised is raised imperishable, in glory, in power (vv. 42–43). Nothing that the fall put into a body is going to be raised with it.

And what age? Scripture does not say, and it is better to admit that than to invent. What it does say is enough: the body will be like his (Phil 3:21). That is the whole promise, and it is a great deal more than a description.
verseByVerse.note: A “spiritual body” is a real body wholly empowered by the Spirit, not a body made of spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.

Paul goes back to Genesis, and the difference between the two halves of his sentence is one word.

Of Adam, Scripture says he became a living being (Gen 2:7, as Paul quotes it). He received life; God breathed it into him and he sat up. Everything about the first man is on the receiving end: he was made from dust he did not gather, given breath he did not take, and put in a garden he did not plant.

Of Christ, Paul says he became a life-giving spirit. Not merely alive — a source. The first Adam was a vessel; the last Adam is a spring. That is why the resurrection of Jesus is not simply the best example of resurrection but its cause. He does not stand at the head of the queue. He is the reason there is a queue.

Paul is not saying that Christ turned into the Holy Spirit; the two remain distinct persons throughout his letters (2 Cor 13:14). He means that the risen Christ, in a body wholly alive with the Spirit, now gives life: he pours out the Spirit (Acts 2:33) and will raise his people by that same Spirit (Rom 8:11). That is what a spiritual body (v. 44) is — not a body made of spirit, but a body fully animated by the Spirit.

Note also the title: the last Adam. Not the second, as though there might be a third. The human race has had two representatives and will have no more. Everything after Christ is a matter of which of the two you belong to.

Then verse 46, which looks like a small logical aside and is doing real work: it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.

Paul is establishing the order of God’s working, and it runs against the instinct of every religious person who has ever wanted to skip a stage. The ordinary comes first. The dust comes before the glory, the natural body before the spiritual one, the long unremarkable life before the transformation. God does not begin with the finished thing.

That is a rebuke to the Corinthian error, which was to believe they had already arrived — already reigning, already filled, already beyond the ordinary business of bodies and patience (4:8). And it is a comfort to anyone who suspects his own Christian life is too plain to be real. The plainness is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is the appointed order. Seed first. Harvest afterwards. Nobody gets the second without going through the first, and the Lord himself did not (cf. Heb 5:8; Phil 2:8–9).

It is a rule with a wide application. The long apprenticeship before the work. The years of faithfulness nobody notices before the door opens. The decades of an ordinary marriage, an ordinary job, an ordinary congregation. Christians are forever looking for a shortcut past the natural into the spiritual, and there is not one; there is only the appointed sequence, and God is not in a hurry.

Thirty years in a carpenter’s shop came before three years of ministry. If the last Adam took the natural first and did not complain about the ratio, nobody else is being short-changed.

parallels.desc: the man became a living creature

verseByVerse.quote: The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.

Two men, two origins, and two families that look like their heads.

A man of dust. Genesis says so and does not apologise for it: God formed the man of dust from the ground (Gen 2:7), and told him after the fall that to dust he would return (Gen 3:19). Every person carries the evidence. We are made of the same elements as the soil in the garden, we require constant maintenance from that soil in the form of food and water, and in the end we go back into it. There is a reason the funeral service says what it says over a grave.

The second man is from heaven. Not made of different material — he had a real body, born of a woman, that got tired and hungry and bled. He is from heaven in origin: he came from somewhere, which no other human being has ever done.

And then the promise in verse 49, and it is one of the great sentences of the Bible. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.

We have borne the first image all our lives, and we know its features intimately: mortality, weakness, the pull toward what we know is wrong, the face in the mirror getting older. Nobody had to be taught to bear that image. It came with the birth.

The second is as certain as the first. Note the tense — we shall also bear, flat future, no condition attached. This is the same thing Paul says in Romans, that those God foreknew he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom 8:29), and what John says in one line: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 Jn 3:2).

Measure that against what is actually broken. The man you have wanted to be and the man you are have never once been the same man; every Christian carries an internal record of the gap. On that day the gap closes. Not by lowering the standard, and not by a lifetime of gradual improvement finally arriving — but because the likeness of Christ, which has been worked into his people slowly and against resistance, will be completed in an instant and will hold. There will be nothing left in you that he would have to overlook.

parallels.desc: you are dust

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Behold! I tell you a mystery.” Paul announces a revelation: not all Christians will die before the Parousia, but all will be transformed. The change will be instantaneous — “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.” The dead will be raised imperishable; the living will be changed. This is not an optional upgrade but a necessary transformation: “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.” The present bodily condition, however good and however beloved of God, is not fitted for the new creation; it must be transformed into what God intends.

Then the doxology — the most triumphant sentences Paul ever wrote, perhaps the most triumphant sentences in Scripture. Death has been swallowed up in victory. The taunt against death: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The answer: nowhere. The sting of death is sin; the power of sin is the law; but God gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Death has been robbed of its sting because sin has been atoned for; sin has been dealt with because the law’s demands have been met in Christ; Christ’s resurrection has declared the victory. The enemy still exists — the last enemy will be destroyed (v. 26) — but it has already been defeated in principle. The resurrection of Christ is the down payment on a victory that is as certain as God himself.

The conclusion drawn from the entire chapter (v. 58) is one of Paul’s most bracing practical statements: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.” The resurrection is not an academic doctrine about the afterlife; it is the foundation of present, costly, patient, unstoppable labour for the Lord. Because the resurrection is certain, no act of faithfulness in this life is lost, no sacrifice is wasted, no patient endurance is pointless. In the Lord your labour is not in vain. This is the word the church has been waiting for throughout fourteen chapters of rebuke, correction, and instruction. It is the word that makes everything else possible.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Foundation of Present Labour

The practical conclusion of the resurrection argument — “your labour is not in vain” (v. 58) — is the most comprehensive positive statement about Christian ethics in the letter. The resurrection does not merely give hope for the future; it validates the present. Every act of love, faithfulness, service, and endurance that has been poured out for Christ is stored up in a creation that will be renewed, not discarded. Herman Bavinck’s great theme was that grace restores nature: the resurrection does not annul creation but redeems and glorifies it.

Anthony Hoekema makes the same point in his study of biblical eschatology: the resurrection is the guarantee that present labour is not in vain, because the God who raised Christ will also raise and renew the creation in which that labour was performed. The resurrection does not make the present world irrelevant; it makes it eternally significant.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed to hear that the deaths of their beloved dead were not permanent losses, that their own present labour was not ultimately futile, and that the God who raised Christ had the power and the intention to complete what he had begun in them. The resurrection doctrine is not abstract comfort; it is the concrete ground of the community’s ability to bear all things, believe all things, hope all things, endure all things (ch. 13). Now: Every generation of the church faces the question that faces every human being: does my life mean anything beyond this brief span? Paul’s answer is the most radical possible: yes, because the God who raised Jesus from the dead is the God who inhabits your story, and he wastes nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.

Flesh and blood is a Jewish idiom for a human being in his present frail condition — not a slur on physical existence, which Paul has spent fifteen verses defending. He is saying that this body as it now is, mortal and running down, is not equipped for the world that is coming. It is not a moral judgment; it is a statement about fitness. You do not go deep-sea diving in a jacket.

Behold! I tell you a mystery. A mystery in Paul is never a puzzle; it is something that could not have been worked out and has now been disclosed. He is about to say something the church did not know.

We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed. There is the new information. The entire chapter so far has assumed the pattern of death and resurrection — sown, then raised. But there will be a generation of Christians alive when Christ returns, who will never be buried at all. They will not miss out on the transformation; they will simply reach it by a different road.

Did Paul expect to be in that generation? He writes we because he speaks as one of the living church, which is always to be ready, and he did not know the day (1 Thess 5:1–2). Elsewhere he speaks just as calmly of his own death (2 Cor 5:1–8; Phil 1:21–23). He was not mistaken about a date; he never set one.

This is where Paul’s teaching here joins hands with what he had already written to Thessalonica: the Lord descending with a cry of command and the sound of the trumpet, the dead in Christ rising first, and then those who are alive being caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air (1 Thess 4:16–17).

Is this the rapture? It is the moment 1 Thessalonians 4 describes, when living believers are caught up to meet the Lord. Christians differ on its timing. Many premillennial Christians hold a pre-tribulation view: Christ will come for his church before a final seven-year tribulation, and then return visibly with his church afterwards. They point to promises that believers are not destined for wrath (1 Thess 5:9) and will be kept from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world (Rev 3:10). Others, including amillennial, postmillennial and historic premillennial Christians, see one coming. They note that Paul ties this moment to the last trumpet (v. 52), the public trumpet of Christ’s coming (Matt 24:31; 1 Thess 4:16), and to the resurrection that ends death (vv. 54–55). The more likely reading is one coming of Christ, visible to all, at which the dead are raised and the living changed together.

Christians hold different convictions about the timing and sequence of these events, and many of them are held by people who love the Scriptures and read them with great care. It is worth being clear about how much is shared before any of that is discussed, because the shared part is nearly all of it: that Jesus Christ will return personally, visibly and bodily; that the dead in Christ will be raised; that those alive will be transformed; that this will happen in an instant and at his initiative; and that no believer of any generation will be left out of it. That is what this passage teaches, and it is what Christians of every persuasion say together at a graveside.

Where they differ is on the arrangement of what follows. The amillennial reading is the more likely: the resurrection of the dead and the end belong together (vv. 23–24, 52), with no earthly kingdom between them. But what this verse settles is the fact and the certainty. It is a poor use of a promise this size to make it the occasion of a quarrel among people who are all waiting for the same trumpet.

verseByVerse.quote: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.

Paul reaches for two measures of time and both of them mean the same thing: there will be no process.

In a moment translates en atomōi — in an uncuttable instant. It is the word from which we get “atom,” and it meant the smallest thing that cannot be divided further. Paul is saying the change will happen in a slice of time too thin to have parts.

In the twinkling of an eye is the homelier version of the same idea. Not the blink — the flicker, the involuntary movement of the eye that is over before it has been noticed. It is the fastest thing a person can observe in himself.

Both images say the same thing and it is worth pausing on, because it is not what anyone would have guessed. Everything else in the Christian life is slow. Sanctification takes decades and moves backwards on many days. Grief takes years. Prayers are answered over the course of a lifetime, or not visibly at all. The whole of a believer’s experience trains him to expect God to work at the pace of growing things.

And then this. No preparation, no ramp, no gradual improvement. A woman who has spent eleven years unable to leave her chair, and in the next instant she is not merely well but imperishable. A man in a churchyard since 1840 whose stone is illegible, and in the same instant he is standing. The slowest work God does and the fastest work God does are both directed at the same person.

At the last trumpet. A trumpet in Israel summoned the assembly, announced the king, and called the camp to move (Num 10). This one does all three at once. And there is something worth noticing in the word last: there will never be another summons after it, because there will never again be anyone who needs calling.

And note who is doing what in the sentence. The dead do not rise; they will be raised — the same passive that was used of Christ at verse 4. Nobody in that vast company contributes anything to his own resurrection. They are not straining at the lid. They are called, and they come, because the voice that calls them is the voice that called light out of nothing and Lazarus out of a tomb.

Which means that the certainty of this does not depend in the least on the strength of the faith of the person waiting for it. Everyone in the churchyard will be raised by the same voice, at the same instant, with the same ease (cf. Jn 5:28–29; 1 Thess 4:16).
verseByVerse.note: A trumpet announced great acts of God and summoned his people.

verseByVerse.quote: For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”

Notice the verb: put on. It is the word for getting dressed — putting on a coat, a garment, clothing. Paul does not say the perishable body is discarded and a better one issued. He says it is clothed, and the thing underneath is still there.

That matters, because it is the difference between resurrection and replacement. The Christian is not going to be swapped for a superior model of person. The same man who has struggled and prayed and failed and hung on is going to be dressed in immortality, and it will be him inside it.

And this perishable body, Paul writes, twice. He might have said the perishable. He says this, and one imagines him gesturing at himself as he dictated — a man in his fifties with a scarred back and failing eyes, saying: this one.

Then the quotation, from Isaiah 25. It is worth knowing what surrounds it there, because Isaiah is describing a feast. On his mountain the LORD will make a banquet of rich food for all peoples; he will destroy the covering that is cast over all nations, the veil spread over everything — and then: He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces (Isa 25:6–8).

The verb is worth having. Death is not defeated in a negotiated settlement. It is swallowed — taken in and gone, the way the sea takes something and closes over it. The thing that has swallowed every human being who ever lived is itself swallowed at last, and there is a rough justice in the image that Isaiah plainly intended.

And the detail that most people need is the one about the faces. God is not described as issuing a decree about grief. He is described as coming close enough to wipe tears off individual faces with his own hand — which is what he is doing at the end of the Bible too (Rev 21:4). Whatever else that day contains, it contains a God who has come near enough to touch the people who have been crying.

One word in these verses is worth pressing, because Paul repeats it: must. This perishable body must put on the imperishable. That is the language of necessity — not what is likely, or hoped for, or reasonable to expect, but what has to happen.

Necessary to whom? Not to us; nobody here arranged anything. It is necessary because God has purposed a new creation and has determined that his people will live in it, and a perishable body cannot. The obligation sits on his side of the transaction. He has bound himself, and the raising of the dead is now something he must do in order to be the God he has said he is.

parallels.desc: he will swallow up death forever

verseByVerse.quote: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.

Paul turns and speaks to death directly, and the tone is not respectful. He is quoting Hosea (Hos 13:14), and the two questions are a taunt — the sort of thing shouted after an enemy who has been beaten and is being watched off the field.

Where is your victory? Death has had a total record. It has never lost a single engagement in the history of the world; every person it has come for, it has taken. And Paul stands in front of it and asks what it has won.

Then the word to concentrate on: sting. It is the word for the barb of a scorpion or a bee — not the size of the creature but the part that can actually kill you.

The old illustration is still the best one, and it is worth stating properly. A bee that has stung has left its sting behind. It can still come at you; it can still fly at your face and make a grown man leave a picnic. What it cannot do is hurt you, because the thing that made it dangerous is gone. And a child who knows that will stand perfectly still while it buzzes round his head.

That is precisely the Christian’s position, and Paul explains the mechanism in the next clause rather than leaving it as a picture. The sting of death is sin. What makes death terrible is not that it ends the body; animals die and it is sad and it is not frightening in this way. What makes death terrible is that it is the doorway to judgment for a guilty person — it is sin that gives death its barb.

And the power of sin is the law. The law is not the villain here; Paul says elsewhere it is holy, righteous and good (Rom 7:12). But the law is what turns wrongdoing into a documented offence. It names it, measures it, and pronounces the sentence, and so it is the law that gives sin its legal force.

So follow the chain backwards to see what has actually happened. Death is fearful because of sin. Sin has its power from the law. And Christ has dealt with both — he kept the law we broke and bore the sentence it pronounced. Pull those two out and death is a bee with no sting. It is still an enemy. It can still frighten. It cannot kill a Christian, and it never will again.

parallels.desc: O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

The argument stops. The proofs are finished, the objections are answered, and Paul does the only thing left to do.

Read the verbs. Nobody in the sentence wins anything. The victory is given — handed over, made a present of — and it is given to people who were not on the field. This is not the language of a struggle in which the believer participated and finally prevailed. Every Christian who will ever be raised was, at the decisive moment, dead in trespasses and sins, and had contributed nothing to the outcome except the problem.

And notice the tense: gives. Present. Not “will give,” though the resurrection is future. The giving is already going on. The victory is being handed over now, to people still in perishable bodies, still burying their friends, still afraid of the diagnosis. The thing has been settled and the settlement is in force.

And the channel is named, as it always is in Paul: through our Lord Jesus Christ. Not through our grasp of the doctrine, our steadiness under pressure, or the quality of our dying. Christians have died well and Christians have died badly — frightened, confused, heavily medicated, saying nothing memorable at all — and it makes no difference whatever to the outcome, because the victory was won by somebody else and is handed over as a gift to people who were not in a position to receive anything.

The word victory has been in the air since verse 54, and it is a battlefield term: the outcome, the thing carried off the field. Paul uses it again in Romans and puts an even stranger word in front of it — in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us (Rom 8:37). More than conquerors. Not merely surviving the engagement, but coming out of it with more than was taken in.

So there is nothing left but thanks, and it is worth letting the sentence be what it is rather than pressing on to the application in the next verse.

He was dead. Properly dead, taken down by men who did this for a living and knew when a job was finished, wrapped and weighted with spices and shut behind a stone by people with no expectation whatever of seeing him again. Everything that has ever terrified the human race had done its complete work on him, and had done it with the full cooperation of the authorities, the crowd, and his own friends.

And on the first morning of the week he got up and folded the cloth that had been on his head and left it lying in the place where it had been, and went out into a garden where a woman was crying, and said her name (Jn 20:7, 15–16).

Thanks be to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.

Fifty-seven verses of the highest doctrine in the letter, and the conclusion is about Monday.

That therefore is doing all the work, and it should stop anybody who has ever thought the resurrection is a subject for funerals. Paul does not say: therefore look forward to heaven. He says: therefore get on with it.

Steadfast, immovable. Two words meaning much the same thing, laid one on the other for weight — seated, settled, not to be shifted. This is the answer to a church that had been blown about by every teacher, every fashion and every clever argument all through this letter.

Always abounding in the work of the Lord. Abounding is an overflow word. Not managing, not maintaining, not doing one’s bit — more than is required, spilling over the edge. And note that a man is being told to spend himself in a body he has just been told is perishable, on the ground that the body is going to be raised. The doctrine does not produce detachment from this life. It produces recklessness in it.

Then the clause the whole chapter has been travelling toward: knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.

The word in vain has been haunting this chapter. If Christ is not raised, the preaching is in vain, the faith is in vain (v. 14); Paul’s grace was not in vain (v. 10). Now it lands where the reader lives. Because Christ is raised, nothing done for him is wasted.

And that needs to be made concrete, because it is exactly the sort of promise that evaporates when it is left general. Consider the mother who has prayed for a son for thirty years and has watched him get worse. The man who taught a Sunday class of eight children for a decade and has no idea what became of any of them. The woman who nursed a husband through seven years of dementia, doing everything, thanked by nobody, remembered by a man who did not know her name. The believer who has held a difficult marriage together in private for a lifetime and will never be commended for it. The missionary who gave forty years to a place and left it with three converts and a small building.

Every one of them has looked at what they have to show for it and thought: that was nothing. And every one of them has been wrong, on the authority of this verse. Not “your labour will probably bear fruit eventually.” Not “God sees your effort even if it failed.” Your labour is not in vain — the work itself is not lost, because it was done in the Lord, and what is done in the Lord belongs to a world that is not going to be thrown away but raised.

That is what the empty tomb finally means for an ordinary Tuesday. The God who did not let his Son’s body stay in the ground is not going to let his people’s work stay there either. He wastes nothing, he forgets nothing, and he is going to raise all of it.

On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.<sup>11</sup>Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you then not even Christ has been raised.<sup>14</sup>And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.<sup>15</sup>We are even found to be misrepresenting God, If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”<sup>33</sup>Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.”<sup>34</sup>Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning.
