16.title: The Collection, the Plans, and the Farewell
16.overview:
After fifteen chapters of theological depth and pastoral intensity, chapter 16 lands with the practicality of a man who has finished his sermon and is now talking about arrangements. The collection for the Jerusalem poor, travel plans, commendations of colleagues, personal greetings — these are the ordinary textures of Christian community life, and Paul handles them with the same theological seriousness as the great arguments of chapters 1–15. The ordinary and the transcendent are not separated in Paul’s world; the collection for the poor is a gospel act; the greeting of a colleague is a theological act; the closing benediction is a doxological act.

The letter closes not with law but with grace. “My love be with you all in Christ Jesus” — the apostle who has rebuked, corrected, warned, and argued for sixteen chapters ends with love. And between the final warning and the final love comes the great cry of the early church: Maranatha — “Our Lord, come!” The pulse of the apostolic community beats with eschatological longing: come, Lord Jesus. Everything that has been argued in this letter — the cross, the resurrection, love, order, holiness, community — points forward to the moment when he who died and rose and is coming again will make all things new.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Collection for the Saints
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The collection for the Jerusalem poor was one of the major projects of Paul’s apostolic ministry — a gathering of financial support from the Gentile churches for the impoverished believers in Jerusalem, which Paul saw as both a practical act of mercy and a symbolic expression of the unity of the one body of Christ across ethnic and geographic lines. He addresses it with practical wisdom: on the first day of every week, each person sets aside whatever they can afford, accumulating it so that there is no need for a last-minute collection when Paul arrives.

The regularity (“on the first day of every week”), the proportionality (“as he may prosper”), and the discipline (“each of you...put something aside”) are the marks of Paul’s teaching on financial generosity across his letters. Systematic, proportionate, habitual giving is not merely a fundraising strategy; it is a spiritual discipline that keeps money in its proper place as a servant of the kingdom rather than a master of the heart.

Verses 3 and 4 add the other half of the instruction, and it is as practical as the first. Paul will not carry the money himself. It travels in the hands of men the Corinthians have chosen and formally accredited. Financial transparency is apostolic practice, not modern governance imported into the church.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Collection as a Gospel Act

Paul’s collection theology, most fully developed in 2 Corinthians 8–9, grounds financial generosity in the grace of Christ: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Cor 8:9). The collection is not a tax but a participation in the logic of the cross — the voluntary sharing of material blessing across economic and ethnic lines that enacts the gospel’s claim that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. The Gentile churches supporting the Jewish church in Jerusalem is the financial expression of Romans 15:27: “if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem church was impoverished, possibly as a result of the famine of Acts 11:28 or the social cost of Jewish Christians being excluded from economic networks following their conversion. The collection was an act of solidarity across the most significant social divide of the ancient world. Now: The principle of systematic, proportionate, habitual giving as a spiritual discipline remains the most practically effective and most theologically grounded approach to Christian financial stewardship. The “first day of every week” rhythm connects giving to worship — it is part of how the community orients itself toward God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do.

After the resurrection, money. The transition looks jarring, and it is not; it is the same transition the whole letter has been making. Paul has just spent fifty-eight verses proving that the dead will be raised, and concluded that therefore no labour is wasted. The very next thing he mentions is a hardship fund for a church some eight hundred miles away.

The collection was one of the great projects of Paul’s life. The believers in Jerusalem were poor — there had been famine (Acts 11:28), and Jewish believers who confessed Christ were often cut out of the family and trade networks that had supported them. So Paul spent years gathering money from Gentile congregations around the Aegean for a Jewish congregation most of them would never meet, and he cared about it enough to risk his freedom delivering it (Rom 15:25–31).

He is not, in other words, raising funds for his own ministry here. The money is going to strangers, and the strangers are of the ethnic group that had caused him the most trouble.

On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come.

Four things in one sentence, and together they are the New Testament’s most practical paragraph on giving.

It is regular — the first day of every week, which is also, incidentally, one of the earliest indications we have that Christians were already meeting on Sunday rather than the Sabbath, because that was the day he rose. Giving is attached to the resurrection day from the beginning.

Does that make Sunday the Christian Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that it does: the fourth commandment still stands, with the day moved to the first day of the week in honour of the resurrection, the Lord’s day (Rev 1:10). The more likely reading is that it does not. Meeting on the first day was the apostolic habit (Acts 20:7), and it is a good and wise one, but nothing here transfers the Sabbath command to Sunday. The Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17), and no day binds the believer’s conscience (Rom 14:5–6).

It is personal — each of you. Not the wealthy patrons, not a committee, not whoever feels moved. Everybody.

It is proportionate — as he may prosper. The sum is not fixed; it is scaled to income. That single phrase protects the poor from a demand they cannot meet and prevents the rich from discharging the duty with something they will not notice.

And it is planned in advance, so that Paul’s arrival is not the occasion of a scramble. There is a small pastoral wisdom here worth having: he does not want his visit remembered as the week they were asked for money.

Which raises the question every reader of this passage actually has, and it deserves an answer rather than a silence. How much? Is a Christian required to give a tenth?

The straight answer is that the New Testament nowhere commands the tithe of believers, and Paul, who had every opportunity to name a figure here and in two whole chapters on giving (2 Cor 8–9), never does. What he gives instead is this principle: as he may prosper. That is deliberately not a number, and it is harder rather than easier, because a fixed percentage can be paid and forgotten while a proportion has to be thought about every year the circumstances change.

The tenth is still a useful benchmark, and Christians who use it as a floor rather than a ceiling are not being legalistic; they are being sensible. But notice what Paul actually appeals to elsewhere when he wants to move people to generosity. Not a rule. A person: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9). The Christian does not give a percentage of his income to a cause. He gives, out of what he has been given, to people who have less — because that is precisely what was done for him, and the one who did it did not calculate a proportion.
verseByVerse.note: The collection was for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The first day of the week is Sunday, the day Christians met.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem. If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem. If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.

An administrative note, and one of the most quietly important sentences in the letter for anyone who has ever wondered how a Christian ministry ought to handle money.

Paul does not carry it. He, an apostle, with a direct commission from the risen Christ and every right to be trusted, arranges that the funds should travel in the hands of men the Corinthians themselves have chosen and formally accredited. He will not be alone with the money.

He explains why elsewhere, and the sentence deserves to be framed in every church office: he takes these precautions so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (2 Cor 8:20–21).

Note the two audiences. A ministry must be honest before God — that is obvious. Paul adds that it must also be visibly, checkably honest before people who are not obliged to think well of it. Being innocent is not sufficient; the arrangements must be such that no reasonable person could suspect otherwise.

This is not modern governance imported into the Bible. It is apostolic practice, and the church has paid a heavy price whenever it has thought itself above such things. Every scandal in which a Christian leader has been found handling money alone, unaccountably, with the records in his own keeping, was preventable by a verse written in the fifties.

And the practical form of it is unglamorous and cheap: two signatures rather than one, an audited account, published figures, a treasurer who is not the preacher, and no one — however trusted, however senior, however long-serving — ever alone with the cash. Not because Christians are suspected. Because the gospel is worth protecting from suspicion.

There is a second thing in these verses that is easy to miss. The men who carry the money are chosen by the Corinthians, not by Paul. It is their gift, and they appoint its escort. He is not managing them; he is serving an arrangement they own.

And the last clause has a quiet dignity: if it seems advisable that I should go also. Even the question of whether the apostle travels with the delivery is left open, subject to what turns out to be wise. There is no assumption that his presence is required, or that a gathering of money is somehow incomplete without him attached to it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s travel plans reveal the missionary network of the early church and the genuine relationships that sustained it. He plans to come to Corinth via Macedonia, possibly spending the winter there — a significant stay, not a brief visit. Timothy will come first as his representative; Paul asks the Corinthians to receive him without intimidation, because Timothy is doing the Lord’s work. Apollos, Paul reports, was urged to visit but was not willing to come now — an interesting note that Apollos is not Paul’s rival but his colleague, acting on his own judgment about timing.

The passage is a window into the texture of early Christian community: genuine relationships, real disagreements about timing and priorities, mutual encouragement across distance. The Apollos note is particularly significant: Paul, who has spent chapters resisting the faction that followed Apollos against him, here speaks warmly of Apollos as a brother, regrets his absence, and trusts his judgment. There is no rancour, no competition, no theological warfare — only two men jointly serving the same Lord.

Two clauses in the middle of the section carry more than their length. Verse 7 ends if the Lord permits — detailed plans held under that clause. And verses 8 and 9 give one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for reading circumstances: a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Missionary Network and the Unity of the Gospel

Paul’s travel plans are not merely logistical; they reflect the theology of the one body of Christ extended across geography. The early church was not a collection of independent local congregations operating in isolation; it was a network of communities bound together by the gospel, by apostolic ministry, by financial sharing, and by personal relationship. Paul’s letters are themselves the literary expression of this network — the apostle’s presence extended across distance through writing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ease with which Paul mentions Timothy and Apollos as co-workers, and the genuine care he shows for Timothy’s reception, models the pastoral culture of the early church: mutual submission, personal warmth, collaborative ministry. Now: The temptation to treat Christian ministry as competitive rather than collaborative is ancient and persistent. Paul’s warmth toward Apollos — the man whose followers had been used as a weapon against him — is a lesson in the largeness of a gospel-formed heart.

verseByVerse.quote: I will visit you after passing through Macedonia, for I intend to pass through Macedonia, and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will visit you after passing through Macedonia, for I intend to pass through Macedonia, and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.

Travel arrangements, and they are more revealing than they look.

The first thing is the warmth. This is the congregation that had divided into parties over his name, questioned his apostleship, taken each other to court, and got drunk at the Lord’s table — and Paul is planning to spend the winter with them. Sailing stopped in the winter months; to winter somewhere was to be stuck there until spring. He is proposing to be shut in for months with the most difficult church he has.

And he says why: I do not want to see you now just in passing. He could have managed a brief, efficient, well-controlled visit and moved on. He wants time with them instead. That is what a man says about people he loves, not about a problem he is managing.

Then the phrase that most needs saying: if the Lord permits.

Paul makes plans. Detailed ones — a route, a season, a length of stay, and an expectation that the church will help him onward afterwards. There is nothing unspiritual about a diary, and this passage should settle it for anyone who has been taught that planning shows a lack of faith.

But every plan he makes sits under a clause. James puts it more sharply: you do not know what tomorrow brings; you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (Jas 4:14–15). It is not a superstitious formula to be attached to sentences. It is a settled awareness that the diary is a proposal and not a contract.

And in fact it did not go as written. Paul’s movements changed, the Corinthians were upset about it, and he had to defend himself in the next letter against the charge of being unreliable (2 Cor 1:15–17). Which is worth knowing, because it tells the reader what if the Lord permits costs. It is easy to say when the plan works. It has to be meant in advance, so that when the year goes differently there is something already in place to stand on.

verseByVerse.quote: But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

Two facts about the same situation, joined by and — and it is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone trying to read his circumstances.

A wide door: an opening, an opportunity, work that is actually going somewhere. Ephesus was proving fruitful, and Luke records what that looked like — two years of daily teaching, the word spreading through the whole province, sorcerers burning their books in public (Acts 19:9–10, 19).

And there are many adversaries. The same city, the same season. Within a short time the silversmiths would start a riot that filled the theatre for two hours and nearly cost him his life (Acts 19:23–41).

Now notice how Paul relates the two clauses. Not “a door has opened, but there is opposition,” as though the second were a qualification of the first. He writes and. The adversaries are part of the report, and they are not a reason to leave; they are named in the same breath as the reason to stay.

That matters, because Christians routinely read the two facts the wrong way round. A door opens, resistance follows, and the resistance is taken as evidence that the door was not from God after all — that if this were really his will it would be going more smoothly. Paul assumes the opposite. Where the gospel is actually advancing, something pushes back. The absence of opposition is not the mark of God’s blessing; it may only be the mark of not having disturbed anything.

The rule cuts both ways, and both halves are needed. Not every difficulty is proof that you are on the right road; some obstacles are God closing a door, and Paul himself was once forbidden by the Spirit to go where he intended (Acts 16:6–7). But opposition by itself never disqualified an opportunity, and a Christian who abandons every good work at the first serious resistance will never finish anything.

The test for telling the two apart is not the size of the difficulty; it is what the difficulty is made of. Opposition from people who do not want the gospel to advance is evidence that it is advancing. A closed road, an exhausted body, a family that needs you at home, a door that simply will not open however hard it is pushed — those are different, and a wise Christian reads them differently.

So Paul stays in the dangerous city until the feast, because the field is ripe and a wide door does not stay open indefinitely.

And there is something worth noticing in effective. The word means a door open for work that works, that gets somewhere. Paul is not staying because the situation is interesting or because he has invested a lot in it. He is staying because something is actually happening, and he can tell the difference between motion and progress. That is a discernment many a ministry has lacked, and it costs years.
verseByVerse.note: Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.

Read that as a letter of introduction and it is almost protective enough to be touching.

Paul is sending a young man into the hardest congregation he has, and he knows exactly what they are like, because he has spent fifteen chapters describing it. So he writes ahead. Put him at ease. Do not despise him. Send him on kindly.

Timothy was young — Paul would later have to tell him to let no one despise him for his youth (1 Tim 4:12) — and by all appearances he was not a naturally commanding figure. He seems to have been prone to timidity; Paul writes elsewhere about his tears (2 Tim 1:4) and tells him that God has not given a spirit of fear (2 Tim 1:7). Corinth was a church that graded people by eloquence, presence and impressiveness, and before long some there would be saying that Paul’s own bodily presence was weak and his speech of no account (2 Cor 10:10). Timothy was walking into that.

The safeguard Paul offers is not a claim about Timothy’s gifts. He does not say Timothy is a fine preacher, or that he has authority, or that he is more capable than he looks. He says: he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. The same work. That is the whole credential.

Which is a standing rebuke to how congregations actually assess people, then and now. A church will weigh a visiting speaker’s confidence, accent, humour and bearing within about ninety seconds, and every one of those measures was in play at Corinth. Paul cuts across all of it with a question about what a man is doing.

And there is something here for anyone who has ever felt like Timothy walking in — too young, too quiet, too unimpressive for the room, aware that he is being measured against somebody more capable. He was, and he was right about it, and the apostle wrote ahead to the whole congregation about it. Timidity is not a disqualification. It is a thing the family is supposed to make allowances for.

And there is a duty in it for the congregation, stated as a command: see that you put him at ease among you. Not merely refrain from crushing him — actively set him at ease. That is work, and somebody has to decide to do it: to be the person who goes over first, who asks the question that lets a nervous newcomer talk about something he knows, who does not leave him standing at the edge of a room with a cup in his hand.

Every church has a Timothy in it on any given Sunday. The command is not to admire him. It is to go and put him at ease.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was young and perhaps timid.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.

A short verse, and remarkable in three directions at once.

Remember who Apollos is in this letter. He is the other name in the faction fight — I follow Paul, or I follow Apollos (1:12) — the eloquent Alexandrian (Acts 18:24) whose admirers had been used as a stick to beat Paul with. Four chapters were spent dismantling that party spirit.

And here is Paul, at the end of the same letter, calling him our brother Apollos and saying he pressed him hard to go to Corinth. That is the first remarkable thing. If there were any rivalry, it is entirely on the Corinthians’ side. Paul is actively trying to send his supposed rival to the church that prefers him.

The second is that Apollos said no. An apostle strongly urged him, and he declined — it was not at all his will to come now — and Paul reports it without a word of complaint, without hinting that Apollos was being difficult, and without appealing to his own authority to overrule him.

That is worth pausing on, because it settles something about how guidance and authority worked in the early church. Apostolic authority was real, and Paul had just used it heavily in this letter. But it did not extend to running another man’s diary. Where Scripture commands, there is no discretion; where it does not, a Christian is free to weigh a matter and reach a different conclusion from someone he respects — and neither man has sinned.

Apollos may well have had a good reason, and the obvious one is staring out of the text: a church divided into a Paul party and an Apollos party is not helped by the arrival of Apollos. Staying away may have been the most loving thing he could do, and it would have cost him a warm welcome.

The third remarkable thing is the last clause: he will come when he has opportunity. No coolness in it, no door shut. Two servants of the same Lord disagreeing about timing, and the friendship entirely intact. A great deal of damage in churches would be avoided if Christians could learn to let a no be a no without treating it as a verdict on the relationship.

There is also a lesson here about how the will of God is actually found in matters Scripture does not settle. Apollos did not receive a revelation telling him to stay where he was. He weighed a request from a man he respected, considered the situation, formed a judgment, and acted on it — and the New Testament records the outcome without a hint that he should have waited for something more supernatural.

That is worth saying to any Christian paralysed over a decision, waiting for a certainty God has not promised to supply. Where the Bible speaks, obey it. Where it does not, use the mind God gave you, take advice, weigh the good of other people, and decide — and then get on with it, as Apollos plainly did (cf. Prov 15:22; Rom 14:5).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final exhortations are compressed, powerful, and perfectly sequenced. “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong.” Four imperatives that read like a military order of the day — vigilance, stability, courage, strength — followed immediately by the fifth and greatest: “Let all that you do be done in love.” The four imperatives without the fifth would be cold and harsh; the fifth without the four would be sentimental and weak. Together they describe the full character of the community Paul has been trying to form throughout the letter: strong and loving, firm and warm, courageous and gentle.

The commendation of Stephanas and his household is Paul’s closing tribute to those who have served the community faithfully. They were the firstfruits of Achaia; they had devoted themselves to service; they had come to Paul in Ephesus and refreshed his spirit. Paul asks the Corinthians to give recognition to such people — not as flattery but as the appropriate honour due to those who have given themselves for the community.
verseByVerse.theology:
Courage and Love: The Paradox of Gospel Character

The sequence of imperatives in vv. 13–14 — watchful, firm, courageous, strong, then loving — captures the full paradox of the Christian character that Paul has been cultivating throughout the letter. The cross demands both: the courage to stand for truth (as Paul has done in every hard section of this letter) and the love that is patient, kind, and bears all things (as chapter 13 demands). Neither without the other is Christian; together they describe the character of Christ himself, who drove the money-changers from the temple and wept on the way to Lazarus’s tomb.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed all five imperatives in exactly the order Paul gave them. They needed watchfulness against the false teachings threatening them; firmness against the cultural pressure to conform; courage to exercise church discipline; strength to endure the costs of faithful community. And they needed all of this wrapped in love, or it would produce the cold and harsh community that pride produces rather than the warm and strong community that grace produces. Now: Every generation of the church needs the same five imperatives in the same order. The church that is watchful and firm but unloving is a fortress, not a family. The church that is loving but not watchful and firm is a sentimentality, not a community.

verseByVerse.quote: Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.

Five commands, fired off like an order of the day, and they are the whole letter compressed into two lines.

Be watchful. The word is a sentry’s: stay awake, keep looking. It is the same verb Jesus used in Gethsemane to men who could not manage an hour (Mk 14:34–38). A church is most in danger when it is comfortable, and Corinth had been asleep in exactly that way — a man in gross immorality in the membership and the church arrogant about it rather than mourning (5:1–2).

Stand firm in the faith. Not “in your faith” — in the faith, the thing believed, the deposit handed over. There is ground to hold, it is not the church’s to renegotiate, and the pressure to move it is constant and usually reasonable-sounding.

Act like men. One word in Greek, and it needs explaining, because a modern reader will stumble. It is built on the word for a man, and it means: be courageous, behave like an adult. In older English “quit you like men” carried the same sense. It is not addressed to the male half of the congregation; it is addressed to a church Paul has already called infants (3:1), and it means grow up and show some nerve. The Greek translation of the Old Testament uses this very verb where Joshua is told to be strong and courageous (Josh 1:6–9) — and God said it there to a man who was frightened.

Be strong. Passive in form: “be strengthened.” The strength is not manufactured. Paul says elsewhere exactly where it comes from — be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might (Eph 6:10).

And then the fifth, which changes everything: let all that you do be done in love.

Take the first four alone and you get a certain kind of Christian, and everyone has met him: watchful, immovable, courageous, strong, and impossible to be near. Vigilance without love becomes suspicion. Firmness without love becomes rigidity. Courage without love becomes belligerence, and there is a species of contender for the faith who is right about everything and has never comforted anyone.

Take the fifth alone and you get the opposite failure: a church so anxious to be loving that it will not stand anywhere, cannot say a hard thing, and has quietly agreed that nothing is worth a disagreement.

Paul will not have either. All four, and all four soaked in the fifth. That is the church he has been trying to build all through this letter, and it is the character of the Lord who drove the traders out of the temple and wept on the way to a friend’s grave.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I urge you, brothers—you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints— be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I urge you, brothers — you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints — be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.

Names at last. After fifteen chapters of problems, Paul points at some people who were getting it right.

Stephanas has appeared once already: his household was one of the very few Paul remembered baptising personally (1:16). They were the first converts in Achaia — the firstfruits of the whole province, the first family in southern Greece to believe. And they had been at it ever since.

This is the household Paul baptized (1:16), and it is sometimes cited for infant baptism. But the description here, a household that had devoted themselves to the service of the saints, describes believers, and nothing in either passage mentions children (cf. Acts 16:34; 18:8).

The verb Paul uses of them is the striking thing. They devoted themselves — the word means they appointed themselves, posted themselves to the duty. Nobody rostered them. No one asked. They looked at what the church needed and put themselves into the gap, and had apparently been doing it for years without a title.

Then the instruction, and it is not the one anyone expects: be subject to such as these. Submit to them.

Consider what that means in a congregation that had spent the whole letter arguing about status. Paul does not tell them to admire Stephanas, or thank him, or put him on a rota. He tells them to place themselves under the people who have proved themselves by serving. In this church, authority is not chiefly a matter of appointment; it is earned in public over time by people who did the work when nothing was in it for them.

Which supplies a test for anyone deciding whom to follow in a church. Not who is the most gifted speaker, or the most confident, or the one everybody quotes. Look for the household that has been quietly serving the saints for fifteen years and has never once been thanked from the front. Then note that the New Testament tells you to submit to people like that.

And note the reach of the last clause — and to every fellow worker and laborer. The word for labourer means someone who works to the point of exhaustion. Paul is not building a hierarchy with two names in it. He is describing a whole category, and the qualification for membership is simply that a person has worn himself out for the church.

There is a warning in this for anybody who is waiting to be asked. Stephanas did not wait. Churches are full of people whose gifts are real and whose service never begins, because nobody approached them and it felt presumptuous to volunteer. This verse quietly removes the excuse: the household Paul holds up as the model appointed themselves, and the apostle commends them for exactly that.

And a warning for those who are already serving. What Paul commends is not the work; it is the direction of it. They devoted themselves to the service of the saints — to people, not to a programme, a building, or a set of arrangements. It is entirely possible to be exhausted by church activity and never once to have served a person.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

verseByVerse.quote: I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence, for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence, for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.

Three men made the journey from Corinth to Ephesus — a crossing of some two hundred and fifty miles by sea, undertaken at their own trouble and expense, very likely carrying the letter of questions that this whole epistle answers.

And look what Paul says about it. They have made up for your absence. He had been missing them. Not the letter, not the news — them. The apostle who has spent fifteen chapters correcting this church tells them that having three of their number in the room went some way toward filling a gap their absence had left.

Then: they refreshed my spirit. The word means to give someone rest, the way a weight is taken off. Paul was in Ephesus with a wide door and many adversaries, carrying, by his own account, the daily pressure of anxiety for all the churches (2 Cor 11:28). Into that came three men from a difficult congregation, and he says they rested him.

It is worth asking what they actually did, since he does not say. There is no record of Fortunatus preaching or Achaicus writing anything. They travelled, they brought a letter, they stayed a while, they went home. Which is to say: the thing that lifted the weight off the greatest missionary in history was some ordinary Christians turning up.

That is a genuinely useful discovery for anyone who has ever wondered what to do for a minister, a missionary, or any believer visibly carrying too much. You do not need a gift for it. Go and see them. Take something. Stay a while. Say the encouraging thing you have thought and never said. It sounds too small to matter, and Paul put three men’s names in Scripture for doing it.

Give recognition to such people. A last small command, and an easy one to obey. Notice them. Say so out loud. Every congregation has its Stephanas, and the reason they are rarely thanked is not unkindness but that quiet service is almost invisible by design — the work only becomes noticeable in the week it stops.

And keep hold of the direction this runs, because it is not what anybody expects. The letter has been a torrent of correction flowing from Ephesus to Corinth for fifteen chapters. Here, for a moment, it flows the other way: a struggling, arrogant, half-converted church sent three men across the sea, and they rested the apostle who was correcting them.

Nobody is only a recipient in the body of Christ. The people being taught refresh the teacher; the ones being carried carry him back. Paul says as much to the Romans about a visit he was hoping for — that they might be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith, both yours and mine (Rom 1:12). He corrected that clause on purpose. He did not want anyone thinking the traffic went one way.
verseByVerse.note: These three men probably brought the Corinthians’ letter to Paul.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter closes with a network of greetings that map the early church’s relational geography: the churches of Asia, Aquila and Prisca (Paul’s closest co-workers), the church that meets in their house, all the brothers. The early church was a house-church movement — communities gathered in the homes of those with enough space to host them — and the home of Aquila and Prisca was evidently one of the centres of Christian life wherever Paul worked.

Paul’s personal closing — written in his own hand after the letter dictated to a secretary — contains two of the most theologically charged farewell statements in the NT. The anathema against those who do not love the Lord Jesus — “let him be accursed” — is not vindictiveness but the flip side of the gospel’s demand: the Lord Jesus must be loved, not merely acknowledged. And then Maranatha — the Aramaic prayer of the early church: “Our Lord, come.” This prayer, preserved in its Aramaic form even in a Greek letter to a Greek-speaking church, is evidence of its antiquity and universality. The whole church, from its earliest days, prayed this prayer. And then grace, and then love — the final words of a letter that began with grace and peace and ends with grace and love in Christ Jesus.

One small command inside the greetings deserves attention: greet one another with a holy kiss (v. 20). The greeting itself was the ordinary affectionate greeting of that world; Paul’s addition is the word holy. What made it remarkable was who exchanged it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Maranatha: The Eschatological Pulse of the Church

“Maranatha” is either maran atha (“Our Lord has come,” a declaration of the incarnation) or marana tha (“Our Lord, come!” a prayer for the Parousia). The context — following the anathema, preceding the benediction, echoing Revelation 22:20’s “Come, Lord Jesus” — strongly favours the prayer. The church that lives with the cross at its centre (ch. 1–2), that loves without condition (ch. 13), that proclaims the resurrection (ch. 15), lives with this prayer on its lips: come. The present is not all there is; the best is yet to come; the One who died and rose is coming again. Maranatha is the heartbeat of the community that has understood what Paul has been saying all letter long.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The early church’s Aramaic prayer preserved in a Greek letter to a Gentile church is a small but moving piece of evidence for the unity of the early church across language and culture. Jewish and Gentile believers shared the same prayer in the same words. Now: The prayer “Come, Lord Jesus” is a prayer Christians in every tradition and century have prayed. It is the prayer that the Revelation ends with; it is the prayer that this letter ends with. To pray it is to join the whole church across time — to live, with Paul, as one on whom the end of the ages has come, watching and waiting for the One whose coming makes all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord. All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord. All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

Greetings, and they are not padding. This paragraph is a map of the early church.

The churches of Asia — plural, a whole province of congregations that had not existed a few years earlier. The church in their house — because for generations that is where churches met. No buildings, no steeples, no signs. A front room, some benches, a table, and a family who had space and were willing to have people tramping through it every week.

Aquila and Prisca deserve to be known. They were a couple, tentmakers like Paul, expelled from Rome when Claudius drove the Jews out, who took him in when he arrived in Corinth alone and discouraged after Athens (Acts 18:1–3; cf. 2:3). They moved to Ephesus with him (Acts 18:18–19). They took the eloquent Apollos aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately (Acts 18:26) — two tentmakers correcting a brilliant preacher, privately, and he took it. And Paul says elsewhere that they risked their necks for his life (Rom 16:4). Notice, too, that they are almost always named together and that Prisca is often named first, which was not the ordinary order.

Then: greet one another with a holy kiss.

A modern reader wants to know whether this is a command. The honest answer is that the greeting was the ordinary affectionate greeting of that world, as it still is in much of the Mediterranean and the Middle East, and that Paul’s addition to it is the important word: holy. The instruction is not that Christians must adopt a first-century custom. It is that the ordinary warm greeting of your own culture is to be given, in church, and given without the social calculation that normally governs it.

Because that is what makes it remarkable. In that room a slave and a slave-owner greeted each other this way. A Jew and a Greek did. The rich patron and the dockworker who arrived late for the supper did. The greeting was the one moment in the week when the world’s seating plan was visibly suspended — which is exactly what this letter has been fighting for since chapter 1, and it turns out the fight comes down to who you are willing to greet warmly on a Sunday morning.

So the practical form of the command in a culture that does not kiss is not complicated, and it is not a licence to do nothing. Greet people. Warmly, physically, in whatever way your place counts as warm — and greet the ones you would not naturally have crossed the room for. That is the whole instruction, and a congregation can be transformed by ten people obeying it for a month (cf. Rom 16:16; 1 Pet 5:14).
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.

The pen changes hands.

Letters in that world were normally dictated to a trained secretary, and Paul used one — the man who took down Romans even signs his own name in it (Rom 16:22). So this letter has most likely been in a professional’s handwriting: even, practised, easy to read.

Now the apostle takes the pen himself, and the script on the papyrus visibly changes. He does this at the end of several letters, and once he draws attention to it: see with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand (Gal 6:11) — big, awkward characters, the hand of a man whose eyes or fingers were not what they had been.

There is a practical reason for it. Forged letters were a real problem in the early churches, and Paul had to warn one congregation not to be shaken by a letter seeming to be from us (2 Thess 2:2). His handwriting was the seal — the mark, as he says elsewhere, in every letter of his (2 Thess 3:17). A congregation that knew his hand could check.

But there is more in it than security, and it is worth seeing. Everything in this letter has been his: the rebukes, the arguments, the hymn to love, the great chapter on the resurrection. Now the last few lines are his in the other sense too — formed by his own fingers, on that sheet, in that room in Ephesus, by a man in his fifties with a scarred back and failing sight, who wanted these particular sentences to arrive in his own writing.

And it is worth remembering what those sentences are going to be. He has picked up the pen in order to write a warning, a prayer, and two declarations of love to a church that had given him more grief than any other. He did not save his own handwriting for the easy people.

There is a small apologetic note in the verse too, and it is worth having. This is not the sort of detail a forger includes. A man fabricating an apostolic letter has no reason to mention a change of handwriting he cannot produce, and every reason not to draw attention to the question of authenticity at all. The habit only makes sense for a real correspondent writing to people who had seen his hand before.

And it is a reminder of what these documents physically were. Not a leather-bound book with gilt edges. A roll of papyrus, dictated over days, carried by hand across a sea, read aloud to a room of people who had been waiting for it — and at the bottom of the last sheet, larger and less tidy than the rest, the writing of a man they knew.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters and added a closing greeting in his own handwriting as a mark of authenticity.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!

Two sentences, and the first is the hardest thing in the letter. The word is anathema — devoted to destruction, handed over to the judgment of God. It is not a temper; it is a formal declaration, and Paul writes it in his own hand.

Begin with what it does not say, because a tender conscience will misread it within seconds. It does not say “if anyone does not love the Lord perfectly.” It does not say “if anyone’s love has grown cold,” or “if anyone struggles to feel anything in church,” or “if anyone has doubts.” Every believer who has ever lived would be under that sentence, including the man writing it.

It says has no love. None. Paul is describing the person for whom Jesus Christ is a matter of complete indifference — who may be in the congregation, may be perfectly orthodox, may know the arguments and enjoy the debates, and has no affection for him at all. That, and not weakness, is what falls under this word.

And if the verse frightens you, that is itself the answer: nobody who has no love for Christ is troubled by a verse about not loving Christ. The fear is the evidence. The people this sentence describes read it and feel nothing whatever, which is precisely the diagnosis.

But it should not be softened, either. Paul is saying that the final question is not whether a person knows the right things about Jesus. This whole letter has been written to a congregation stuffed with knowledge and gifts, and here at the end the apostle names the one thing that cannot be substituted for. Christianity is not agreement. It is love for a Person, and there is no version of it in which that is optional.

Then, immediately, the other sentence — and Paul leaves it in Aramaic. Maranatha. Our Lord, come.

Its survival is a small marvel. Here is a Greek letter to a Greek-speaking church in Greece, and this one phrase is left in Aramaic, untranslated, because everyone already knew it. It was the prayer of the first believers in Jerusalem, and it had travelled across the Mediterranean without ever needing to be put into another language. It is among the oldest recorded prayers of the church, and it is two words long.

And it is still the last prayer in the Bible, in Greek this time: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus (Rev 22:20). The church has been saying it for two thousand years, and one day it will be interrupted.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Our Lord, come!” translates Maranatha, an Aramaic prayer of the earliest church.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.

Look at where this letter ends, and then look at where it began.

It opened with grace to you and peace (1:3) and it closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. Everything in between — the factions, the immorality, the lawsuits, the idol meat, the head coverings, the disgraceful supper, the tongues, the denial of the resurrection — is enclosed by grace at both ends. Whatever this church was, it was a church, and Paul never once wrote to them as though they were not.

Then the last line, and it is unlike anything else he wrote. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Paul ends letters in a variety of ways; he does not usually end them like this. It is unique in his correspondence, and it is addressed to the congregation that had given him the most pain.

Count what he had taken from them. They had split into parties over teachers. They had questioned whether he was an apostle at all. They had put up with a scandal that shocked pagans. They had sued each other in front of the city. They had got drunk at the Lord’s table while poor members went hungry. And they had written him a list of questions, several of which were really challenges.

He answered every one of them, at enormous length, holding nothing back and softening almost nothing. And then he took the pen out of the secretary’s hand and wrote, in his own difficult script: my love be with you all.

All. Not the ones who had stayed loyal. Not the party that still called itself his. The whole quarrelsome congregation, including the men who thought him a fool.

And the last three words say where such a thing comes from, because it does not grow in human ground: in Christ Jesus. Paul had no natural stock of affection for people like this, and neither has anybody else. What he had was a share in the love of the One who had looked at a world exactly this arrogant, this divided and this ungrateful, and had not withheld himself from it. That love reached Corinth, and turned some of the least promising people in the Roman Empire into saints, and then came back out of them in a letter.

Sixteen chapters of correction, and the last word is love. It was always going to be.
